His central conviction never moves: God works through people, not arrangements, and the person God can use is the one who has learned to pray.

Talking to men for God is a great thing, but talking to God for men is greater still.

— E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer

He is buried in Washington, Georgia, under a modest stone. He held no great office, founded no movement, and died with his best work unpublished. He simply got up, nineteen years running, while the town was still dark — and the church has been reading what came out of those mornings ever since.

faq.q: Who was E. M. Bounds?
faq.a: Edward McKendree Bounds (1835–1913) was an American Methodist pastor, Civil War chaplain and former attorney who gave the last years of his life to rising at four in the morning to pray. He died largely unknown outside the churches he had served, leaving a stack of manuscripts; a century later his books on prayer have been translated into dozens of languages and never gone out of print. He is one of the clearest cases of a life whose fruit came almost entirely after its end.

faq.q: What was his early life?
faq.a: Born in Missouri in 1835 and named for the frontier bishop William McKendree, he lost his father at fourteen and, like many of his generation, went west in the gold-rush years before coming back to read law, admitted to the bar as one of the youngest attorneys in the state. Converted under a Methodist revival, he gave up the practice — worth noting in a man trained to argue — and in 1859, at twenty-four, was ordained.

faq.q: What did the Civil War cost him?
faq.a: In 1861 he was arrested by Union troops as a suspected Southern sympathiser and required to swear an oath of allegiance or pay a fine; he refused both, not out of politics but because he would not be compelled in a matter of conscience, and was held some eighteen months. He then served the rest of the war as a Confederate chaplain and was struck by a sabre at Franklin. The cause he served fought to preserve slavery, which nothing he later wrote alters.

faq.q: What happened at Franklin after the war?
faq.a: He went back to Franklin — the town where he had been wounded, whose fields still held men he had buried — to pastor its Methodist church, and his method was almost absurdly simple. He looked for a handful of men who actually believed prayer did something, found about half a dozen, and every Tuesday night they knelt together and prayed for themselves, the church, the town, and revival in a wrecked and bitter country.

faq.a: That decade shaped the rest of him. faq.q: Was he a successful churchman?
faq.a: By ordinary reckoning, yes. He pastored in Alabama and Missouri and served as editor of the St Louis Christian Advocate and then associate editor of the Nashville Christian Advocate, for a time one of the more influential desks in Southern Methodism. The man who wrote so insistently about praying at four in the morning was not a monk with an empty house but a father with a full one.

faq.q: What were the hours before daylight?
faq.a: Around 1894 he left the editor's chair for Washington, Georgia, held no prominent pulpit again, and made prayer his principal work — in the plain sense of work. He rose at four in the morning and prayed until seven, and those who knew him described a man walking and praying aloud in the dark hours, often carrying a single text for days until it burned. Almost nobody was watching.

faq.a: Eight manuscripts on prayer, covering its necessity, its possibilities, its reality, its weapons, and the men who had prayed in Scripture. Only one, "Preacher and Prayer" (1907, later retitled "Power Through Prayer"), found a publisher while he lived; the other seven sat in manuscript, and he had no reason to believe they would ever be read. "The men who have done the most for God in this world have been early on their knees," he wrote.

fields.name: Richard Sibbes
fields.bio: Richard Sibbes (1577–1635) was an English Puritan preacher known in his own day as “the heavenly Doctor”. Where much Puritan preaching pressed hard on the conscience, Sibbes was famous for gentleness toward people who had already given up on themselves; his best-known book takes its title from Isaiah's promise that the bruised reed will not be broken.
fields.bio_html:
Richard Sibbes preached in one of the harshest religious ages England has known, and became famous for gentleness. Where much of the Puritan pulpit pressed hard on the conscience, Sibbes went looking for the people who had already given up on themselves — the doubting, the downcast, the believer so bruised he could barely pray — and spoke to them with such tenderness that his own century nicknamed him “the sweet dropper,” and, after his doctorate, “the Heavenly Doctor Sibbes.” His most enduring book takes its title and its whole spirit from a single promise of Isaiah, carried over into the Gospels: that the Messiah will not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax.

There is more mercy in Christ than sin in us.

— Richard Sibbes, The Bruised Reed

A wheelwright’s son

He was born in 1577 at Tostock, a village in Suffolk, the son of Paul Sibbes, a wheelwright — a maker and mender of wheels. It was not a home from which scholars were expected to come, and his father is said to have wished the boy would take up the family trade rather than bury himself in books. But the local minister and friends saw the promise in him. From the grammar school at Bury St Edmunds he went up to St John’s College, Cambridge, in 1595, took his degree in 1599, and was elected a Fellow of the college in 1601. The wheelwright’s son had become a Cambridge man.

Converted under a quiet preacher

Learning, though, is not the same as life, and the decisive turn came around 1603 under the preaching of Paul Baynes — the man who had succeeded the great William Perkins in the pulpit of St Andrew’s, Cambridge. Baynes was no celebrity; he lived and died in relative obscurity and difficulty. But under his plain, searching ministry Sibbes was converted, and he never forgot the debt, speaking of Baynes ever after as his father in the gospel. It placed Sibbes in a remarkable spiritual lineage — Perkins to Baynes to Sibbes — and Sibbes would extend that line further than any of them, becoming spiritual father to a whole generation.

The Heavenly Doctor

Ordained in his early thirties, Sibbes became a lecturer at Holy Trinity Church, Cambridge, around 1610, and the town discovered a preacher. His ministry drew crowds and, inevitably in the reign of the anti-Puritan bishops, suspicion; the old story that he was formally stripped of his posts for nonconformity has been overturned by modern research, but there is no doubt he preached under pressure and watchful eyes. Through it all he kept his footing. In 1617 he was chosen preacher to the lawyers of Gray’s Inn in London, one of the most influential pulpits in the country. In 1626 Cambridge called him back as Master of St Catharine’s Hall, which he set about restoring, and in 1627 he was made Doctor of Divinity — the title that fixed his nickname forever. In 1633 the Crown itself presented him to the vicarage of Holy Trinity, the very church where he had begun. A man supposedly ruined for his Puritanism had instead been entrusted, again and again, with the care of souls.

The ministry of the bruised reed

What made Sibbes Sibbes was not his rise but his tone. He built his most famous book on the words of Matthew 12:20 — “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench” — and turned it into a sustained, patient argument that Christ does not despise weak, struggling, half-extinguished faith, but tends it. He read the two images with a physician’s care. The bruised reed is the soul crushed by a sense of its own sin, and Sibbes held that such bruising is not a sign of Christ’s absence but the very ground He works on. The smoking flax is faith reduced to a barely glowing wick, all smoke and little flame; and the whole burden of the book is that Christ comes not to snuff that smoke but to fan it back into fire. To the believer convinced that his repentance was too shallow and his grace too faint, Sibbes insisted that the smallest true spark is Christ’s own kindling, and that Christ will not blow it out. “This bruising is required before conversion,” he wrote, “that so the Spirit may make way for himself into the heart by levelling all proud, high thoughts.” And he was as shrewd as he was tender: “Weakness with watchfulness will stand,” he warned, “when strength with too much confidence fails.”

This gentleness was not softness of temperament but a settled conviction about how God actually saves people. Sibbes believed that harsh, hectoring preaching drove wounded consciences away from the very Christ they needed, and that the gospel wins its way by drawing rather than driving — by wooing the soul to the loveliness of Christ until it comes willingly. It earned him the affectionate name of “the sweet dropper,” for a ministry that fell on hearers like a gentle, steady rain. His companion treatise, The Soul’s Conflict with Itself, is a whole book on the discipline the psalmist practised when he turned on his own despondency and demanded, “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?”

Sibbes taught the downcast believer to do what the psalmist did — to reason with his own sinking heart rather than sink with it. His Soul’s Conflict is a manual for that inward wrestling: preaching to yourself, arguing your soul back from despair to God, until “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?” gives way to renewed hope in Him.

Father to a generation

Sibbes sat at the warm centre of a wide circle of friendships — ministers, students, and London gentry — that historians call the Puritan “spiritual brotherhood,” much of it hubbed at Gray’s Inn. Through his preaching John Cotton was converted, later carrying that faith to New England. Thomas Goodwin was turned by him from Arminianism toward a warmer, experiential Calvinism, and John Preston was drawn from clever, ornamental preaching to the plain proclamation of Christ. But the most famous fruit of his ministry Sibbes never lived to see, and it came through a book, not a sermon. A poor travelling pedlar sold a copy of The Bruised Reed at the door of a Shropshire household, and the father of the family bought it. His teenage son read it — a boy named Richard Baxter, who would become one of the greatest pastors England ever produced. Baxter recorded what it did:

It opened the love of God to me, and gave me a livelier apprehension of the mystery of redemption, and how much I was beholden to Jesus Christ.

— Richard Baxter, on reading Sibbes’s The Bruised Reed

It is a fair picture of Sibbes’s whole legacy: a gentle book, quietly sold, opening the love of God to a soul the author would never meet. Because he published little himself, much of what we have of Sibbes was gathered from his sermon notes by friends and printed after his death; the standard collection runs to seven volumes, and nearly all of it carries the same errand — to draw the wavering to Christ rather than drive them.

Heaven in him before he was in heaven

Sibbes died in the summer of 1635, on the 5th of July, at Gray’s Inn, unmarried, having spent himself on the souls in his care. About a week before the end he had preached to the lawyers on the fourteenth chapter of John — “Let not your heart be troubled” — fitting last words for the great comforter of troubled hearts. When someone at his bedside asked how his soul stood, he gave an answer that only a lifetime of nearness to God could make sound humble rather than presumptuous: he said he should do God much wrong if he did not say, very well. His will, dictated the day before he died, bequeathed his soul “into the hands of my gracious Saviour, who hath redeemed it with his most precious blood.”

Among those who loved him was Izaak Walton, the writer, who kept a copy of Sibbes’s sermons and wrote in it two lines that have outlived every controversy of the age:

Of this blest man, let this just praise be given, / Heaven was in him, before he was in heaven.

— Izaak Walton, of Richard Sibbes

Nearly four centuries later that is still the truest word on him. Sibbes left no great institution and courted no power; he left books that go on doing gently what he did — finding the bruised reed, and refusing to break it. To anyone who has feared that his faith is too weak to count, the Heavenly Doctor still says what he said to Cambridge and to Gray’s Inn: that there is more mercy in Christ than sin in us, and that the One who lit even the faintest spark has promised never to let it go out.

fields.name: John Owen
fields.bio: John Owen (1616–1683) was the foremost theologian of English Puritanism — chaplain to Cromwell, Dean of Christ Church and Vice-Chancellor of Oxford, and after 1662 a dissenting minister barred from the universities he had led. He is famous for the density of his prose and for an unusually exact understanding of how sin actually works on a person, which is why The Mortification of Sin has outlived almost everything else written in its century on the subject.
fields.bio_html:
John Owen was the most formidable theological mind English Puritanism produced, and one of the most searching physicians of the soul who has ever written in the language. He sat at the very centre of national power — chaplain to Oliver Cromwell, Dean of Christ Church, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford — and then watched it all be taken away, spending his last twenty years as a hunted Nonconformist barred from the universities he had once governed. Out of both the height and the loss came the same preoccupation: an almost unbearably exact understanding of how sin works on a person, and how grace works deeper still. It is why his little book on killing sin has outlived nearly everything else his century wrote on the subject.

Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

— John Owen, The Mortification of Sin

A Puritan boyhood

He was born in 1616 at Stadhampton, a village in Oxfordshire, the second son of Henry Owen, a Puritan minister who conformed to the established Church only as far as his conscience would let him. The exact day of John’s birth was never recorded — a small reminder that greatness announces itself late. He went up to Queen’s College, Oxford, at about twelve, took his degree at sixteen, and read with the ferocious discipline that marked him for life; he is said to have allowed himself only four hours of sleep a night, a regimen he later regretted as a theft from his own health. He earned his master’s degree in 1635 and began further study, but by 1637 he could not in conscience submit to Archbishop Laud’s new church statutes, and he left the university rather than bend. It cost him his prospects. He became a private chaplain and tutor instead, and waited.

The assurance he could not find

For all his learning, Owen spent his young manhood under a long and crushing spiritual darkness. He believed the gospel; he could not feel that it was his. For months he could scarcely pray, and doubted whether he was converted at all. The turn came, as it so often does, sideways. Around 1642 he went to hear the celebrated London preacher Edmund Calamy at St Mary’s, Aldermanbury. Calamy did not appear. In his place an unknown country minister — a man Owen never afterwards managed to identify — stood up and preached on a single question of Christ to His frightened disciples: “Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” Under that plain sermon, from a preacher whose name is lost to history, the assurance Owen had begged God for finally came. The bondage broke. He had gone looking for a famous voice and been met by God through a nobody.

Owen had prayed for months, in near-despair, for the assurance that he truly belonged to Christ. It came under a substitute preacher he could never afterwards name, on the text “Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” — the settled peace he had sought, given where he least expected it.

Chaplain to Cromwell

Now his pen made him known. A Display of Arminianism (1642) won him the living of Fordham in Essex, and then the vicarage of Coggeshall, where his study of the New Testament persuaded him toward a Congregational understanding of the church. He preached before the Long Parliament, and in 1649 — the day after the execution of Charles I — he preached before it again, and there met the man who would carry him to the centre of the nation. Oliver Cromwell recruited Owen as an army chaplain and took him to Ireland and then Scotland. In 1651 Cromwell made him Dean of Christ Church, Oxford, and the following year Vice-Chancellor of the whole university, a post he held until 1657, receiving his Doctor of Divinity in 1653. For a season the boy who had walked out of Oxford on principle now ran it — reforming, protecting scholars of every party, and preaching still.

The anatomist of sin

The Oxford years produced the books for which he is still read. In 1647 came The Death of Death in the Death of Christ, his massive defence of the particular, purposeful love of God in the cross. But it was the shorter, sharper works that lodged in the conscience of the church. Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656), an exposition of a single verse of Romans, remains the classic Christian handbook on the daily, deliberate war against indwelling sin — and its most quoted sentence is a whole spirituality in nine words:

Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

— John Owen, The Mortification of Sin (1656)

If Mortification shows Owen’s severity, its companion shows his sweetness. Of Communion with God (1657) argues that the believer enjoys a real, distinct, experienced fellowship with each Person of the Trinity — with the Father in His love, the Son in His grace, the Spirit in His comfort. It is the warm centre of everything Owen was. “So much as we see of the love of God,” he wrote, “so much shall we delight in him, and no more.” The man the world remembers as a hammer against sin was, in his own study, chiefly occupied with the enjoyment of God.

Communion with God was the beating heart of Owen’s inner life — a daily, unhurried fellowship with Father, Son, and Spirit that he insisted was not the privilege of the advanced but the birthright of every believer. His last book was simply that habit written down: a long, adoring meditation on the glory of Christ.

Ejected

Then the tide went out. At the Restoration in 1660 Owen lost the deanery, and the Act of Uniformity in 1662 drove him and some two thousand other ministers out of the Church of England altogether. For the rest of his life he was a Nonconformist — preaching to gathered congregations that met at risk, writing tirelessly for toleration, refused the pulpits and the university he had led. He became the acknowledged leader and defender of Independency, and though offers came, including the invitation to lead a church in Boston, he stayed to shepherd the persecuted flock at home.

One friendship from these years has passed into legend. Owen prized the preaching of John Bunyan, the imprisoned Bedford tinker, and is credibly said to have used his standing at court to help win Bunyan’s release. When Charles II expressed surprise that so learned a doctor would cross London to hear an unschooled mender of pots, Owen is reported to have answered that he would gladly give all his learning for the tinker’s power in the pulpit. The exact words come down to us only through later tradition — but the humility in them is entirely his.

A house of sorrows

The private cost of Owen’s public life was staggering. He married Mary Rooke around 1644, and by her he had — so his biographers report — some eleven children. All but one died young; the single daughter who reached adulthood came home after an unhappy marriage and soon died of consumption. Mary herself died in 1675. The man who wrote most exactingly about grief bearing believers up had buried nearly his whole family. He remarried a widow, Dorothy D’Oyley, who brought him some comfort and ease in his final years, but the sorrows were never far, and they give his writing on suffering and assurance the weight of a thing paid for.

The long looked-for day

Owen died on 24 August 1683 at Ealing, near London. Two days before, dictating a farewell letter to his old friend Charles Fleetwood, he set down words that gather his whole life into a sentence:

I am going to Him whom my soul hath loved, or rather who hath loved me with an everlasting love, which is the whole ground of all my consolation.

— John Owen, letter to Charles Fleetwood, 22 August 1683

“I am leaving the ship of the church in a storm,” he added; “but whilst the great Pilot is in it, the loss of a poor under-rower will be inconsiderable.” On his last morning, the minister William Payne came to tell him that his final book, Meditations on the Glory of Christ, had gone to the press. Owen answered, “I am glad to hear that that performance is put to the press; but, O brother Payne, the long looked-for day is come at last, in which I shall see that glory in another manner than I have ever done yet, or was capable of doing in this world.” That evening — the anniversary week of the ejection that had cost him everything — he died. They buried him at Bunhill Fields among the dissenters he had loved.

He left a mountain of writing that has outlasted the empire he served: the Hebrews commentary in four volumes, the great works on the Spirit and on justification, and above all the two small books on killing sin and enjoying God that still do their work in any reader honest enough to sit under them. Owen never made the truth easy. He believed the human heart too devious and the glory of Christ too great for shortcuts. But to those willing to follow his hard, exact sentences, he offered the thing he had himself been given under an unknown preacher’s voice — the settled, unbreakable assurance of being loved by God with an everlasting love.

When Charles II expressed surprise that so learned a doctor would cross London to hear an unschooled mender of pots, Owen is reported to have answered that he would gladly give all his learning for the tinker's power in the pulpit — the exact words come down only through later tradition, but the humility in them is entirely his.

faq.q: What did his private life cost him?
faq.a: It was staggering. He married Mary Rooke and by her had, his biographers report, some eleven children — all but one dying young, and the single daughter who reached adulthood came home after an unhappy marriage and soon died of consumption. Mary herself died in 1675. The man who wrote most exactingly about grief bearing believers up had buried nearly his whole family, and the sorrow gives his writing on suffering and assurance the weight of a thing paid for.

faq.q: How did he die?
faq.a: Owen died on 24 August 1683 at Ealing. Two days before, dictating a farewell to his old friend Charles Fleetwood, he wrote, "I am going to Him whom my soul hath loved, or rather who hath loved me with an everlasting love, which is the whole ground of all my consolation." Told on his last morning that his book Meditations on the Glory of Christ had gone to press, he answered, "the long looked-for day is come at last." He was buried at Bunhill Fields among the dissenters he had loved.

fields.name: Martin Luther
fields.bio: Martin Luther (1483–1546) was the German monk whose recovery of justification by faith alone sparked the Protestant Reformation. fields.bio_html:
Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 in Eisleben, in the mining country of Saxony, and baptised the next morning on the feast of St Martin, whose name he bore. His father, Hans, had climbed by hard work from peasant stock into the copper trade and was determined that his clever son should rise higher still — into the law, and a secure and prosperous life. Martin was an obedient boy under a strict and sometimes brutal discipline, and he did as he was told, taking his master's degree at the University of Erfurt and beginning the study of law. He was twenty-one, dutiful, and outwardly on his way. And then, on a summer road, God knocked him flat.

A Vow in the Storm

On 2 July 1505, returning to Erfurt after visiting his parents, Luther was caught in the open by a violent thunderstorm near the village of Stotternheim. A bolt of lightning struck so close that it threw him to the ground, and in raw terror of death and judgement he cried out a vow to the patron saint of miners that his father had taught him to invoke.

Help me, Saint Anne, and I will become a monk!

— Martin Luther, in the thunderstorm at Stotternheim, 1505

He kept the vow. Two weeks later, over his furious father's protests, he sold his law books and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt, and in 1507 he was ordained a priest. He threw himself into the monastic life with a desperate seriousness. He fasted, watched, prayed, and confessed his sins for hours at a stretch until his weary confessor told him to go away and come back when he had done something worth confessing. But peace would not come. Luther was crushed by an overwhelming sense of the righteousness of God — a God who demanded a perfection Luther knew he could never reach — and the harder he laboured to make himself acceptable, the more hopeless he grew. He would later say that if ever a monk got to heaven by his monkery, it would have been he, and it very nearly destroyed him.

The Gate of Paradise

His superiors, hoping study would settle him, pressed him toward a doctorate and a chair of biblical theology at the new University of Wittenberg. It was the best thing they could have done, for it set Luther to lecturing his way slowly through the Psalms and the letters of Paul. And there, wrestling above all with a single phrase in Romans — the righteous shall live by faith — the whole terrifying edifice of his fear gave way. He saw at last that the righteousness of God in the gospel is not a standard God demands of us and by which He damns us, but a gift God gives us, received by faith alone in Christ. The discovery broke over him like sunrise.

I felt that I had been altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates. This passage of Paul became to me a gate to heaven.

— Martin Luther, recalling his discovery of justification by faith

Everything flowed from that. If a sinner is set right with God by faith in Christ and not by works or payments, then the whole machinery of merit — pilgrimages, penances, and above all the sale of indulgences, those certificates that claimed to buy the release of souls from purgatory — was a lie that robbed people of the free grace of God. On 31 October 1517, Luther posted ninety-five theses for academic debate on the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, protesting the traffic in indulgences. He meant to start a scholarly argument. He started the Reformation. Printed and carried across Germany within weeks, the theses lit a fire that no one could put out.

Here I Stand

Rome moved against him. Summoned, examined, and at last excommunicated by a papal bull he publicly burned, Luther was called in 1521 to answer before the Emperor Charles V and the assembled princes of the Holy Roman Empire at the Diet of Worms. His books were piled on a table and he was ordered to recant. He asked for a day to think, and returned the next evening to give an answer that has echoed for five centuries. He would not recant, he said, unless he were convinced by Scripture and plain reason, for he could not trust popes and councils who had so often contradicted one another and themselves.

My conscience is captive to the Word of God. To go against conscience is neither right nor safe. Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me. Amen.

— Martin Luther at the Diet of Worms, 1521

It was, in effect, a sentence of death; the Edict of Worms declared him an outlaw whom anyone might kill. But his prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, spirited him away in a staged ambush and hid him in the Wartburg Castle, where for the better part of a year Luther lived in disguise as a bearded knight, "Junker Jörg." He was often ill and battered by depression and by what he took to be the direct assaults of the devil. And he worked. In eleven weeks he translated the entire New Testament from Greek into a vigorous, singing German that ordinary people could read for themselves — a gift that shaped the German language itself and put the living Word into the hands of the plough-boy and the housewife, exactly as he intended.

A Home in the Black Cloister

Returning to Wittenberg, Luther gave the movement its shape: German services, congregational hymns, catechisms to teach the faith to children, and a recovered vision of ordinary life — marriage, work, parenthood — as the arena of holy obedience. He lived that vision himself. In 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a runaway nun who two years earlier had escaped her convent hidden among the fish barrels of a merchant's wagon. It scandalised half of Europe and delighted Luther. Katharina, whom he called "my Katie" and teased as "the morning star of Wittenberg" for her early rising, took charge of the vast, chaotic household of the old Augustinian cloister — the children, the boarding students, the endless guests — and ran it, and him, with a firm hand he cheerfully acknowledged, joking that in domestic affairs he deferred to Katie and was otherwise led by the Holy Spirit.

Out of that home came some of the warmest devotional writing of the Reformation. When his barber, Peter Beskendorf, asked him plainly how to pray, Luther wrote him a little book, A Simple Way to Pray, counselling him to make the Lord's Prayer and the Commandments his daily school and never to let prayer grow cold or hurried. And out of the same years came the hymn that became the anthem of the whole movement — Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, "A mighty fortress is our God, a bulwark never failing" — his defiant paraphrase of Psalm 46, sung in the teeth of every danger.

Prayed Back from the Grave

Prayer for Luther was not a discipline of calm but a wrestling, and he prayed as a man who believed God had bound Himself to His own promises and could be held to them. The most famous instance came in the summer of 1540, when his dearest friend and fellow-labourer Philip Melanchthon fell so gravely ill at Weimar that he seemed already dying, his eyes glazing and his speech failing. Luther rushed to his side, and turning to the window he prayed with an almost frightening boldness, reminding God of every promise in Scripture to hear prayer and refusing to let his friend go.

At Melanchthon's deathbed Luther flung the whole of God's promises before Him and would not be refused, pleading that God must not let his friend die. Melanchthon, already sinking, began to revive, took food, and recovered. Luther said afterward, God gave me my brother Melanchthon back in direct answer to prayer. Philip lived and laboured another twenty years.

Luther's own health, worn by decades of overwork, illness, and strain, failed steadily in his last years. In the winter of 1546 he travelled, unwell, back to Eisleben — the town where he had been born — to make peace in a quarrel between two noble brothers. He completed the work of reconciliation, and then his heart gave out. In the early hours of 18 February 1546, as death came on, his friend Justus Jonas asked whether he was ready to die trusting Christ and the gospel he had preached. Luther answered, clearly, "Yes." He died within sight of the font where he had been baptised sixty-two years before.

On a scrap of paper beside him they found his last written words, a sentence that gathers his whole life and message into a breath. The man who had tried so hard to climb to God, and who had found instead that God comes down in free grace to the empty-handed, laid down his pen at the only place he had ever truly rested.

We are beggars. This is true.

— Martin Luther, his last written words, 1546

fields.name: John Calvin
fields.bio: John Calvin (1509–1564) was the leading theologian of the second generation of the Reformation and the pastor of Geneva for over twenty years. A French lawyer and humanist turned reformer after a “sudden conversion,” he wrote the Institutes of the Christian Religion — the fullest statement of Reformed faith — and shaped Protestantism across Europe through his preaching, his commentaries on nearly the whole of Scripture, and the Academy of Geneva.
fields.bio_html:
John Calvin was born on 10 July 1509 in Noyon, a cathedral town in the French province of Picardy. His father, Gérard Cauvin, was a legal officer in the service of the local bishop, an ambitious man who meant his gifted second son for the priesthood and later, as ambitions shifted, for the more lucrative career of the law. Neither plan reckoned with God, who would take this precise, reserved, bookish Frenchman and set him at the very centre of the Reformation — not as a firebrand but as its patient teacher, the man who, more than any other, gave the movement a mind. Everything Calvin became is gathered into the motto he took for his own and stamped on his seal: a hand holding out a flaming heart.

My heart I offer to you, O Lord, promptly and sincerely.

— John Calvin, his personal motto

A Scholar Redirected

Sent to Paris as a boy of around fourteen, Calvin passed through the Collège de la Marche and the austere Collège de Montaigu, taking his master's degree while still in his teens. He was, by every account, a formidable student — disciplined to the point of severity, quick, and already marked out by his teachers. When his father fell out with the cathedral chapter at Noyon, he abruptly redirected his son from theology to law, and Calvin went to study at Orléans and then Bourges under the finest jurists in France. There he also drank deeply of the new humanist learning, teaching himself Greek and Hebrew and reading the classics and the Church Fathers in their own tongues. His first book was not a work of religion at all but a scholarly commentary on the Roman philosopher Seneca. He looked set for the life of a quiet Renaissance man of letters.

But France in the early 1530s was a dangerous place to think freely about God. The evangelical ideas coming out of Germany were seeping across the border, and Calvin, moving in reform-minded circles in Paris, found the ground shifting beneath his feet. He never wrote at length about the crisis of his own soul — he was too self-effacing for that — but in the one place he let the curtain lift, the preface to his commentary on the Psalms, he described what happened in a single, unforgettable sentence.

God by a sudden conversion subdued and brought my mind to a teachable frame, which was more hardened in such matters than might have been expected from one at my early period of life.

— John Calvin, preface to the Commentary on the Psalms

He tells us almost nothing of the circumstances — no date, no place, no vision. He tells us only who did it. God subdued him. The proud, self-possessed scholar was mastered, and once mastered he could not go back. As persecution of the evangelicals sharpened in France, Calvin fled, moving under assumed names from city to city, and in 1535 settled for a time in Basel. There, still only in his mid-twenties, he wrote the first edition of the book that would occupy him for the rest of his life: the Institutes of the Christian Religion, a clear and ordered account of the evangelical faith, offered partly as a defence of his hunted fellow-believers before the king of France. It began as a slim handbook. Across the next twenty-three years he revised and enlarged it again and again until, in its definitive 1559 form, it stood as the most complete and influential statement of Reformed theology ever written.

Seized for Geneva

Calvin wanted a scholar's life — a desk, his books, and quiet. God wanted him in Geneva. In the summer of 1536, meaning only to spend a single night in the city while travelling to Strasbourg, he was recognised. The fiery reformer Guillaume Farel, who had wrenched Geneva loose from Rome but had not the gifts to build what must replace it, came to the inn and begged Calvin to stay and help. Calvin refused; he pleaded his studies, his temperament, his need for peace. And then Farel, in a moment Calvin never forgot, turned prophet and thundered that God would curse Calvin's studies and his quiet if he ran from the work to which he was plainly called. Calvin was undone by it. He took the terrible words as the voice of God Himself, and he stayed.

It went badly at first. Calvin and Farel pressed reforms and a discipline the city was not ready to bear, and in 1538 the magistrates threw them both out. For Calvin the exile felt less like a defeat than a deliverance — he could return to his books. He went to Strasbourg and spent what may have been the happiest three years of his life, pastoring a congregation of French refugees under the wing of the gentle reformer Martin Bucer, lecturing, and learning how a church was actually to be run. It was there, too, that he married. In August 1540 he wed Idelette de Bure, the widow of a converted Anabaptist, a woman of quiet strength who brought two children into the marriage and became, in Calvin's own word, the faithful helper of his ministry.

Then Geneva, in disarray without him, called him back. Everything in Calvin recoiled — he wrote that he would rather die a hundred deaths than take up that cross again. And yet, weighing the plain call of God against his own longing for peace, he surrendered. The heart in the open hand was not a slogan; it was the hardest act of his life.

To Farel, agonising over the summons back to Geneva, Calvin wrote the words that became his motto: I offer my heart to the Lord, promptly and sincerely. He returned in September 1541 to a city he dreaded, believing that the offering of the heart to God meant going wherever God pointed, however costly — and there he stayed, without a break, for the twenty-three years that were left to him.

The Pastor of Geneva

Calvin never held political office in Geneva and never became a citizen until near the end. He was, simply, a pastor and a teacher, and his authority was the authority of the pulpit and the Word. He preached constantly — often daily, working straight through books of the Bible verse by verse — and lectured, and wrote commentaries on nearly the whole of Scripture, and carried on an enormous correspondence that reached persecuted Protestants across Europe. He laboured to order the church after what he found in the New Testament: pastors to preach, teachers to instruct, elders to oversee, and deacons to care for the poor and the flood of refugees pouring into the city. In 1559 he crowned the work by founding the Academy of Geneva, a school and seminary that sent trained preachers back into France, Scotland, the Netherlands, and beyond, so that the little city became, in John Knox's phrase, the most perfect school of Christ since the apostles.

His years there were not serene. He fought bitter battles with powerful Genevan families who resented the church's discipline, and for a long stretch he seemed the losing party. And in 1553 came the episode that has shadowed his name ever since: the arrest, trial, and burning of Michael Servetus, who had denied the Trinity and taunted Calvin for years. Calvin sought his conviction and consented to his death — a judgement shared by nearly every authority of that harsh age, Catholic and Protestant alike, but a grievous thing to set beside the gospel of grace Calvin preached. It is no service to him to hide it. The same man who wrote so movingly of the tenderness of God could be hard, and knew it.

Prayer, the Chief Exercise of Faith

For all the weight of doctrine and government he carried, the beating heart of Calvin's religion was communion with God in prayer. In the longest chapter of the Institutes he taught that prayer is nothing less than the chief exercise of faith, the daily means by which believers dig up the treasures God has promised in the gospel. It was no theory to him. He closed each of his Old Testament lectures with a short, extemporary prayer that his hearers took down as he spoke — dozens of them survive, and they are the private devotion of the public man, laid bare.

Grant, Almighty God, that as thou art pleased daily to exhort us to repentance, and dost not suddenly execute thy judgment against us, so we may not abuse this thy forbearance.

— John Calvin, a closing prayer from his lectures on the Minor Prophets

His household knew grief. The one son Idelette bore him, Jacques, was born early in 1542 and lived only a few days; there were no other children who survived. And in March 1549 Idelette herself died, after a long decline. Calvin, who kept his feelings under such tight rein, let one line of his sorrow into a letter to a friend, and it is the more moving for its restraint.

Although the death of my wife has been exceedingly painful to me, yet I subdue my grief as well as I can.

— John Calvin, letter to Pierre Viret, 1549

How Long, O Lord

Calvin's body had never been strong, and the punishing regime of work broke it early. He was plagued for years by migraines, fevers, gout, kidney stones, and a lung ailment that finally burst a blood vessel as he strained to preach. He gave his last sermon in February 1564. In April he gathered the ministers of Geneva to his bedside and took his leave of them with a plainness that hid nothing — reminding them how little there had been when he first came, how bitter the struggle had been, and asking their pardon for any sharpness his affliction had drawn out of him.

He died on 27 May 1564, not yet fifty-five, worn to nothing in the service he had never wanted and never abandoned. At his own insistence he was buried in an unmarked grave, so that no shrine could ever gather at his bones; to this day no one knows the exact spot. He had spent himself in obscurity on purpose, wanting only that God be glorified and himself forgotten. The last words his companions recorded from him were not his own but the psalmist's ancient cry of longing — How long, O Lord — the prayer of a heart that had, at the very end, nothing left to offer but itself, promptly and sincerely, into the hands of God.

faq.a: At the centre of Calvin's religion stood the conviction that God is truly and actively Lord of all things — that nothing falls out by chance, and that a believer's whole comfort lies in resting under the care of a Father who governs every circumstance. He held that God's providence is not a distant, general oversight but a near and particular ruling of the world, and he taught that prayer is the chief exercise of faith, the daily means by which believers lay hold of what God has promised. fields.name: Erica Sabiti
fields.bio: Erica Sabiti (1903–1988) was the first African Archbishop of the Church of Uganda. Ordained in 1933, he met the balokole of the East African Revival in 1939 while travelling with his bishop in Rwanda and Burundi, and became one of the movement's leaders. His election as archbishop in 1966 was opposed on ethnic grounds and the division was healed only when the province's nine diocesan bishops confessed their own part in it and united behind him.

The East African Revival is remembered for its laymen and its martyrs — the health officer who would not settle, the deacon who died with one word on his lips, the archbishop murdered for refusing to be quiet. Erica Sabiti was none of those things. He was a clergyman, ordained and licensed and doing the work, when the fire he is now numbered among reached him almost by accident on somebody else's journey. He was the first African to lead the Church of Uganda, and his path to that office ran through one of the ugliest quarrels in its history — a quarrel settled, in the end, not by negotiation but by nine bishops standing up and confessing their own sin.

A chief's son from Ankole

He was born in 1903 at Rwebishuru, in Ankole in the south-west of Uganda, into a country of hills and cattle a long way from the Buganda kingdom where the church's power sat. His father was a chief, and he died while Erica was still young.

He went to King's College, Budo — the school that trained a generation of Uganda's leadership — and afterwards to Makerere. It was at Budo that the decisive thing happened, and it happened through a window. The chapel carried words of Christ in its glass, and Sabiti later traced the impetus of his whole life to reading them there:

I did all this for you, what have you done for me?

— the words in the Budo chapel window, which Sabiti said gave him his life's impetus

It is worth pausing on how ordinary that is. No crisis, no meeting, no preacher — a boy at school reading a sentence set in glass by somebody he never met, and carrying it for eighty years.

He taught in a primary school. He was ordained deacon in 1933 and priest in 1934.

Six years an ordained man, and something still missing

Here the story becomes unusual, and more useful than the usual shape.

Sabiti was not a man waiting to be converted. He was a believing, trained, ordained Anglican clergyman with a parish ministry — by every measure his church used, a finished article. And for six years after his ordination, the thing that would define the rest of his life had not yet touched him.

In 1939 he accompanied the Bishop of Uganda on a visit to churches in Rwanda and Burundi. The East African Revival had been running there for several years by then, out of the mission station at Gahini where Joe Church and Yosiya Kinuka worked. Sabiti met the balokole — the saved ones — on that trip, and his ministry was transformed.

He had not gone looking. He was travelling as somebody's companion, in another country, among people who were not his responsibility. From that year onward he is named in every serious list of the revival's leaders, alongside Simeon Nsibambi, William Nagenda, Yosiya Kinuka and Festo Kivengere.

For any reader who has been a Christian a long time, or who is employed by the church and quietly dry, Sabiti is the more relevant witness of the two great names. Nsibambi was a layman who forced the question. Sabiti was already inside the machine, doing the job well, when the thing arrived sideways.

Twenty-six years, then a mitre

What followed his revival was not a rocket. It was two and a half decades of ordinary ministry.

He was ordained in 1933 and consecrated Bishop of Rwenzori in 1960 — twenty-six years in between, of parish work, teaching, and the unrecorded labour that makes up most of a faithful life. We know almost nothing about those years, which is the honest situation with most of the church's best people. There was no crisis worth writing down. There was a man doing the work.

The office at the end did not make those years worthwhile. They were already the ministry.

The archbishop nobody could agree on

In 1965 Leslie Brown, the expatriate archbishop of the province, retired. Uganda's bishops chose Sabiti to succeed him, and in 1966 he became the first Ugandan — the first African — to hold the office, over a province then covering Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Boga-Zaire.

It should have been a moment of pure celebration. It was not.

Sabiti was a Munyankore from the south-west. The archbishop's seat was at Namirembe, in Buganda, and there was bitter opposition from those who would accept only a Muganda in that chair. The dispute was not about doctrine or competence. It was ethnic, it was public, and it dragged on for years, leaving the new archbishop leading a church a substantial part of which would not acknowledge him.

This is the part of his life that most deserves to be remembered, and it is not really about him at all.

The deadlock was eventually broken when the president — Idi Amin, of all people — summoned the province's bishops to Kampala to settle the matter. In that meeting the nine diocesan bishops confessed the sins that had contributed to the division, and then together recognised Erica as their archbishop.

Years of ethnic division in the Church of Uganda ended in a single meeting when its nine diocesan bishops each confessed their own part in it aloud, and then jointly acknowledged Sabiti as archbishop. It was the revival's oldest practice — naming your own sin in company — applied to a bench of bishops in a national crisis.

That is not a diplomatic settlement; a diplomatic settlement divides the difference and leaves everyone's dignity intact. It is the method Nsibambi and Kinuka had been practising in small rooms for thirty years, scaled up to the leadership of a national church. The revival's central claim — that specific sin, named out loud in company, is what breaks things open — was tested at the highest level available in that country, and it held.

Sabiti's own conduct through those years is notable for what is absent from it. There is no record of him campaigning for himself, denouncing his opponents, or gathering his supporters to split off. He waited, and let the confession be theirs to make.

The bag with the Bible in it

In early 1972 — the year Amin expelled Uganda's Asian population, and the beginning of the regime's worst period — Sabiti was called to the Command Post at short notice.

He was diabetic and always travelled with a flask of tea. His assistant carried the bag, and the bag also held his Bible. They were received at the Command Post and taken to the president.

Amin threatened him. He repeated the threat. When it came a third time, the archbishop reached into the bag and took out his Bible.

He was almost seventy, in front of the most dangerous man in the country, and what he reached for was the book he had been carrying since a schoolboy read a sentence in a chapel window.

Accounts of what was said vary and this account will not pretend to more than the gesture. The gesture is not ambiguous.

Retirement, and the man who followed him

He became the first Bishop of Kampala in 1972 and served two more years. In 1974 he retired, and the House of Bishops elected Janani Luwum to succeed him.

Three years later Luwum was dead, murdered by Amin's regime after delivering the bishops' protest against the killings. Sabiti outlived his successor by eleven years — an old man in retirement, watching the church he had held together be attacked, and watching the man who took the chair from him pay for it with his life.

He died at Kinoni on 15 May 1988, aged eighty-five.

What he leaves

Sabiti wrote no famous books and left few of his own words. What he left is a demonstration of two things the church keeps forgetting.

The first is that ordination is not the same as being filled. He had every credential his church could issue and was still six years short of what he most needed, and he received it while travelling as somebody's assistant. Nobody is too far in to be given more.

The second is that the revival's method works on institutions. We are used to the idea that personal confession heals marriages and friendships. Sabiti's archbishopric is the evidence that it also heals churches — that a division which negotiation could not settle in years was undone in one meeting by men who stopped defending their positions and named their own part in the wreck.

He is the least dramatic figure the East African Revival produced, and in a way the most encouraging. He was not a martyr and not a founder. He was a clergyman from a small place who was given more than he had, waited twenty-six years, took an office that half the country would not grant him, refused to fight for it, and lived to see it handed on.

I did all this for you, what have you done for me?

— the question he first read at school, and answered for fifty-five years

fields.name: Jarena Lee
fields.bio: Born free in New Jersey, Jarena Lee was converted under Richard Allen and became the first woman authorized to preach in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, travelling thousands of miles to proclaim the gospel.
fields.bio_html:
Jarena Lee was born free on February 11, 1783, in Cape May, New Jersey — a rare thing for a Black child in revolutionary America, and a mercy she never took for granted. Freedom did not spare her hardship. At seven years old she was sent sixty miles from her parents to work as a servant girl, and she grew up lonely, far from home, and hungry for something her circumstances could not give her. Long before she understood the gospel, she was aware of God: a tender conscience, a fear of death, a sense that she was made for more than service in another family's house.

That hunger drew her, as a young woman, to Philadelphia — the cradle of the free Black church. There she came under the preaching of the Reverend Richard Allen, the former slave who had founded Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church and would soon become the first bishop of the AME denomination. She had passed through years of religious searching first — trying one congregation and then another, convicted of sin, at times so oppressed in spirit that the tempter pressed her toward taking her own life. But God, she believed, was "mercifully striving" with her the whole while. Under Allen's ministry, about 1804, her long seeking came to its end.

My soul was gloriously converted to God, under preaching, at the very outset of the sermon.

— Jarena Lee

Conversion did not settle her; it set her seeking a deeper work. For years she wrestled with her own sinfulness, with doubt, even with temptation to despair. Then one day, alone, the assurance she had prayed for broke over her like a storm of light.

For weeks she had pleaded to know that she was wholly the Lord's. "That very instant," she wrote, "as if lightning had darted through me, I sprang to my feet, and cried, 'The Lord has sanctified my soul!' There was none to hear this but the angels who stood around to witness my joy."

The call she could not silence

Not long after, Jarena Lee heard what she could only describe as a voice — an inward, unmistakable command to preach the gospel. It frightened her. She was a poor, unlettered Black woman in a church, and an age, that reserved the pulpit entirely for men. But the call would not leave her, so she carried it to Richard Allen himself.

She told him plainly "that the Lord had revealed it to me, that I must preach the gospel." Allen, kind but bound by the Methodist Discipline, answered that their book made no provision for women preachers. Lee submitted — outwardly. Inwardly, the conviction only deepened, and she came to see the refusal as the age's blindness rather than God's will. In her narrative she set down a defense of women's preaching that still rings:

If the man may preach, because the Saviour died for him, why not the woman? seeing he died for her also. Is he not a whole Saviour, instead of a half one?

— Jarena Lee

In 1811 she married the Reverend Joseph Lee, pastor of a Black congregation at Snow Hill, some distance from Philadelphia. The marriage carried her away from the Bethel community that had nurtured her, into isolation she felt keenly. Then grief came in waves: within about six years she had buried her husband and several of her children, and found herself a widow with a young child and almost nothing. Yet the sorrow did not extinguish the call — it clarified it. Stripped of the supports she had leaned on, she leaned harder on God, and the old command to preach returned with new force.

"An altogether supernatural impulse"

The breakthrough came about 1819, in the very church where she had been converted. A visiting preacher rose to expound a text, faltered, and seemed to lose the Spirit's help. What happened next Jarena Lee never claimed as her own doing.

The same instant, I sprang, as by altogether supernatural impulse, to my feet, when I was aided from above to give an exhortation on the very text which my brother had taken.

— Jarena Lee

She preached — extemporaneous, unauthorized, on fire — and then sat down trembling, certain she had disgraced herself and would be expelled. Instead, Bishop Allen rose before the whole assembly. Eight years earlier, he told them, this woman had come to him asking leave to preach, and he had put her off; but he now believed, as fully as of any preacher present, that God had called her to the work. It was the answer to a prayer she had carried, like Jonah, for nearly a decade.

For eight years Jarena Lee had asked to preach and been refused, until the day she rose unbidden and exhorted a faltering congregation. When she sat down expecting disgrace, Richard Allen stood and publicly declared her called of God — the very permission she had prayed for, granted at last before the whole church.

With that blessing she became the first woman authorized to preach in the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

Thousands of miles for the gospel

What followed was one of the most extraordinary preaching lives of the nineteenth century. For decades Jarena Lee travelled — on foot, by wagon, and by the new railroad "cars" — thousands of miles a year, across the free states and into slave territory, preaching in churches and camp meetings, homes and open fields, to Black and white congregations alike. In a single year she recorded travelling more than two thousand miles and preaching nearly two hundred sermons. She was often the only woman in the pulpit, and just as often met with suspicion, exhaustion, and poverty. Her journal, kept faithfully across the 1820s, 30s, and 40s, is the record of a woman who simply would not stop.

It is also, page after page, a record of prayer. She prayed her way into strange towns and hostile meetings; she prayed over the sick and the seeking; she prayed when her body failed and her purse was empty, and she wrote down, with a diarist's plainness, how God met her.

Again and again her journal turns, mid-account, into petition and thanks — a preacher who treated prayer not as a duty bracketing the work but as the engine of it, "succored when tempted, and every where upheld by his hand."

Her travels carried her into real danger. She preached in the slave states of Maryland and beyond, where a free Black woman proclaiming the gospel — and the equal worth of every soul Christ died for — was a provocation, and where she once preached with enslaved men and women weeping before her and their masters looking on. She never separated the gospel she preached from the bondage she witnessed; the God who had made her free in Christ, she was certain, had not made anyone a slave. Her whole ministry was a living argument that the good news belongs to the poor, the enslaved, the unlettered, and the woman as fully as to anyone else.

She counted her hardships as fellowship with Christ, not grounds for complaint. Opposition to a woman in the pulpit she answered by preaching better; poverty she answered by trusting God for the next meal and the next mile; loneliness she answered by pressing into the presence she had known since that night the lightning of assurance struck her soul. She had no formal education and no earthly patron — only a call, a Bible, and a conviction that the One who gave the call would supply the strength.

A book, and a long silence

In 1836, Jarena Lee did something no African American woman had done before: she published her autobiography, The Life and Religious Experience of Jarena Lee, paying for the printing herself so that her testimony would outlast her. In 1849 she expanded it into the fuller Religious Experience and Journal of Mrs. Jarena Lee, adding the travel journal that makes up most of this volume. Both books she carried in her own bags and sold at her own meetings — a Black woman evangelist self-publishing her call in defiance of every convention of her day.

After 1849 the record goes quiet; she is thought to have died about 1864, in her early eighties, her later years unrecorded. For a long time her name was quiet too, remembered mostly by the church she had served. But her testimony did outlast her, exactly as she hoped. In 2016 the African Methodist Episcopal Church posthumously ordained her, formally granting the standing that the age had denied and God had plainly given. Jarena Lee had never really waited on that permission. She had a whole Saviour, and a whole gospel to preach, and she had spent her life proving that the good news is no respecter of persons — that the God who died for the woman as surely as for the man will use whom he calls, and answer the prayers of those who will not let him go.

fields.name: Julia A. J. Foote
fields.bio: Born to formerly enslaved parents, Julia A. J. Foote was a holiness evangelist who was excommunicated for preaching as a woman and later became the first woman ordained a deacon in the A.M.E. Zion Church.
fields.bio_html:
Julia A. J. Foote was born on May 21, 1823, in Schenectady, New York, the fourth child of parents who had known slavery firsthand. Her father was born free but was stolen as a child and enslaved; her mother was born a slave in the State of New York and served a cruel master and mistress before the family won its freedom. Out of that hard inheritance came a girl of fierce conscience and quick mind, sent out at ten to work as a servant in a family some miles from home, and hungry — long before she could name it — for God.

Her childhood was marked by the casual cruelties of a world built on slavery even where slavery was ending. She was whipped, once, for a theft she had not committed; a beloved schoolteacher was hanged for a crime; and everywhere she felt the weight of being poor, Black, and a girl. Yet she also remembered mercies — a family that treated her, for a time, almost as their own, and above all a growing sense that God was near. She learned to read chiefly so that she could read the Testament for herself, sounding out its words by firelight.

At fifteen she was converted. It happened, as she tells it, on a Sunday evening at a quarterly meeting, in a rush of assurance she never doubted afterward. But conversion only opened a deeper hunger. She had heard the Methodists speak of a second work of grace — entire sanctification, a heart made clean and wholly Christ's — and she would not rest until she had it. In an age when many Christians treated the new birth as the end of the matter, Foote believed the gospel promised more: not only forgiveness for what one had done, but cleansing for what one was.

The work of full salvation

After her marriage, about 1836, to George Foote, a sailor, she moved to Boston, and it was there that the longing was answered. She entered into what she called, all her life, "the work of full salvation" — sanctification as a distinct, definite gift of the Holy Spirit — and from that day holiness was the burden of her testimony. When she rose in class-meeting to tell of it, some crowded round to ask how they too might find it; others drew off in suspicious little groups. That division would follow her for the rest of her life. To preach holiness in her day, and to be a Black woman doing it, was to feel, in her own words, that "every man's hand is against us" — and to answer that not with bitterness but with communion.

In this severe trial I had constant access to God, and a clear consciousness that he heard me.

— Julia A. J. Foote

A call she fought, then obeyed

The call to preach came slowly and against her will. For months she found herself drawn out in prayer and exhortation from house to house, her "whole soul seemed drawn out for the salvation of souls." Friends warned that she was too forward. And when the conviction sharpened into a summons, she resisted it as Jonah had.

Pressed in spirit to preach, she recoiled at her own unfitness — "I thought it could not be that I was called to preach — I, so weak and ignorant" — and answered God plainly: "No, Lord, not me." Day by day the impression only deepened, until she could no longer refuse and gave herself to the work.

When she began to preach, the minister of her own African Methodist Episcopal Zion congregation in Boston moved against her. She asked only to be heard; he refused, put her name before the church, and had her cut off. She was tried and expelled from the church she loved — excommunicated for the double offense of preaching holiness and preaching as a woman. She appealed to the conference of ministers, trusting that a body of Christian men would judge righteously, and was disappointed again. It was a wound that never fully closed. Yet she refused to let it stop her, and refused, too, to let it turn her bitter. She simply kept preaching, now as an independent evangelist with no denomination behind her and no salary before her, trusting God alone to open the doors and supply the way.

Women in the Gospel

Out of that cost came one of the clearest defenses of women's preaching in nineteenth-century America. Foote had searched the Scriptures for herself, and she could not find the God who had so plainly called and used her forbidding her to speak. Her argument was disarmingly simple: whatever the Spirit gives, he gives to women and men alike.

If the power to preach the Gospel is short-lived and spasmodic in the case of women, it must be equally so in that of men; and if women have lost the gift of prophecy, so have men.

— Julia A. J. Foote

For decades she carried that conviction across the country — through New England and New York, into Ohio and the Midwest, up into Canada — travelling constantly, often poor, often ill, preaching in churches when they would have her and in halls, homes, and camp meetings when they would not. She became one of the best-known evangelists of the Wesleyan-Holiness movement. In 1878 she preached to an estimated five thousand people at a holiness meeting in Lodi, Ohio. Everywhere she went she pressed the same message: not merely pardon, but purity; not merely a first work of grace, but a full salvation that cleanses the heart and fits it for God.

The life cost her dearly. She travelled when she was sick and when she had no money for the fare; she preached in places where a Black woman in a pulpit drew scorn or worse; she was parted, for long stretches, from home and from her husband, whose work at sea already kept them apart, and she outlived him and the child she had buried. She met opposition not only from white congregations but from her own people's leaders, who feared that a woman preacher would bring their churches into disrepute. Through all of it she held that the hardship was fellowship with a suffering Saviour, and that the call which had cost her so much was worth more than the cost.

Her travels were sustained, as her memoir records on nearly every page, by unceasing prayer. She prayed her way into hostile meetings and prayed her way through sickness and want; she asked God for her daily bread and her next appointment and wrote down how he supplied them. The trials she met she counted as the fellowship of Christ's sufferings, and the deliverances she met she counted as proof that the God who called her would not abandon her.

Cast out of her own denomination and left without support, Julia Foote found her ministry not ended but enlarged: doors opened across the North and into Canada, thousands came to hear her, and the very church that had expelled her would, near the end of her life, ordain her — the deliverance of a woman who had committed her whole cause to God.

Vindicated at the last

Foote grounded her whole ministry in Scripture, not in defiance of it. She pointed to the prophet Joel's promise, fulfilled at Pentecost, that God would pour out his Spirit on daughters as well as sons, so that they too would prophesy; she pointed to the women who followed Christ and the women who labored beside Paul. If God had once spoken through such women, she reasoned, he had not fallen silent — and the same Spirit who sanctified a heart could surely fill a mouth. It was, for her, not a matter of rights to be demanded but of a gift to be obeyed.

In 1879, settled in Cleveland, Ohio, Foote published her autobiography, A Brand Plucked from the Fire — the title taken from the prophet Zechariah's vision of a soul snatched from the flames. It is a plain, fervent book, unashamed of visions and holy joy, and it stands among the most important spiritual narratives left by a Black woman of her century. She wrote it, she said, not for her own name but so that her testimony to full salvation might outlast her and lead others into the same liberty.

Vindication came slowly, and then fully. The church that had cast her out as a young woman received her, at the last, as one of its own ministers. She died that same year, in her late seventies, a brand indeed plucked from the fire — and one that had set many others alight.

faq.q: Who was Julia Foote?
faq.a: Born to formerly enslaved parents in 1823, Julia A. J. Foote was a holiness evangelist who was excommunicated for preaching as a woman and later became the first woman ordained a deacon in the A.M.E. Zion Church. She carried a message of full salvation across the North and into Canada for decades, and the very church that had cast her out received her, near the end of her life, as one of its own ministers.

faq.q: What was her hard inheritance?
faq.a: She was born on 21 May 1823 in Schenectady, New York, to parents who had known slavery firsthand: her father, born free, had been stolen as a child and enslaved, and her mother was born a slave in New York and served a cruel master before the family won its freedom. Sent out at ten to work as a servant, whipped once for a theft she had not committed, she learned to read chiefly so that she could read the Testament for herself, sounding out its words by firelight.

faq.q: How was she converted?
faq.a: At fifteen she was converted on a Sunday evening at a quarterly meeting, in a rush of assurance she never doubted afterward. But conversion only opened a deeper hunger: she had heard the Methodists speak of a second work of grace — entire sanctification, a heart made clean and wholly Christ's — and she would not rest until she had it, believing the gospel promised not only forgiveness for what one had done but cleansing for what one was.

faq.q: What was "the work of full salvation"?
faq.a: After her marriage about 1836 to George Foote, a sailor, she moved to Boston, and there the longing was answered. When she rose in class-meeting to tell of it, some crowded round to ask how they too might find it; others drew off in suspicious little groups, a division that would follow her for the rest of her life.

faq.q: What was the call she fought?
faq.a: The call to preach came slowly and against her will. For months she was drawn out in prayer and exhortation from house to house, her whole soul, she said, seemed drawn out for the salvation of souls; friends warned she was too forward. When the conviction sharpened into a summons she resisted it as Jonah had, recoiling at her own unfitness — "I thought it could not be that I was called to preach — I, so weak and ignorant" — and answering, "No, Lord, not me," until she could no longer refuse.

faq.q: Why was she excommunicated?
faq.a: When she began to preach, the minister of her own African Methodist Episcopal Zion congregation in Boston moved against her. She asked only to be heard; he refused, put her name before the church, and had her cut off. She was tried and expelled from the church she loved — excommunicated for the double offense of preaching holiness and preaching as a woman — and her appeal to the conference of ministers was disappointed again. It was a wound that never fully closed, yet she refused to let it stop her or turn her bitter.

faq.q: How did she defend women's preaching?
faq.a: Out of that cost came one of the clearest defenses of women's preaching in nineteenth-century America. Searching the Scriptures for herself, she could not find the God who had so plainly called and used her forbidding her to speak, and her argument was disarmingly simple: "If the power to preach the Gospel is short-lived and spasmodic in the case of women, it must be equally so in that of men; and if women have lost the gift of prophecy, so have men."

faq.q: What was her preaching life?
faq.a: For decades she carried her message across New England and New York, into Ohio and the Midwest, up into Canada — travelling constantly, often poor and often ill, preaching in churches when they would have her and in halls, homes and camp meetings when they would not. In 1878 she preached to an estimated five thousand people at a holiness meeting in Lodi, Ohio, becoming one of the best-known evangelists of the Wesleyan-Holiness movement — sustained, her memoir records on nearly every page, by unceasing prayer.
