fields.name: Rees Howells
fields.bio: Rees Howells (1879–1950) was a Welsh coal miner turned intercessor whose life of costly, sacrificial prayer became the pattern taught in his biography by Norman Grubb. He founded the Bible College of Wales at Swansea in 1924, running it without fees or fundraising appeals, and led its community in sustained wartime intercession for Britain.
fields.bio_html:
Rees Howells left school at twelve for the tinplate mill and the coal mine, and he is remembered today for something almost the opposite of that hard, ordinary start: a life given over so completely to prayer that his biographer could find no better word for him than intercessor. He founded a Bible college that took no fees and made no appeals, and during the Second World War he gathered a hundred people in a Welsh house to pray every night for months. What he taught about prayer — that it can cost the one who prays as much as it asks of God — is the reason his name has outlived him. His story is also a study in how carefully a devotional life must be told, because the most dramatic claims made for it are claims of faith, not of proof.

A collier from Brynamman

He was born on 10 October 1879 at Brynamman, in Carmarthenshire, the sixth child of Thomas and Margaret Howells. It was a Welsh-speaking mining district, and there was no money for a long education. He left elementary school at twelve and went to work in a local tinplate mill and then in the coal mine, as boys of that valley did.

In 1901 he emigrated to America, following the tinplate trade to the mills of Pittsburgh and Connellsville in Pennsylvania. It was there, and not in chapel-going Wales, that his faith came alive. Under the influence of a Jewish convert and evangelist named Maurice Reuben, and of the writings of Professor Henry Drummond, he was converted — somewhere around 1902 to 1904; the exact time and place were never firmly recorded. What is clear is that a young Welsh miner went to America for work and came home, in 1904, a changed man.

He returned to a country that was itself on fire. The Welsh Revival of 1904–05, under Evan Roberts, had swept the valleys, and Howells came back into the middle of its aftermath, working again as a coal miner among people newly awakened. But conversion, for him, turned out to be only the first door.

The surrender at Llandrindod

In 1906 he attended the convention at Llandrindod Wells — the Welsh equivalent of the Keswick holiness meetings. Norman Grubb, whose biography Rees Howells: Intercessor is the source for almost everything intimate that we know about him, calls what happened there the most revolutionary event of his life after his conversion. Howells described it as a total and unconditional surrender, and he spoke of it ever afterward as a meeting in which the Holy Spirit asked to take possession of him.

Howells said the Spirit spoke to him in terms that left no room to bargain — that if God came in, He came as God, and the old self would have to go out. In his own recollection the words were plain and severe:

I am God, and I am come to ask you to give your body to Me that I may work through it… But if I come in, I come as God, and you must go out… I shall not mix Myself with your self.

— the words Howells said the Spirit spoke to him at Llandrindod Wells, 1906 (as recorded by Norman Grubb)

It is worth being exact about what this is. It is Howells, years later, recounting an inner voice — a thing told from the inside, not a transcript. But the effect on his life was outward and lasting. From that surrender he dated everything that followed: the giving away of money and comfort, the long nights of prayer, the strange and costly ministry that made his name.

What he meant by intercession

Howells drew a sharp line between ordinary prayer and what he called intercession, and it is here that Grubb's account is most useful. In Grubb's telling, Howells's intercession had three marks — identification, agony and authority.

Identification meant that the one who prayed did not stand at a distance from the person he prayed for, but stepped into their place — sharing their poverty, their hunger, their loneliness, modelled on the way Christ took the place of sinners. In practice this was not a feeling but a cost: Howells gave away money he needed, food he wanted, hours he could not spare, and lived among the people he was burdened for. Agony meant travailing in prayer, praying through, until an inward assurance came that Grubb reports Howells calling gaining the position. And authority was what remained once identification and agony had done their work — a settled confidence to pray for the outcome and expect it.

Identification, agony and authority.

— Norman Grubb's account of the three marks of Rees Howells's teaching on intercession

Each such victory Howells called a position of intercession — a permanent place of prevailing prayer, won once, at real personal cost, and never surrendered. His early positions were among the poorest: tramps and homeless men, orphans, and the sick and dying. He took them as burdens, not as projects, and he paid for them out of his own means and his own comfort.

One of those early burdens marked him more deeply than any other. Grubb records that a close acquaintance was dying of consumption, and Howells was drawn into an intense and prolonged intercession over her sickness. In the best-known telling, the dying woman, brought to a settled assurance of God's love, prayed not that she would be healed but that no one else would ever have to suffer as she had. She died. Howells came out of it having learned, as he had not before, what it means to stand in another person's place and not be spared.

He was drawn to pray for a woman dying of consumption, and could not pray her free of it. In the telling that has come down through Grubb, she asked only that no one else suffer as she had, and died at peace — and Howells emerged having learned the cost of standing in another's place. It was, he said, his first great position of intercession.

Africa: the Rusitu revival

Around 1912 the Howellses — he had married Elizabeth Hannah Jones, "Lizzie," of Brynamman in December 1910 — believed themselves called to Africa. They joined the South Africa General Mission and were given charge of the Rusitu station in Gazaland, on the border of Mozambique and what was then Southern Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe. They reached the field in 1915.

What happened there is one of the few large episodes of his life attested well beyond Grubb's devotional pages. Within about six weeks of Howells beginning to preach on revival, the meetings changed. Dated from October 1915, a revival broke out that lasted some fifteen months, centred on Rusitu and Silinda and spreading through the region. Howells, who had spent years learning to pray one dying woman into peace, now watched a whole country-side moved at once. The line remembered from him, reported through Grubb, is a plain man's astonishment:

You can never describe those meetings when the Holy Spirit comes down!

— Rees Howells on the Rusitu revival, as reported by Norman Grubb

Six weeks of intercession at the Rusitu station, and then, from October 1915, revival — meetings that ran for some fifteen months and spread through southern Africa. Of all the answers Howells is remembered for, this is the clearest and the best attested: a sustained work he had prayed toward and then could only stand inside of.

The Howellses returned to Wales around 1920, and Rees turned to the work that would occupy the rest of his life.

A college built on prayer

After an American preaching tour in 1922 he resolved to found a Bible college, loosely modelled on Moody Bible Institute in Chicago. He bought the Glynderwen estate at Swansea, and the Bible College of Wales opened on Whit Monday, 1924.

Its distinctive was its economy. There were no fixed fees and no fundraising appeals; the needs of the college were, in the language of that world, prayed in. The tradition preserved by Grubb says he began with only a few shillings and that money came, again and again, at the very hour it was needed — enough to buy not only Glynderwen but Sketty Isaf, Derwen Fawr, and later the Penllergaer estate. The exact sums and dates belong to devotional memory rather than to an audited ledger, and are best left as what they are: a testimony that the college met its bills without ever asking a donor for them.

The college's own testimony is that its estates were bought without a single appeal — that Howells and his students prayed, and the money arrived, often at the last possible hour. Told honestly, the miracle is not in any one figure, which memory has smoothed, but in the settled fact that a large work ran for years on prayer and refused to beg.

Those who sat under him did not always have words for the impression he made. Grubb preserves one listener's:

There is someone here among us, and I feel like going round the country with him, carrying his bag and cleaning his boots.

— a listener describing the effect of Rees Howells, as recorded by Norman Grubb

On Boxing Day, 26 December 1934, at Derwen Fawr, Howells received what he called the Every Creature vision — a burden to intercede that the whole world should have the chance to hear the gospel. Staff and students gave New Year's Day 1935 to prayer and fasting over it. It set the pattern for the college's most famous, and most delicate, chapter.

The war years — what is documented, and what is believed

When war came in 1939 the college turned its whole life toward prayer. This much is documented, in Grubb and in the college's own prayer diaries: from the outbreak of the war they held prayer meetings every evening, running from around seven o'clock to midnight and beyond, and did not miss a single day. Grubb describes something like a hundred people praying as though they had been called to fight on the Western Front. The diaries record intensive intercession for Dunkirk over 22–29 May 1940, and the college prayed its way through the Battle of Britain. Howells put his conviction into print in a 1940 book, God Challenges the Dictators.

That is the documented part, and it is remarkable enough. But it is important to say clearly what is not established. The college believed — and many who tell its story still believe — that this praying turned the tide: that it lay behind the halt before Dunkirk and the outcome over southern England. That is a conviction of faith, a reading of a real correlation between the nights of prayer and the events of the war. It is not a demonstrated historical cause, and it would be dishonest to present it as one. What can be said without exaggeration is that a community of Christians prayed, night after night, for the deliverance of their country, and that they believed their prayers were heard. The praying is a matter of record. The verdict on it is a matter of faith.

Death and legacy

Rees Howells died on 13 February 1950, aged seventy-one. His son, Samuel Rees Howells, succeeded him as director of the college, and the work he had prayed into being outlived him.

He wrote little that is widely read, and much of what we know of his inner life reaches us through one devoted biographer, which is a reason for care rather than for doubt. The care is the point. Howells taught that prayer is not a way of getting God to do easy things at a distance, but a way of being drawn so far into another's need that the praying costs you something — your money, your comfort, your peace, sometimes your health. That teaching does not depend on any wartime claim being proved. It stands on a dying woman prayed into peace, on tramps and orphans taken in, on a mission station in Gazaland where the roof seemed to lift, and on a college that paid its way for a generation without ever passing a plate. Those are the things Rees Howells actually did, and they are enough.

fields.name: John Hyde
fields.bio: John “Praying” Hyde (1865–1912) was an American Presbyterian missionary to the Punjab, remembered above all as a man of prayer — founder of the Punjab Prayer Union and a leader of the Sialkot Convention, who asked God for a soul a day and saw hundreds converted. Much of his vivid reputation comes from Francis McGaw’s 1923 devotional book “Praying Hyde,” written after his death.
fields.bio_html:
There is a difficulty at the heart of any life of John Hyde, and it is better to name it at the start than to pretend it away. Almost everything vivid that we know about the man called “Praying Hyde” — the whole nights on the floor, the finger laid on his lips, the heart said to have shifted in his chest — comes to us through a single small devotional book: Francis McGaw’s Praying Hyde, published in 1923, more than a decade after Hyde was dead, and drawn in part from what other people remembered. The hard, checkable facts of his life are thinner and quieter than the legend. This account keeps the two apart on purpose. Where the record is solid, it says so plainly; where the story rests on McGaw and the memories he gathered, it says that too. Hyde does not need to be inflated. What is verifiable is remarkable enough.

A minister’s son from Illinois

John Nelson Hyde was born on 9 November 1865 in Illinois, one of six children of the Reverend Smith Harris Hyde, a Presbyterian minister. His father was a man who prayed, in particular, a specific prayer — that God would send out labourers into the harvest — and it is one of the few threads that runs unbroken from the well-attested record into the legend: the son became, in the end, an answer to the kind of prayer the father had prayed. The household knew the cost of that prayer, too. An elder brother, Edmund, had set out toward the mission field himself and died of fever while still a student.

Hyde graduated from Carthage College in Illinois with high honours in 1887, and went on to McCormick Theological Seminary in Chicago, finishing his training there in 1892. In October of that year he sailed from New York for India. He was twenty-six.

He carried a real disadvantage with him. Hyde was partly deaf — “slow of speech and hearing,” as the phrase went — and this made the early work of learning a new language slow and discouraging. It is worth holding onto, because the man who would later be remembered for fluent, tender preaching in two Indian languages did not begin as an obvious success. He studied at Dehra Dun, and from around 1894 took up village evangelism in the districts around Ludhiana and Lahore in the Punjab, and in time became closely bound to the town of Sialkot. The deafness never fully lifted, but he became genuinely fluent in Urdu and Punjabi.

The turn toward prayer

The early years were hard and the converts were few. It seems to have been out of that hardness, rather than out of any easy success, that Hyde’s praying life grew. From about 1899 he began to spend whole nights in prayer. This is the root of everything the later devotional writers made of him, and it grew from the least romantic soil there is: a discouraged missionary with little to show, who decided that the answer was not to work harder in front of people but to wait longer before God.

Father, give me these souls, or I die!

— John Hyde, as remembered in Francis McGaw’s Praying Hyde (1923)

That cry is McGaw’s, and its exact wording varies from telling to telling — some render it “O God, give me souls or I die.” It should be read as the shape of the man’s burden as those close to him remembered it, not as a transcript. But the burden itself is not in doubt.

In April 1904, alongside the first of the great annual Sialkot Conventions, Hyde and several fellow missionaries founded the Punjab Prayer Union. Its purpose was to pray for a “quickening” — a revival — across the Punjab and across India. Hyde led both the Union and the Convention for years. The members of the Union bound themselves to a simple, checkable discipline: to set apart half an hour each day, as soon after noon as they could manage, to pray for the awakening — and to keep on, in the Union’s own words, until the awakening comes.

Every member of the Punjab Prayer Union pledged the same half hour: as soon after noon as possible, each day, to pray for a spiritual awakening across India — and not to stop asking until it came. It was ordinary, repeatable, and open to anyone. That, as much as the whole nights, is the discipline Hyde actually built.

What the praying was said to do

Out of the Prayer Union and the Sialkot Convention came what mission accounts of the time describe as a genuine outpouring — conventions marked, from 1904 onward, by deep conviction, open confession and renewal. Those who were there credited Hyde’s long, hidden intercession with much of it. This is the most solid of the answers to his prayer: not a private marvel, but a public work that many witnesses saw and named.

The most famous single claim about his fruitfulness belongs partly to the record and partly to tradition, and the two should be kept distinct. Reference works confirm that in 1908 Hyde prayed for one soul a day, and that something on the order of four hundred people were brought into the church that year. That much is soberly reported. The rest is McGaw’s: it was said that Hyde then raised his asking to two souls a day, and near the end to four, and that on any day the full number was not reached, there lay on him at night a weight so heavy that he could neither eat nor sleep. Those escalating totals rest on devotional memory alone. The one-a-day, and the four hundred, do not.

In 1908 Hyde asked God for one soul a day. By the year’s end, the reference accounts agree, about four hundred had been gathered in. It is the plainest, best-attested answer to prayer in his life — a whole year of it, counted one day at a time.

The accuser of the brethren

Among the many scenes McGaw recorded, one stands out as both the most trustworthy and the most searching, and it turns not on triumph but on a rebuke Hyde believed he received from God himself. He was praying for revival in the life of an Indian pastor whose faith had gone cold, and he began, as we all begin, by telling God the man’s faults: “O Father, thou knowest how cold —” and got no further. He felt, he said, a finger laid on his lips, and heard the words, He that toucheth him, toucheth the apple of Mine eye. Hyde stopped. What came out of him next was not accusation but repentance.

Forgive me, Father, in that I have been an accuser of the brethren before Thee!

— John Hyde, in Praying Hyde (1923)

From that moment, the account runs, he could only praise the man he had come to criticise. It is among the most reliable of McGaw’s stories, and among the most useful, because it works against the grain of hero-worship. The great intercessor is caught in the oldest sin of the praying person — running down a brother in the presence of God — and is stopped, and turned. Whatever else the legend made of Hyde, this scene shows a man being corrected, not a man being admired.

A worn-out body

The nights and the burden took a toll on his health, and here the honest telling has to be most careful, because it is exactly here that devotion has most often outrun the evidence. The story that was handed down is this: a doctor who examined Hyde found his heart displaced from the left side of his chest to the right, and in the worst condition he had seen, and gave him only months to live unless he rested — the strain of prayer, the telling goes, had physically moved his heart.

It is a moving image, and it should be handled with care. A condition in which the heart sits on the right side of the body has a plain medical name — dextrocardia — and is very often something a person is simply born with. It is entirely possible that this is what the examining doctor found. The reading that prayer shifted a healthy heart is a devotional interpretation laid over the fact, not a medical finding. The right way to hold it is to tell the story as Hyde’s friends told it, and to leave the miracle unclaimed.

Hyde had already gone home to America once, on furlough for his health in 1902, returning to India in 1904. He left India for the last time in March 1911. For a season he travelled in Britain, sharing in the evangelistic work of J. Wilbur Chapman. Back in the United States the doctors found the real thing that was killing him — a malignant tumour of the brain.

Northampton, 1912

Here a smaller act of honesty is owed to the reader, because the popular devotional accounts often get the ending wrong. They will tell you Hyde died on the first of February at Clifton Springs. He did not. He died on 17 February 1912, at Northampton, Massachusetts, at the age of forty-six, and was buried at Carthage, Illinois, near the college where he had begun. The wrong date and place have been copied from book to book for a century; the corrected facts are worth restating simply because they are true.

The last words attributed to him were not in English but in the language of the people he had given his life to. He is remembered to have cried out, in Punjabi: Bol, Yisu Masih, ki jai! — “Shout the victory of Jesus Christ!” The transliteration shifts from source to source; the sense of it is steady. A man who had spent his strength asking God for the souls of the Punjab died with a Punjabi shout of triumph on his lips.

Bol, Yisu Masih, ki jai! — Shout the victory of Jesus Christ!

— the last words remembered of John Hyde, Northampton, 17 February 1912

What he leaves

John Hyde wrote no great book; the book that carries his name was written about him, by another man, after he was gone. He left almost nothing in his own hand. What he left instead was a pattern — a discouraged, half-deaf missionary who, finding little fruit in front of people, went behind them and waited on God, and a small prayer union with a half-hour rule that anyone could keep. The father had prayed for labourers; the son became one, and prayed for the harvest itself.

The legend around him should be read for what it is: a devotional tradition, rooted in one 1923 book and in the memories it gathered, that has sometimes said more than can be proved. But strip the tradition back to what the record will bear, and a real man is still standing there — one who asked for a soul a day and saw four hundred come, who was stopped mid-prayer from accusing a brother and turned to praise instead, and who died far from the Punjab still shouting its Saviour’s victory in its own tongue. That is enough. It was always enough.

fields.name: Gregory the Great
fields.bio: Gregory the Great (c.540–604) was Prefect of Rome who renounced the city’s highest civil office to become a monk, and the reluctant pope who wrote the West’s most influential manual of pastoral ministry, the Pastoral Rule. He fed Rome through famine and plague, ransomed captives, and sent the mission that converted the English.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the shepherds the church remembers were poor men who climbed. Gregory of Rome was the opposite: a man at the very top of Roman society who climbed down, on purpose, into a monastery — and then was hauled back up against his will to carry the heaviest office in the Western church. He is remembered as a pope, a saint, one of the four great Latin Doctors. But the truer name for him, the one that runs under everything else he did, is pastor. He wrote the book that taught the West how to care for souls, and he tried to live it while feeding a starving city, ransoming its captives, and walking it through a plague.

The prefect who walked away

He was born around 540 in Rome, into a wealthy patrician family of the old senatorial rank — the kind of household that had governed the city for generations. It was also a devout house, and church-tied: his mother, Silvia, and two of his aunts are venerated as saints. He was given the best education the sixth century could offer, and he rose fast. By about 573, still only in his early thirties, he had become Prefect of the City of Rome — the highest civil office the city had to give. He had, in worldly terms, arrived.

And then, around 574, he gave it all away. Not in a moment of collapse, and not lightly. The record says he came to the decision only after long prayer and a hard inward struggle, and then he acted with the thoroughness of a man who does not do things by halves. He turned his own family home on the Caelian Hill into a monastery under the patronage of St Andrew, and became a monk there. The Sicilian estates he had inherited he gave up as well, using them to found six more monasteries on the island. The prefect of Rome became one of the brothers.

It is worth being careful here, because the sources are. He is often called the abbot of St Andrew's, but there is no firm evidence he ever held that title; what is certain is that he lived there as a monk, and by his own later testimony those were the happiest and most settled years of his life. He had found the thing he wanted, and it was quiet.

Dragged back into the world

The quiet did not last. In 579 he was made a deacon and sent to Constantinople as apocrisiarius — the pope's envoy at the imperial court — to plead for help against the Lombards, the people then overrunning Italy. He spent years in that role before returning to Rome and to St Andrew's, around 585 or 586, hoping to resume the monastic life he loved.

Then, in 590, the plague took Pope Pelagius II, and the city turned to Gregory. He is widely described as the first monk to become pope, and he wanted no part of it. He tried to refuse. Everything we know of him says the refusal was sincere — that he genuinely dreaded the office, and grieved the loss of his monastery. When he could not escape it, he did a very Gregory thing: he sat down and wrote a book about why a man in his position should be terrified, and how, having been given the burden anyway, he must carry it.

The art of arts

That book is the Book of Pastoral Rule — in Latin the Regula Pastoralis — written around 590. It began partly as his own apologia, an explanation of why he had wanted to flee such an office. It became something far larger: for roughly the first millennium and a half of Western Christianity, the single most influential book ever written on the care of souls. In 813 its study was made obligatory for bishops under Charlemagne. Three centuries after Gregory's death, King Alfred the Great had it translated into Old English and sent a copy to every bishop in England. Few books have shaped so many pastors for so long.

Its argument is set out in a single sentence that has never been improved upon:

The government of souls is the art of arts.

— Gregory the Great, Book of Pastoral Rule, Book I

He meant it as a warning before it was a compliment. If leading souls is the highest of all the arts, then no one should presume to practise it who would not presume to practise medicine or teaching without training and fear. The whole of his first book is an argument against entering the office lightly. The pastor must be humble; he must want the work for the work's sake and not for the standing it brings; and — this is the note Gregory returns to again and again — he must not let the crush of outward business hollow out his inner life.

Gregory knew that danger from the inside, because his own days were now buried in administration. Rome's poor had to be fed, its captives ransomed, its enemies negotiated with; the letters and accounts never stopped. And he watched what that kind of load does to a man's soul, and named it exactly:

The mind, occupied with earthly cares, is emptied of the solidity of inward fear; and, estranged from the business of self-examination, it does not even consider the losses it is suffering.

— from the Book of Pastoral Rule, Book I

That is not the observation of a theorist. It is a man describing his own temptation — the pastor so consumed with running things that he stops examining himself, and does not even notice how much he is losing. Gregory's remedy was never to withdraw from the work; it was to keep the inner watch alive in the middle of it. His long third book is a catalogue of contrasted people — rich and poor, joyful and grieving, the meek and the quick-tempered — each, he insists, to be admonished differently, because souls are not interchangeable and a good shepherd learns them one at a time.

Servant of the servants of God

The title Gregory chose for himself has outlived every grander one. He called himself servus servorum Dei — the servant of the servants of God. He did not coin the phrase; it is older than he is. But he took it up as his own name for the office and made it the standard style of the popes, and he did so pointedly, as a rebuke of pride. When the Patriarch of Constantinople styled himself the "Universal Bishop," Gregory recoiled from the arrogance of it, and answered the swelling title with a shrinking one. The man who governed the Western church would be known, in his own hand, as the servant of God's servants.

He governed as the title promised. When famine and plague pressed on Rome, he administered the church's own estates — the "patrimony of Peter" — to feed the hungry, and he emptied the papal treasury to buy back the captives the Lombards had carried off. Pastoral care, in Gregory's hands, was not only counsel; it was bread and ransom money. And when imperial authority in Italy grew too weak to protect the city, it was Gregory who negotiated with the Lombards to spare Rome.

Leading a city in repentance

His very first act as pope set the pattern. Rome in 590 was a plague city, and Gregory's answer to it was not administrative but pastoral: he called the whole population out to walk the streets in penitence, imploring God to lift the pestilence, the new shepherd leading his frightened flock in repentance and prayer.

His first act as Bishop of Rome was to lead the whole city through its plague-stricken streets in a penitential procession — not to organize relief first, but to bring the people to their knees together, begging God to end the pestilence. The shepherd's first move was to pray, out loud, at the head of his flock.

Later ages could not leave the story plain. A medieval legend grew up that as the procession wound past Hadrian's great mausoleum, the Archangel Michael was seen atop it sheathing his sword — the sign that the plague was ending — and that the building has been called the Castel Sant'Angelo, the Castle of the Angel, ever since. That is a beautiful story and it is a legend; the sober fact underneath it is simply a pope who met a plague by leading his people in prayer.

Not Angles, but angels

Gregory's most enduring pastoral legacy reached a people he never saw. In 596 he sent a monk named Augustine — Augustine of Canterbury — with a band of brothers to carry the gospel to the pagan Anglo-Saxons of Britain. Augustine landed in Kent in 597, and from that mission the English church grew; English tradition still calls Gregory the Apostle of the English.

There is a cherished story about why he sent them. The historian Bede, writing around 731 — well over a century after Gregory's death — records that Gregory once saw fair-haired boys for sale in the Roman slave market, and asked where they were from. Told they were Angli, Angles, he is said to have answered that they were not Angles but angels, non Angli sed Angeli, and to have resolved from that moment to send the good news to their people. It is one of the most repeated stories in the history of the English church. It is also Bede's telling, set down long after the fact, and it should be received as the church has cherished it — as tradition, not as a documented saying from Gregory's own mouth. What is certain, and enough, is the mission itself: an old, overworked pope in a shrinking city who still found it in him to send the gospel to the edge of the known world.

The song under his name

Gregory died on 12 March 604. The church named him one of its four great Latin Doctors and called him, simply, the Great. His writings shaped Western worship, and he did reorganize the liturgy of Rome — which is almost certainly the seed of the tradition that his name became attached to. For centuries the plainsong of the Western church has been called Gregorian chant. But the attribution is traditional and grew up long after him; historians doubt that Gregory composed or codified that body of music, and honesty requires us not to hand him a legend as a fact. His name rests on the chant the way it rests on the slave-market pun — lovingly, and at a distance.

What he leaves the shepherds

Strip away the legends and a very solid man remains, and he is more useful than the legends. Gregory is the pastor who did not want the job, said so, and did it faithfully for fourteen years anyway. He is the administrator who knew that administration could eat a soul alive, and kept watch against it in himself. He fed the poor from his own church's lands, spent its treasure on ransoming slaves, met a plague on his knees at the head of his people, and sent the gospel to a nation he would never meet — all while insisting, in the book that outlived him by more than a thousand years, that the care of souls is the highest and most fearful art there is.

To every pastor since who has felt too small for the work, Gregory is a strange comfort: the man who felt exactly that, and was right, and served anyway.

The government of souls is the art of arts.

— Gregory the Great, who spent fourteen years proving how hard he meant it

fields.name: George Herbert
fields.bio: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and Anglican priest who left an aristocrat’s path to court to become a humble country parson at Bemerton. His devotional poems, published after his death as The Temple, and his pastoral manual The Country Parson made him a model of the devout parish priest.
fields.bio_html:
Some lives are remembered for what a man built or won. George Herbert is remembered for what he gave up. He was born into an aristocratic Welsh-border family, educated at the best schools England had, and elected to one of Cambridge’s most coveted offices — a post that pointed, as everyone around him understood, toward the royal Court and a career in the service of the King. He walked away from all of it to become the rector of two tiny country churches in Wiltshire, a post so obscure that most of his own century would have thought it a waste. He held it for less than three years before he died. And yet the book of poems he never saw printed, and the small manual he wrote for his own use, have outlived every courtier he might have become.

The fifth son of a great house

He was born on 3 April 1593 at Montgomery, in the Welsh Marches, the fifth son of a family that stood near the top of the country’s life. His elder brother Edward — later Lord Herbert of Cherbury — became a philosopher and diplomat of real note. His mother, Magdalen Herbert, was a woman of learning and a patron of poets; she was a friend and patron of John Donne, who would one day preach at her memorial. Into that cultured, well-connected household George was born the youngest of a crowd of sons, and he was marked early as the clever, delicate, bookish one.

His father died when George was three, and Magdalen raised the children herself. He went to Westminster School, and from there to Trinity College, Cambridge, admitted in 1609. He took his degrees in course — a bachelor’s in 1613, a master’s in 1616 — and was made a Fellow of Trinity in 1614. He was, by every outward sign, a young man of the university, at home in Latin and music and the manners of learned men, moving smoothly toward whatever the world might offer him.

What the world offered, in 1620, was the office of Public Orator of the University of Cambridge. It is hard now to convey what that meant. The Orator was the university’s public voice — the man who wrote and delivered its formal addresses, who spoke for Cambridge to the great and, above all, to the Court. It was understood to be a stepping-stone. The two men who had held it before Herbert had both gone on to become Secretaries of State. He sat briefly in Parliament for Montgomery in 1624. Everything was arranged. A brilliant young aristocrat, holding the university’s most public office, with the ear of the Court and the favour of the King almost within reach.

The blocked road, and the turn

Then the road closed. Herbert’s worldly hopes had rested on royal favour, and within a short span the men who might have carried him upward were gone: two of his patrons, the Duke of Richmond and the Marquis of Hamilton, died, and then in 1625 King James I himself died. The “Court-hopes,” as they were called, quietly collapsed. At the same time Herbert’s health, never strong, was failing — the consumption that would eventually kill him was already at work in him.

It would be too simple, and untrue, to say he became a priest because his ambitions were disappointed. The honest picture is a convergence. A genuine and deepening piety, a set of blocked prospects, and a body that was plainly not made for the long climb of public life all pressed him the same way at once. He turned from the Court to the Church. He was ordained deacon around 1626 and made a canon of Lincoln Cathedral that same year. And on 19 September 1630 he was ordained priest — the pivot of every account of his life, the well-connected aristocrat and Public Orator becoming, deliberately, an obscure country parson.

Contemporaries were baffled. For a man of his birth and gifts, the parish of a rural church was not a step down so much as a disappearance. He seems to have known exactly what he was choosing, and to have chosen it as the more excellent thing.

Bemerton

In 1630 he was instituted rector of Fugglestone St Peter with Bemerton, a small country parish just outside Salisbury. He had married Jane Danvers the year before. And there, in under three years, he became the enduring English picture of what a devoted country priest could be.

He did not treat the smallness of the place as beneath him. He paid, out of his own means, for the restoration of the decayed Bemerton church. He catechised the children and the unlearned. He visited the poor of his parish and supported them materially, out of his own pocket. Whatever he had given up in worldly scale, he poured into this handful of souls with a thoroughness that made the parish, and not the university, the true theatre of his life.

He was also a real musician — an accomplished lutenist and player of the viol, and a composer. By the account of his early biographer Izaak Walton, written some thirty-seven years after Herbert’s death, he walked the mile or so into Salisbury about twice a week for the Cathedral’s Evensong, and stayed afterward to make music with friends. Walton tells us he called that his “Heaven upon earth.” Walton also tells a much-loved story of Herbert ringing the church bell and praying the daily offices at set hours so that the labourers in the surrounding fields, hearing it, might pause and pray along with him. These warm scenes come to us through Walton, a devout admirer writing long after the fact, and are best received as his testimony rather than as documented record — but they are testimony that has shaped how the English church has remembered its country parson ever since.

The book he never saw

Out of those few years came two works, both published only after he was dead. The first was A Priest to the Temple, or The Country Parson, a plain prose manual of pastoral ministry, written at Bemerton around 1632 for his own guidance and printed in 1652. The second, and the reason the world still says his name, was The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations — a collection of more than a hundred and sixty English devotional poems, printed in 1633, the year he died.

The poems are the record of a soul’s dealings with God: struggle, rebellion, comfort, surrender, all in a plain and exact English that has never gone out of fashion. In “The Elixir” he set down the whole doctrine of hallowing ordinary work that his own life at Bemerton had become:

A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine; / Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th’ action fine.

— George Herbert, “The Elixir”

In “The Collar” he wrote the great poem of resistance dissolving into obedience — a man raging against the restraints of his calling until a single word undoes him:

Methought I heard one calling, Child! / And I replied, My Lord.

— George Herbert, “The Collar”

And in “Love (III)”, the last poem in the book, the soul that draws back “guilty of dust and sin” is welcomed anyway, and sat down, and fed. It is one of the tenderest treatments of grace in the language. Herbert’s whole theology of prayer he compressed into a single sonnet, “Prayer (I)”, which piles image upon image and then, refusing every definition, closes on two quiet words.

Prayer the church’s banquet, angel’s age, / God’s breath in man returning to his birth… — so begins Herbert’s sonnet “Prayer (I)”, which runs through a cascade of names for prayer and abandons them all at the end for two words: “…something understood.”

The message to Little Gidding

The consumption that had shadowed him for years took him quickly at the last. He died at Bemerton on 1 March 1633, not yet forty years old. His ministry there had lasted less than three years.

The most cherished account of his dying comes, again, from Walton, and should be received as his. Walton tells that as Herbert lay near death he sent the manuscript of his poems — the collection we now call The Temple — to his friend Nicholas Ferrar, the founder of the devout community at Little Gidding. His instruction, by Walton’s report, was that Ferrar should read it and judge; if it might “turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul,” let him publish it, and if not, let him burn it. He would not press it on the world as a thing of value in itself.

Publish it if it may turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul, else burn it; for I and it are less than the least of God’s mercies.

— George Herbert’s dying message to Nicholas Ferrar, as reported by Izaak Walton

Ferrar did not burn it. He had The Temple printed that same year, 1633. What its author called less than the least of God’s mercies has fed dejected souls for four centuries.

What he leaves

Herbert left no dynasty and won no office worth recording. He held the most promising post at Cambridge and let it go; he took a country parish that his peers thought a burial; he served it for a handful of years and died young. By the measure he was raised to, it was a small life thrown away.

By another measure it is one of the most complete lives the English church has produced. He had discovered — and, more rarely, had lived — that the sweeping of a room could be made divine, that the ordinary offices of a country priest were not a step down from greatness but the substance of it, and that a man might do the humblest work “as for thy laws” and so make it fine. He did not tell his poems they were good; he thought them, and himself, less than the least of God’s mercies, and asked that they be burned if they helped no one. That they were not burned, and that they have never since stopped helping, is the quiet answer his life was given.

faq.q: Who was George Herbert?
faq.a: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and Anglican priest who left an aristocrat's path to court to become a humble country parson at Bemerton. His devotional poems, published after his death as "The Temple," and his pastoral manual "The Country Parson" made him the enduring English picture of the devout parish priest. He is remembered less for what he built or won than for what he gave up.

faq.q: What was his background?
faq.a: He was born on 3 April 1593 at Montgomery, in the Welsh Marches, the fifth son of a family near the top of the country's life; his elder brother Edward became a noted philosopher, and his mother Magdalen was a woman of learning and a patron and friend of the poet John Donne. His father died when George was three, and Magdalen raised the children. He went to Westminster School and then Trinity College, Cambridge, becoming a Fellow in 1614 — a young man at home in Latin, music, and the manners of learned men.

fields.name: John Newton
fields.bio: John Newton (1725–1807) was a slave-ship captain who, after a gradual conversion begun in a 1748 Atlantic storm, became an Anglican pastor at Olney, wrote “Amazing Grace,” and — late in life — a leading voice against the slave trade he had once plied, mentoring William Wilberforce.
fields.bio_html:
Almost everyone has sung his most famous line without knowing whose life it describes. “Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me” is not a poet reaching for a strong word. It is a plain report. The man who wrote it had been an infidel, a runaway, a servant of slaves on the African coast, and — this is the part the hymn does not let us skip — a captain of slave ships, carrying human beings chained below his own deck while he kept a pious routine above it. He knew exactly what he meant by a wretch. That is why the line has never worn out.

A mother’s Scripture, and the sea

John Newton was born in London, in the riverside district of Wapping, on 24 July 1725. His mother, Elizabeth, was a devout Dissenter who filled his early childhood with Scripture and hymns and hoped he would grow up to be a minister. She died of consumption in July 1732, when he was not quite seven. It is the first of the losses that shaped him, and the seed she planted lay buried a long time before it grew.

He went to sea at about eleven, sailing with his father, a merchant-ship commander. The boy raised on his mother’s hymns became, over the next years, a hard and profane young man. Around 1743 he was press-ganged into the Royal Navy aboard HMS Harwich. His father’s influence made him a midshipman; his own recklessness undid it. He attempted to desert, was caught, publicly flogged, and reduced to the rank of common seaman — a humiliation in front of the whole ship.

He then got himself transferred into the service of a slave trader, and the descent continued. From about 1745 he lived on the Sierra Leone coast, on the Plantain Islands, in destitution and something close to bondage under a slave-dealer and his African wife. Sick, half-starved, and mistreated, the man who would one day command slave ships was for a season treated almost as a slave himself. He remembered the degradation plainly.

Whenever he left the vessel, I was locked upon deck, with a pint of rice for my day’s allowance.

— John Newton, An Authentic Narrative

This is where his own story becomes useful rather than merely dramatic. Newton did not fall from a great height. He was already at the bottom — mocked, hungry, and by his own later account an enemy of God — when grace began, slowly, to reach him.

The storm off Donegal

The turning point came at sea. On 10 March 1748 — by the old-style calendar he kept all his life — Newton was aboard the merchant ship Greyhound, returning across the Atlantic, when a violent storm struck off the coast of Donegal in Ireland. The ship was nearly torn apart. A sailor was washed overboard and lost. Water poured in faster than the crew could work, and Newton, lashed to the pump through the long hours, did something he had spent years mocking other men for doing. He cried out to God for mercy.

Lashed to the pump of a sinking ship in the dark, a man who had made a sport of ridiculing religion prayed for the first time in earnest — asking the God he did not yet trust to have mercy on him.

The Greyhound did not sink. Newton lived, and he never treated his survival as luck. He kept the anniversary as his spiritual birthday for the rest of his life, and he set it down in his own words.

The 10th (that is in the present style the 21st) of March, is the day much to be remembered by me.

— John Newton, An Authentic Narrative

It would be neat to end the conversion there, and many retellings do. Newton himself was more honest. He always insisted his conversion was gradual, not instantaneous. The storm woke him; deeper conviction came slowly, over years, and one uncomfortable fact stands in the middle of that slow work and refuses to be tidied away.

The captain who kept praying

Newton’s cry for mercy in 1748 did not end his slaving. This is the hard centre of his life, and to soften it is to lose the point of everything he later became. After the storm he continued in the trade — as a mate, and then as captain of slave ships. He commanded the Duke of Argyle in 1750 and the African from 1752 to 1754. On those voyages he kept a devout shipboard routine, holding to religious observance on deck while the cargo he was paid to carry lay chained below. He was, by then, a praying man and a trafficker in human beings at the same time, and he stayed that way for years.

He left the sea around 1754, after a seizure that ended his fitness for such command, and even then he did not immediately renounce the trade — for a time he still had money invested in it. The awakening of his conscience about slavery itself, like his conversion, came gradually and late.

An honest reader has to sit with this rather than explain it away. It is precisely because Newton was not made instantly good that his witness to grace carries such weight. He is not a trophy of a clean rescue. He is evidence that God works on a real person over real time, and that the light can dawn in a heart while great sin still darkens the hands. When he finally understood what he had done, he did not plead that he had meant no harm. He called himself what he had been.

Olney, Cowper, and Amazing Grace

Grace made a minister of him, though the door opened slowly. Newton became tide surveyor at the Port of Liverpool in 1755, and in his spare hours taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and theology. He sought ordination and was at first refused. At last, on 29 April 1764, he was ordained deacon in the Church of England, and priest that June, and sent as curate to the small town of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where he served for some sixteen years.

At Olney he formed one of the great friendships of English letters, with the poet William Cowper. Cowper suffered from severe recurring melancholia and seasons of suicidal despair, and Newton became his close pastor and friend, drawing him into the writing of hymns partly as a kind of therapy for a mind that tormented itself. The two were seldom apart.

I believe … we were not seven hours without being together.

— John Newton, on his friendship with William Cowper

Out of that partnership came the Olney Hymns of 1779, to which Newton contributed around 280 hymns and Cowper about 68 — among them Cowper’s “God moves in a mysterious way.” Newton’s own most enduring hymn had first been sung a few years earlier. He wrote it for a New Year’s Day service on 1 January 1773, to accompany a sermon on King David’s prayer of wonder in 1 Chronicles. He called it “Faith’s Review and Expectation.” The world came to know it by its first two words.

Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me! I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see.

— John Newton, “Amazing Grace,” 1779

Speaking against the trade he had plied

In 1780 Newton became rector of St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, where he preached until near the end of his life. The previous year he had published Cardiphonia; or, The Utterance of the Heart — a celebrated volume of his spiritual letters that carried his warm, searching pastoral voice far beyond any one pulpit.

It was from this later ministry that he did the work for which the world owes him most, apart from the hymn. In 1788 he published Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade, a public confession and eyewitness indictment of the traffic he had once captained. Coming from a former slave-ship commander, it carried a weight no abolitionist theorist could match; he had seen with his own eyes what he now testified against, and he did not spare himself in the telling. That same year he gave evidence before the Privy Council committee examining the trade.

He also shaped the campaign through the men he counselled. When the young, newly-converted William Wilberforce considered leaving politics for the ministry in 1785, it was Newton who urged him to stay in public life. That counsel helped keep Wilberforce in the House of Commons, where he would lead the long parliamentary fight against the trade. The old man mentored the young one, and lived just long enough to see the fruit. The Slave Trade Act abolishing the British slave trade passed in 1807, only months before Newton died.

The captain who had once carried human beings in chains lived to see Parliament outlaw the British slave trade — and had spent his last years telling the truth about it, and steadying the man who carried the fight into law.

Two things he remembered

Newton’s wife, Mary Catlett Newton, died in 1790, and he outlived her by seventeen years. He died in London on 21 December 1807, aged eighty-two. He had directed that no other monument mark him but the words he wrote for himself, and they remain the truest summary of his life — a confession and a thanksgiving in one breath.

John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy.

— John Newton’s self-written epitaph, St Mary Woolnoth

Two sayings cling to his memory from his final years, and honesty requires a word about them. Newton is remembered as saying, “I am not what I ought to be, but by the grace of God I am what I am” — a line true to everything he taught, though it comes down to us through later collections rather than anything he is known to have published. And those who attended him near the end reported a simpler word still, offered when his memory was failing: that he was a great sinner, and Christ a great Saviour. Whether or not the phrasing is exact, no summary of the man could be more faithful.

That is finally why his hymn endures where grander ones have faded. Newton never let anyone, least of all himself, forget what he had been. He did not present a cleaned-up conversion or a hero’s progress. He put “a wretch like me” into the mouth of every singer, and meant it first about the man who had chained others below his own praying deck. The grace he sang about was amazing because he had measured, exactly, how far it reached to find him.

faq.q: What is John Newton best known for?
faq.a: He wrote “Amazing Grace,” whose opening line — “Amazing grace! how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me” — is one of the most sung phrases in the English language. For Newton the word “wretch” was not poetic exaggeration but plain autobiography, since he had been a runaway, a blasphemer, and a captain of slave ships before grace found him. He is remembered, too, as the Anglican pastor and letter-writer who late in life became an outspoken witness against the very slave trade he had once plied.

faq.q: Was John Newton really a slave trader?
faq.a: Yes, and honesty requires facing it squarely. After a wretched season on the African coast — where he was himself half-starved and treated almost as a slave — he rose in the trade, commanding the slave ships Duke of Argyle in 1750 and the African from 1752 to 1754, carrying chained human beings below the same deck on which he kept a devout routine. Troublingly, this continued for years after the 1748 storm that began his conversion; his conscience about slavery itself awakened only gradually and late, which is exactly why his later repentance carried such weight.

faq.q: How did John Newton's conversion begin?
faq.a: On 10 March 1748, aboard the merchant ship Greyhound returning across the Atlantic, Newton was caught in a violent storm off the coast of Donegal that nearly tore the vessel apart. Lashed to the pump through the long hours as water poured in, the man who had made a sport of mocking religion cried out to God for mercy for the first time in earnest. The ship survived, and he kept that date as his spiritual birthday for the rest of his life, writing, “The 10th (that is in the present style the 21st) of March, is the day much to be remembered by me.”

faq.q: Did John Newton become a Christian all at once during that storm?
faq.a: No, and he was careful never to let anyone think so. Newton always insisted his conversion was gradual rather than instantaneous — the storm woke him, but deeper conviction came slowly over years, even as he went on captaining slave ships. He is not a story of a clean, immediate rescue but evidence that God can work on a real person over real time, with the light dawning in a heart while great sin still darkens the hands.

faq.q: How did a former sailor end up a pastor at Olney?
faq.a: After a seizure ended his fitness for command around 1754, Newton became tide surveyor at the Port of Liverpool and taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and theology in his spare hours. He sought ordination in the Church of England and was at first refused, but on 29 April 1764 he was ordained deacon and that June a priest, then sent as curate to the small Buckinghamshire town of Olney, where he served for some sixteen years. In 1780 he moved to become rector of St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, where he preached until near the end of his life.

faq.q: When and why did Newton write “Amazing Grace”?
faq.a: He wrote it for a New Year's Day service at Olney on 1 January 1773, to accompany a sermon on King David's prayer of wonder in 1 Chronicles. He gave it the title “Faith's Review and Expectation,” and only later did the world come to know it by its first two words. It appeared in print in the Olney Hymns of 1779, the collection to which Newton contributed around 280 hymns.

faq.q: What was Newton's friendship with the poet William Cowper like?
faq.a: At Olney, Newton became close pastor and friend to the poet William Cowper, who suffered from severe recurring melancholia and seasons of suicidal despair. The two were seldom apart — Newton once recalled that “I believe … we were not seven hours without being together” — and he drew Cowper into writing hymns partly as therapy for a tormented mind. Their partnership produced the Olney Hymns of 1779, to which Cowper contributed some sixty-eight, including “God moves in a mysterious way.”

faq.q: Did Newton ever speak out against the slave trade he had once profited from?
faq.a: He did, and with a weight no theorist could match. In 1788 he published Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade, a public confession and eyewitness indictment of the traffic he had once captained, and that same year he gave evidence before the Privy Council committee examining the trade. Having seen the horror with his own eyes, he testified against it without sparing himself.

faq.q: What was Newton's role in William Wilberforce's fight against slavery?
faq.a: When the young, newly converted William Wilberforce considered leaving politics for the ministry in 1785, it was Newton who urged him to remain in public life. That counsel helped keep Wilberforce in the House of Commons, where he led the long parliamentary campaign against the trade. Newton lived just long enough to see its fruit: the Slave Trade Act abolishing the British slave trade passed in 1807, only months before he died.

faq.q: What was Newton's marriage to Mary like, and how did his life end?
faq.a: Newton's devotion to his wife, Mary Catlett — whom he called Polly — ran through his whole life, and her death in 1790 left him to outlive her by seventeen years. He died in London on 21 December 1807, aged eighty-two, having directed that no monument mark him but the words he wrote for himself: an epitaph naming him “once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa,” who was “by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy.” Those near him at the end reported a simpler word still — that he was a great sinner, and Christ a great Saviour.

fields.name: Robert Murray M’Cheyne
fields.bio: Robert Murray M’Cheyne (1813–1843) was the minister of St Peter’s, Dundee, remembered for his pursuit of personal holiness and tender pastoral care. He drew up a still-used Bible-reading calendar, joined the 1839 mission of inquiry to the Jews, and died of typhus at 29, mourned by a whole city.
fields.bio_html:
Robert Murray M’Cheyne was a minister for barely seven years and dead at twenty-nine, and yet two centuries of Christians have kept his name in a way they have kept few others of his generation. He wrote no great book. He founded no movement, ran no institution, held no high office. He was the pastor of one parish in one Scottish town, and he did that work with such transparent nearness to God that people who never heard him preach have been changed by reading the record of his life. His friend Andrew Bonar gathered his diary and letters after his death into a Memoir that has never gone out of print, and through it a young man who has been in the grave since 1843 still teaches ministers what they most need and cannot manufacture: holiness.

A brother who could not die

He was born on 21 May 1813 in Edinburgh, the youngest child of Adam McCheyne, a Writer to the Signet — a respectable lawyer of the Scottish capital. He was quick, gifted, musical, and by his own later reckoning careless of the things that mattered most. He went to the High School of Edinburgh and, from November 1827, to the University of Edinburgh, a bright student who was not yet a converted one.

The turn of his life came through a death in his own house. His eldest brother David was devout, and had pleaded with Robert about his soul. On 8 July 1831 David died of a fever. That grief did what all the arguments had not: it woke Robert to his need of grace. Bonar, who knew him, dated the first streaks of dawn in his soul to that year. M’Cheyne himself never forgot the debt. Years later, on the anniversary, he wrote a line in his diary that holds the whole of his conversion in a single breath:

This day eleven years ago, I lost my loved and loving brother, and began to seek a Brother who cannot die.

— Robert Murray M’Cheyne, diary (in Bonar’s Memoir)

A brother who cannot die — that was the discovery, and it reordered everything. In the winter of 1831 he entered the Divinity Hall of the University of Edinburgh under Thomas Chalmers, the towering churchman of the age. He was licensed to preach on 1 July 1835, served as an assistant at Larbert and Dunipace, and on 24 November 1836 was ordained minister of St Peter’s, Dundee — a new parish in a crowded, industrial town. He was twenty-three.

A holy minister is an awful weapon

Dundee was a hard field: mills and closes, poverty and drink, thousands of souls in a young man’s charge. M’Cheyne threw himself into it with a tenderness people remembered for the rest of their lives. He visited the sick and the dying. He preached Christ plainly and directly, more concerned to hold up the Saviour than to display himself. But the engine underneath the ministry was hidden, and it was the thing he cared about most: his own walk with God.

He rose early to pray and to read the Scriptures. He kept a diary of self-examination, watching his own heart with a severity he never turned on others. He prepared for the Sabbath with a seriousness that treated the pulpit as a place a man had no right to enter carelessly. He was convinced — and this is the conviction he is most remembered for — that what his people needed from him was not chiefly his cleverness or his eloquence but his personal holiness; that a pastor’s likeness to Christ was the true instrument God used. He put the principle into words that have followed ministers ever since:

It is not great talents God blesses so much as great likeness to Jesus. A holy minister is an awful weapon in the hand of God.

— Robert Murray M’Cheyne (in Bonar’s Memoir)

He did not aim the demand outward. He aimed it at himself, and his prayers show it. Among the petitions his friends recalled from his letters was one that asked for the only holiness a sinner can honestly ask for — not the sinless perfection of one who never fell, but the cleansing given to one already forgiven:

“I often pray, Lord, make me as holy as a pardoned sinner can be made.” It was the prayer of a man who knew exactly what he was — pardoned, and nothing more — and who wanted every inch of what pardon makes possible.

To a correspondent he distilled the same secret into counsel that has outlived every sermon he preached: Live near to God, and so all things will appear to you little in comparison with eternal realities. That was not a phrase he coined for effect. It was the daily practice of his short life reduced to a sentence.

A harvest gathered while he was away

In 1839 the Church of Scotland sent a small party on a mission of inquiry into the condition of the Jews — to Palestine and the lands of the eastern Mediterranean, to see for themselves and report. M’Cheyne was one of the four, travelling with Andrew Bonar, Alexander Black, and Alexander Keith. He was away from his parish from 12 April to 6 November 1839. The journey was arduous, at times dangerous to his fragile health, and the report the party later published helped launch Scotland’s missions to the Jewish people.

But the great thing that happened in 1839 did not happen to M’Cheyne in Palestine. It happened at St Peter’s, in his absence. He had long prayed and laboured for revival among his people, and it had not come. While he was gone, the pulpit was supplied by William Chalmers Burns, and in August 1839 revival broke out and swept through the town. When M’Cheyne came home in November, he returned not to the parish he had left but to a congregation transformed — awakened, weeping, seeking God in numbers he had prayed for and not seen.

The pastor who had prayed for years to see his people awakened was on the far side of the world when the awakening came. The harvest fell not to the sower’s presence but to his prayers and God’s own timing — and M’Cheyne, far from resenting that another man had reaped it, rejoiced that it had come at all.

There is a lesson in that providence that only a certain kind of man could receive without bitterness. The revival he had begged for arrived under someone else’s preaching while he was hundreds of miles away. He took it as pure gift. A man less near to God would have grieved that it was not his own hand on the harvest; M’Cheyne grieved for nothing and gave thanks.

One of the most enduring things he ever made was one of the simplest. In 1842 he drew up a calendar for reading through the Bible in a year, and had it printed early in 1843 — only months before he died — for his own congregation. He called it Daily Bread. It set four portions for each day: two for family worship and two for private reading, so that over a year a household would read through the Old Testament once and the Psalms and the New Testament twice.

What he wanted was not merely completeness but company. His aim, he wrote in the preface, was a scheme so that the whole Bible might be read once in the year by his people, and all of them might be feeding in the same portion of the green pasture at the same time. It was pastoral to its core — a shepherd wanting his flock to graze together. Two days after the pulpit

His health had never been strong, and Dundee in 1843 was visited by an epidemic of typhus. M’Cheyne would not stay away from the sick. He went on visiting the fever-stricken among his people, and he caught the disease from them. Two days after preaching on 12 March 1843 he was seized with fever. He never recovered. He died on 25 March 1843, weeks short of his thirtieth birthday.

The grief of the town was extraordinary. He was buried on 30 March in the churchyard of St Peter’s, and some seven thousand people came. A minister of one parish, dead before thirty, mourned as though the whole of Dundee had lost a son — which, in a way, it had.

Live near to God, and so all things will appear to you little in comparison with eternal realities.

— Robert Murray M’Cheyne, in a letter (in Bonar’s Memoir)

The life that outlived him

The year after his death, Andrew Bonar published the Memoir and Remains of the Rev. Robert Murray M’Cheyne, weaving together a life-sketch with M’Cheyne’s own diary and letters. It became one of the most influential Christian books of the nineteenth century, printed in well over a hundred English editions and carried across the world. Through it, a ministry of seven years reached lengths it could never have reached had M’Cheyne lived to be old.

That is the strange arithmetic of his story. He accomplished, by the ordinary measures, very little — one parish, a few years, a bundle of letters, a Bible-reading calendar, and an early grave. Yet he is remembered where far busier men are forgotten, because what he offered God was not achievement but himself: a heart kept near, watched, cleansed, and given wholly to the work of loving a town into the presence of Christ. He believed that a holy minister was an awful weapon in the hand of God, and he made his own life the proof of it. The brother he lost sent him seeking a Brother who cannot die; having found him, he spent the little time he had making that Brother known — and then, at twenty-nine, went to be with him.

fields.name: Christmas Evans
fields.bio: Christmas Evans (1766–1838) was the greatest of the Welsh preachers — a poor, self-taught farm laborer, blinded in one eye by an assault in his youth, who became known as the “Bunyan of Wales.” For more than thirty years he oversaw the scattered Baptist churches of Anglesey on a stipend of £17 a year, preaching to thousands in vivid, dramatic open-air sermons. His ministry was revived after a famous covenant with God below Cadair Idris.
fields.bio_html:
Christmas Evans was born on Christmas Day, the 25th of December, 1766, in a low thatched cottage at Esgair-wen, near Llandysul in Cardiganshire, Wales. The day gave him his name. It gave him almost nothing else. His parents, Samuel and Joanna Evans, were poor — his father a shoemaker — and when Christmas was nine years old his father died, and the boy was passed to the keeping of an uncle who worked him hard and taught him nothing. He grew up a farm servant, moved from place to place, exposed to rough company and rougher habits, and at seventeen he still could not read a single word, in Welsh or in English. Few lives that God would one day fill to overflowing began so empty.

The filling began in a revival. Somewhere about his seventeenth year the young laborer was drawn into the congregation of David Davies, a Presbyterian minister at Llwynrhydowen, and there, under plain and searching preaching, he was converted. Hungry now to read the Book that had wakened him, he learned his letters as a grown youth, borrowing what light and what pages he could, and made such astonishing progress that within a year or two he was reading Welsh and English and reaching after more. A single eye did all this labor. For while he was still young, a band of youths who bore him a grudge set upon him on the road at night and beat him until he lay senseless; one of them struck him a blow on the left eye that destroyed its sight for the rest of his life. Wales would come to know him as "the one-eyed preacher," and the scarred, half-blind face became one of the most loved in the land.

He never stopped teaching himself, and the wonder of it grew with the years. Books were scarce and dear, and Evans gathered his learning piecemeal, late, and against every disadvantage, yet he pressed at last into the original languages of Scripture. "I was about forty years old," he wrote, "when I learned to read the Hebrew Bible and the Greek Testament, and use Parkhurst's Lexicons in both languages." What he took in he gave out again in the one tongue his hearers loved; the pulpit, never the study, was where all his learning caught fire.

He could not keep the gospel to himself. Coming to Baptist convictions, he was baptized and began to preach, and after early labors in the wild peninsula of Lleyn he crossed, in 1791, to the island of Anglesey. There he settled for more than thirty years as the overseer of its scattered Baptist churches — a bishop in all but stipend, for the pay was a pittance and the roads were long, and he walked or rode them in every weather to preach. It was here that his extraordinary gift came to its height. He preached in the open air to thousands, in the surging, singing cadence the Welsh call the hwyl, and he preached in pictures: whole sermons built as one unfolding scene. His most famous, The Fall and Recovery of Man, tells the entire gospel as a single drama of ruin and rescue, and it earned him a title he has never lost — the Bunyan of Wales.

The secret of it, all who heard him agreed, was an imagination of rare power harnessed wholly to the truth. He did not decorate his sermons with images; he thought in them, until doctrine became landscape and the hearer found himself standing inside the scene. Under such preaching whole congregations were, in the words of his own journals, melted down in tenderness — weeping and crying out together, so that one might suppose the entire assembly, male and female, was dissolved by the gospel, as the word of God became to them "a sharp two-edged sword."

But the gift did not exempt him from the winter of the soul. In the early years of the new century a bitter controversy — the cold, hair-splitting spirit its opponents called Sandemanianism — crept into the Welsh churches and into Evans himself. His congregations were divided and thinned; worse, his own heart went dead. He described the season in a single unforgettable phrase: he was "as dry as Gilboa," barren in the pulpit, in the study, and in secret prayer. For a man whose whole power lay in a burning heart, it was a kind of death.

The thaw came on a lonely mountain road, and it came through prayer. Riding from Dolgelley toward Machynlleth and climbing up toward the great peak of Cadair Idris, Evans judged that he ought to pray, however hard and worldly he felt — and he began, in the name of Jesus, without waiting to feel better first.

Climbing toward Cadair Idris with a cold and reluctant heart, he resolved to pray anyway, "however hard I felt my heart, and however worldly the frame of my spirit was." He spent hours on that ascent in secret wrestling with God — weeping, pleading, and naming his churches one by one — until the numbness broke.

What happened on that ascent he never forgot, and it is his own account, from his journal, that gives the scene its power: the fetters loosening, the hardness softening, the very mountains of frost and snow melting within him.

Having begun in the name of Jesus, I soon felt as it were the fetters loosening, and the old hardness of heart softening, and, as I thought, mountains of frost and snow dissolving and melting within me.

— Christmas Evans

He came down from Cadair Idris a thawed man, and there and then he bound himself to God in a solemn written covenant — thirteen articles, each signed with his initials, giving himself, soul and body, to Christ and pleading for his churches. The first of them set the tone of all the rest.

I give my soul and body unto thee, Jesus, the true God, and everlasting life — deliver me from sin, and from eternal death, and bring me into life everlasting.

— Christmas Evans, from his covenant with God

The prayer on the mountain was answered, in his own words, as "a remarkable refreshing from the presence of the Lord." The deadness lifted and the old fire returned, and the awakening he had begged for came down on the churches of Anglesey: within two years his ten preaching stations on the island had grown to twenty, and some six hundred converts were added to the churches under his care.

The later road was not smooth. His wife Catherine, who had shared the poverty and the endless journeys, died in 1823; he married again in his later years. Troubles and misunderstandings at last drew him away from Anglesey, and the aging preacher — who might have been left to rest — took up new charges instead: at Caerphilly, then at Cardiff, and finally at Caernarvon, still preaching, still traveling, still renewing his covenant with God upon his knees. He had entered the ministry with nothing, and he left it with little; but the churches he had watered were many, and the Welsh nation had taken his sermons into its very memory.

Through it all he remained a poor man, and a humble one. His salary on Anglesey was seventeen pounds a year, and for twenty years he never asked for more, having learned with the apostle that "having food and raiment" a servant of Christ may therewith be content. Yet the little he had he gave away — the sight of want, it was said, always opened his purse — and those who had wronged him found him quick to forgive. Cheerful, self-forgetful, and tender toward every kind of distress, he wore his greatness so lightly that a stranger meeting the shabby, one-eyed traveler on a mountain road would never have guessed he had passed the most powerful preacher in Wales.

In the summer of 1838 he was on a preaching tour in South Wales, an old man of seventy-one, when his last illness overtook him at Swansea. Death held no terror for the one-eyed preacher who had so long proclaimed a risen Christ. At the end he repeated a Welsh verse of trust in his Redeemer, and then, as though the journey were merely changing horses, spoke his last words in English.

Good-bye! Drive on!

— Christmas Evans, his last words, 19 July 1838

With that he turned over as if to sleep, and was gone. He was buried at Swansea. He had come into the world with a pauper's portion and no letters at all, and he went out of it as the greatest preacher Wales had produced — a man whose one eye had seen, and had made a whole people see, the glory of the crucified and risen Lord. Long after his death the Welsh still spoke of his sermons as of scenes they had witnessed rather than words they had heard, and they gathered and translated them so that readers who never knew the hwyl might feel a little of its heat. Those printed sermons remain, and in them the mountain-road fire still burns.
