She presided over disputes, gave judgment, and was obeyed; later, in 1905, she took up a similar role at Ikot Obong. A former mill girl, barefoot and plain in speech, ruled on the quarrels of a district because the people had decided they trusted her.

faq.q: How central was prayer to her work?
faq.a: It was the ground of everything. Often gravely ill with the malaria that never left her, frequently alone and worn past what her body could bear, she prayed about everything — her health, her decisions, the dangers she walked into, the food that had to appear when there was none — and rated prayer above the labour it undergirded: "Praying is harder work than doing, at least I find it so, but the dynamic lies that way to advance the Kingdom."

faq.q: What was her testimony of answered prayer?
faq.a: She summed up nearly forty years in one sentence: "My life is one long, daily, hourly record of answered prayer. For physical health, for mental overstrain, for guidance given marvellously... for food provided at the exact hour needed, for everything that goes to make up life and my poor service, I can testify, with a full and often wonder-stricken awe, that I believe God answers prayer." It was not a doctrine held at arm's length but the ledger of a life spent alone in dangerous country and somehow carried through it.

faq.q: How is she remembered?
faq.a: She died on 13 January 1915 at Use, near Itu, of the fever that had hunted her all her life, aged sixty-six; the colonial government gave her a state funeral, and she was mourned across Calabar and Scotland alike. Among the people she had lived with she was Eka Kpukpru Owo — "mother of all the peoples" — a name earned one rescued child and one settled quarrel at a time. She is proof that God does his largest work through the least likely instruments: a poor girl from a Dundee mill, given nothing but nerve, a language, and a habit of prayer.

fields.name: Gladys Aylward
fields.bio: Gladys Aylward (1902–1970) was an English parlourmaid, rejected by the missionary society, who spent her savings to travel overland alone to China in 1930. She ran an inn that told Bible stories and led about a hundred children over the mountains to safety during the Japanese invasion — insisting she was not God’s first choice, only a willing one.
fields.bio_html:
Most people who have heard of Gladys Aylward met her by accident, through a film she came to hate. In 1958 Hollywood turned her life into The Inn of the Sixth Happiness, gave her Ingrid Bergman's face and a love affair she never had, and sent the story around the world. The real woman was a small London parlourmaid who was turned down for the mission field as unteachable, who bought a one-way railway ticket she could barely afford, and who crossed a continent alone to reach a country that had not asked for her. The truth is stranger and better than the film, and it is worth telling straight — beginning with the fact that even the inn's name was wrong. It was not the Sixth Happiness. It was the Eight.

A parlourmaid who would not settle

She was born on 24 February 1902 in Edmonton, in north London, into a working-class family, and went into domestic service in her early teens. She was a parlourmaid — the servant who answers the door and lays the table in another family's house. Her schooling had been undistinguished and her prospects were exactly what her class and era allotted her: a lifetime of other people's rooms.

She became convinced, as a young woman, that God meant her to go to China. It was not a sentimental wish; she acted on it. She applied to the China Inland Mission, the great missionary society of the day, and offered herself for training.

They rejected her. The judgement was that she was unlikely ever to master the Chinese language, given her poor academic record — and there was her age against her too, for she was by then in her late twenties, old to be starting. By every measure the mission used, she was not a candidate. She was a servant with no gift for study who had already, in their eyes, left it too late.

This is the hinge of her whole life, and she never pretended otherwise. She was not the church's first choice for China. She was not its choice at all.

The long way to China, alone

What she did next is the part the film could not improve on, because it needed no improving. Refused the mission's training and the mission's money, she went anyway, and she went the cheapest way there was.

In the autumn of 1930 — on 15 October, not the 1932 that some tellings give — she left London by train, alone, to cross Europe and Siberia overland on the Trans-Siberian Railway. It was a genuinely dangerous route. An undeclared border conflict was under way between the Soviet Union and China, and a lone Englishwoman travelling east into it had no protection at all. She was detained by the Russians along the way, got free of them with the help of local people, and completed the last stages of the journey into China by mule. She arrived with almost nothing.

It is easy to say those sentences quickly. Hold them still for a moment: a parlourmaid who had been told she could not learn the language crossed most of the known world on her own to go and learn it. The mission board had weighed her and found her wanting. She had weighed the call and found it heavier than the verdict.

She made her way to Yangcheng, in the mountainous province of Shanxi, and joined an elderly missionary already at work there, Jeannie Lawson.

The Inn of the Eight Happinesses

The two women hit on a plan that suited the country they were in. Yangcheng sat on a mule-train route, and the muleteers who drove the caravans needed food and a bed for the night. So Lawson and Aylward opened an inn for them — The Inn of the Eight Happinesses. (The 1958 film renamed it the Inn of the Sixth Happiness; the real inn was the Eight.) They fed the muleteers, stabled their animals, and, over the evening meal, told them the stories of the Bible. The men carried both the meal and the stories on to the next town.

When Jeannie Lawson died, Gladys carried the work on alone. She learned the language she had been told she could never learn — well enough that the local Mandarin appointed her a "foot inspector," sending her from village to village to enforce the new ban on the binding of women's feet. It was a government job, and it opened every door in the region to her; where she went to measure feet, she could also speak of Christ. In 1936 she took the step that sealed her belonging: she became a national of the Republic of China. The people gave her a Chinese name, Ai-weh-deh — "The Virtuous One" — and it stuck to her for the rest of her life.

I wasn't God's first choice for what I've done for China. There was somebody else… I don't know who it was — God's first choice. It must have been a man… a well-educated man. I don't know what happened. Perhaps he died. Perhaps he wasn't willing. And God looked down… and saw Gladys Aylward. And God said — "Well, she's willing!"

— Gladys Aylward (a much-repeated recollection of her own)

That is the sound of her whole theology, and it is the honest opposite of self-importance. She did not think herself specially gifted. She thought herself specially available. The gap the mission board had measured so accurately was real; she simply did not believe it was the decisive thing. Willingness was.

Here is a rebuke to everyone who has ever declined a call by pleading unfitness. She agreed she was unfit. She went anyway, on the grounds that God seemed to be reduced to using whoever would actually say yes — and she would.

A hundred children over the mountains

Then came the war. The Japanese invasion reached Shanxi, and by the spring of 1940 the fighting had made Yangcheng deadly and put a price on Gladys Aylward's head. She had gathered a crowd of orphaned and refugee children around her over the years, and now she could not leave them to the war.

So she took them out. With about a hundred children in her care, she set off on foot over the mountains toward Sian — Xi'an — and safety, a journey of roughly twelve days across hard country, including a crossing of the Yellow River. She did it while wounded and increasingly ill; she was carrying typhus by the end of it. This is the exploit her name is now attached to, and its core is solid fact: one woman, a hundred children, the mountains, the river, and no way back.

The most vivid versions of the trek — the snatches of conversation, the perfectly timed rescues — come from Alan Burgess's 1957 book The Small Woman and the film that followed, and they are dramatizations. What her biographers hand down, and it is worth receiving as their account rather than as documented minute-by-minute record, is a march sustained by prayer and small providences: food that appeared, shelter that opened, soldiers who fed and guarded the children, boats found at the river's edge when the children had to cross. Strip away the invented dialogue and the shape that remains is still astonishing — that they nearly all came through.

As her biographers tell it, the journey was carried on prayer for provision and safe passage, and provision kept arriving — a meal, a roof, a guard of soldiers, a boat at the water. No prayer of hers was written down word for word. What is beyond dispute is the result: she brought about a hundred children over the mountains and the Yellow River, and lived, barely, to see them safe.

She reached Sian to find the city closed to refugees. She had to move on again, and then her body finally gave out: she collapsed with typhus, spent and gravely sick, the hundred delivered and their guide undone.

The film she resented, and the end she chose

She recovered, and went on working in China for years. In 1949 she returned to Britain. And it was in Britain, safe at last, that the strangest ordeal of her life caught up with her — her own fame.

Burgess's book made her famous; the 1958 film made her a legend and, in the same stroke, mortified her. The screen version invented a romance for her, complete with love scenes and an ending in which she abandons the orphans to go away with an army officer. There had been a real Colonel Linnan in her life, but the on-screen affair was fiction. She was deeply distressed by it. She felt the love scenes damaged her reputation, and she said plainly that she had never kissed a man. The world had fallen in love with a Gladys Aylward who did not exist, and the real one had to watch.

She did not stay to be a celebrity. In 1958 she settled in Taiwan, where she founded the Gladys Aylward Orphanage and returned to the only work she had ever wanted — small rooms, other people's children, the stories of the Bible told at the day's end. She died there on 3 January 1970, aged sixty-seven.

What she leaves

Gladys Aylward left few of her own words and no famous books. What she left is a life shaped like a single argument, made against the estimate of a mission board that was, by its own reasonable standards, correct.

They were right that she could not pass their examinations. They were right about her age and her schooling. They were wrong about the one thing that turned out to matter, because they were measuring the wrong thing. She could not have told you why God would pass over the well-educated man she imagined and reach down for a parlourmaid. She only knew that when God looked for someone willing, she was there, and she said yes — to the railway, to the mule, to the inn, to the mountains, to the hundred children — every time it cost her something.

She was not the first choice. She was the willing one. It turned out to be the same thing.

fields.name: Evelyn Christenson
fields.bio: Evelyn Christenson (1922–2011) was an American pastor’s wife whose six-month prayer experiment among a handful of reluctant women grew into the bestselling “What Happens When Women Pray” and a worldwide prayer-seminar ministry. Through the loss of four children she made Romans 8:28 her philosophy: “God is not making a mistake.”
fields.bio_html:
Some books are written from a study. Evelyn Christenson’s most famous one was written from a small experiment that nearly did not happen — a handful of reluctant women, asked to pray together and watch what God did, and a pastor’s wife given six months to keep a record. What came out of those six months reached, by the publisher’s reckoning, several million readers. But the more durable thing she left was not a sales figure. It was a way of praying together that ordinary people could actually do, and a single sentence she taught them to pray: Lord, change me.

A pastor’s wife in Minnesota

She was born in 1922. The details devotional readers usually want — where she was born, the maiden name, the schoolroom she grew up in — the reliable record does not preserve, and it is better to admit that than to invent it. What is certain is that her life’s work grew out of an ordinary calling: she was married to a pastor, the Reverend Harold L. Christenson, and her ministry began in and around his church in Minnesota. She was not a celebrity brought in from outside. She was the minister’s wife, doing the unglamorous work of a congregation, when she was handed the assignment that changed everything.

Before that, though, she had already walked through the sorrow that would quietly govern the rest of her teaching.

Four babies, and a settled conviction

Evelyn and Harold lost four children. There were miscarriages and a stillbirth during the war years, and a daughter, Judy, born with spina bifida, who lived only seven months. Three children — Jan, Nancy, and Kurt — grew up. But a mother who has buried four does not arrive at a theology of prayer by way of theory. She arrives at it by way of grief, and either it holds or it does not.

Hers held, and it fastened onto one verse: Romans 8:28, that God works all things together for good to those who love him. She did not treat it as a slogan to soften a loss. She treated it as a decision she had made and would not revisit.

I accepted it from the Lord, and I not only accepted it, but I made it my philosophy.

— Evelyn Christenson, on losing a child (Revive Our Hearts)

And underneath it, the plainer conviction she came back to again and again: God is not making a mistake. It is a hard thing to say over a small grave, and she said it, and meant it, and it became the ground from which she later comforted grieving women for the rest of her life. The teacher who told others what happens when women pray had first learned, in the worst circumstances a mother can face, what happens when a woman keeps trusting God after the answer is no.

The experiment: about eight reluctant women

In 1967 and 1968 her denomination asked her to run an experiment. The brief was simple and a little daunting: gather some women, have them pray together over a set period, and record what actually happened. It was, in effect, six months of praying with a notebook open.

She began with about eight women, and they were reluctant. That detail matters, because it is the opposite of the way these stories are usually told. There was no revival atmosphere, no crowd, no momentum to ride. There were a few ordinary women, unsure about praying aloud in front of one another, agreeing to try for six months.

Eight reluctant women, asked to meet and pray together for half a year and simply write down what God did — not knowing that the notebook they were keeping would become the seed of a worldwide ministry.

What she watched happen over those months became both a method and a message. She saw that when women prayed together honestly — aloud, about real things — God moved, and the women themselves were changed first. The experiment quietly outgrew its own modest terms. From 1968 onward she was leading prayer seminars, and she went on leading them, across the world, for decades.

A denominational assignment that started with a handful of hesitant women became, over more than forty years, a seminar ministry that circled the globe. Evelyn always told it as an answer to prayer rather than an achievement — the women prayed, and God did the rest.

What she taught: praying so anyone can join in

Out of the experiment came the book, What Happens When Women Pray, published in 1975. By the publisher’s figures it reportedly sold over three million copies — a number worth stating cautiously, since such counts come from promotional copy rather than any audit. However it is counted, it was a genuine bestseller, and it carried her method far beyond Minnesota.

The method itself was refreshingly practical. She had noticed something that surprises people when they first hear it: roughly two-thirds of the women in her audiences had seldom or never prayed aloud with another person. The reason was almost never unbelief. It was fear — the fear of praying a long, polished, public prayer in front of others who seemed better at it. So she took that fear apart.

She taught what she called the six S’s of praying together. Pray subject by subject, one thing at a time, so the group stays together instead of scattering. Pray short prayers, and simple ones — no performance, no eloquence required. Make the requests specific, so an answer can actually be recognized when it comes. Leave silent periods, room to listen. And keep the groups small, small enough that no one can hide and no one is on stage.

It was conversational prayer — aloud, subject by subject, everyone welcome. She framed prayer’s parts as praise, thanksgiving, confession, and intercession, and she made each of them something a frightened beginner could do in a sentence. The effect was to hand the practice of shared prayer back to the ordinary Christian who had always assumed it was for someone more qualified.

Lord, change me

Her second great theme arrived in 1977, in a book whose title was its whole argument: Lord, Change Me! Where much prayer runs quietly toward fixing other people, she turned it back on the one praying.

I have discovered through the years that surprising things happen when I pray, ‘Lord, change me — don’t change my husband, don’t change my children, don’t change my pastor, change me!’

— Evelyn Christenson, Lord, Change Me! (1977)

It is a disarming prayer because it removes the escape route. It is far easier to intercede for a difficult husband than to ask God to work on oneself first. Christenson had discovered — in a marriage, a family, a church, and four gravesides — that the prayer God most readily answers is the one that offers him the person praying. Her two books are really one lesson from two sides: what happens when women pray is that, more often than they expect, the woman herself is the first thing that changes.

Other books followed — What Happens When God Answers Prayer, A Time to Pray God’s Way, and more — and she founded United Prayer Ministry in St. Paul, which she led as its president. The teaching stayed the same. Prayer was not a technique for managing God. It was the place where a person was remade.

Around the world, and to the end

By the early 1990s her reach had gone global in a formal way. She served as co-chairperson of the North American Women’s Track of the AD2000 & Beyond Movement, a worldwide evangelism effort, and her Study Guide for Evangelism Praying was distributed in 84 countries and translated into eight languages. Later publicity would inflate those figures; the contemporaneous numbers are impressive enough without help. A woman who had started with eight reluctant friends was now teaching the same simple prayers on nearly every continent.

She kept at it to the end. According to the Revive Our Hearts tribute published at her death, about a month before she died she was still leading people to Christ — at her own assisted-living home, an old woman past the reach of the podium, still doing in a corridor what she had done on platforms for forty years.

In her last month, in an assisted-living home in Minnesota, Evelyn Christenson was still praying people into the kingdom of God — the seminar over, the crowds gone, the work unchanged.

Evelyn Christenson died of heart failure on 1 November 2011, in Minnesota, at the age of eighty-nine. She had outlived her husband and buried four of her children, and she went to her death holding the verse she had chosen over the first of those graves.

She left no dramatic story — no martyrdom, no founding of a great institution. She left something quieter and more usable: permission for ordinary women to pray aloud together without fear, a method simple enough for the most reluctant, and a single sentence that keeps its edge every time it is prayed honestly. Lord, change me. She had prayed it first, and it had.

fields.name: William Carey
fields.bio: William Carey (1761–1834) was an English cobbler and self-taught linguist whose 1792 call to missions helped launch the modern missionary movement. He gave forty years to India at Serampore, translating the Bible into six Indian languages and campaigning against sati, and is remembered as the “father of modern missions.”
fields.bio_html:
He was a shoemaker who never went to university, a man who learned his Greek and Hebrew and Latin at a cobbler's bench with a book propped open beside the leather. He would spend the last forty years of his life in India and never once come home. He would translate the whole Bible into six of India's languages and parts of it into some thirty more, watch a lifetime's manuscripts burn in a single night, bury a son, lose his wife to madness, and wait seven years to see one man believe. William Carey is called the father of modern missions, and the title is deserved. But the more useful thing about him is how ordinary his gifts were, and how far plain perseverance carried them.

The bench and the map

He was born on 17 August 1761 at Paulerspury in Northamptonshire, into a family of weavers. There was no money for education and no expectation of greatness. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a shoemaker at Hackleton, and it was there, mending shoes, that he began the self-teaching that would define him. He taught himself languages at the bench — Latin, then Greek, then Hebrew — reading while his hands worked. He drew a crude map of the world and hung it before him, and covered it with everything he could learn about the peoples of the earth and how few of them had ever heard the gospel.

In 1783 he was baptised as a Baptist. He began to preach, and took a small pastorate at Moulton, where the stipend was so meagre that he kept on cobbling and ran a little school besides to feed his family. This is worth holding onto: the man who would move the church of his century to look outward was, for years, a poor village pastor mending shoes and teaching children their letters, with no platform and no prospects.

What he had instead was a conviction that would not leave him alone. The older ministers of his circle held that if God intended to convert the nations, God would do it without their help. Carey could not accept it. He believed the command of Christ to go and make disciples of all nations still bound Christians as plainly as it had bound the first apostles — and that believing it obliged him to do something about it.

Expect great things

In 1792 he put the argument into print, in a long tract with a longer title: An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens. Its plainness is its power. He surveyed the whole known world, counted its peoples and its religions, and argued — against the caution of his elders — that the Great Commission was not a relic but a standing order, and that Christians were obliged to use ordinary means to obey it.

That same year, on 31 May, he preached a sermon at Nottingham on the text of Isaiah — "Enlarge the place of thy tent" — that would be remembered ever after as the "Deathless Sermon." Its full text has not survived. What has survived is a couplet drawn from it, in two forms. It is most often quoted as "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." But careful scholarship notes that the earliest recorded form was shorter — simply "Expect great things; attempt great things" — and that the familiar "from God" and "for God" appear to be a later expansion. Since the sermon itself is lost, honesty asks us to hold the short form as the likely original and the fuller version as the one tradition has loved. Either way the burden is the same, and it was aimed squarely at men who expected little and attempted less.

For years he pressed the cause on ministers older and more cautious than himself, who thought the whole idea presumptuous. He did not have influence, or money, or standing. He had only a conviction he could not put down and a persistence that would not take a settled no for an answer — and he kept praying, and kept asking, until the door opened.

It opened on 2 October 1792, at Kettering, where Carey and Andrew Fuller and a handful of others founded the Baptist Missionary Society — the first English Protestant missionary society. Carey is remembered as offering the image that became its motto: he would be willing to go down into the mine, if others would hold the ropes. The exact wording varies in the telling, but the arrangement was real. In June 1793 he sailed for India. He reached Calcutta on 11 November 1793. He was thirty-two, and he would never see England again.

The long cost of the work

The early years were brutal, and the hardest of the hardship was at home. Carey's wife, Dorothy, had not wanted to go. She was a countrywoman with young children and no appetite for the far side of the world, and she went unwillingly. In India the family met fever and want. Carey took work superintending an indigo works at Mudnabati to keep them. He fell ill with malaria. Their son Peter died of dysentery at five years old. Under the weight of it all Dorothy's mind gave way. She sank into delusions from which she did not recover, and for years Carey did his enormous labours alongside a wife who was, by every account, seriously and lastingly ill; she was confined for her own safety and died in 1807. It is not a detail to hurry past. The father of modern missions carried his family's grief and his wife's madness through the very years of his greatest work, and the record does not pretend the two were ever reconciled into something tidy.

And the work itself yielded nothing, for a long time. For about seven years there was not a single convert. Seven years of preaching and translating and waiting, with the ledger empty. Then, in December 1800, a Bengali carpenter named Krishna Pal came to faith and was baptised in the river Ganges — the first Bengali believer, the first fruit of all those years.

Seven years of labour without a single soul to show for it, and then Krishna Pal — one Bengali carpenter, baptised in the Ganges in December 1800 — the first of a harvest Carey had begun to fear he would never see. He had told the church to expect great things; here, after long waiting, was the first of them.

Serampore

Because the East India Company was hostile to missionaries, the work found a home at Serampore, a small Danish settlement where it could not be shut down. There Carey was joined by Joshua Marshman, an educator, and William Ward, a printer — the three of them remembered as the "Serampore Trio." From 1801 Carey also held a professorship at Fort William College in Calcutta, teaching Bengali, Sanskrit and Marathi, and turning his salary back into the mission.

What he produced from that base is almost hard to believe. The complete Bible in six Indian languages — Bengali, Oriya, Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Assamese — and portions of Scripture in some twenty-nine more. In his lifetime the Serampore press issued around 212,000 copies of Scripture. He compiled grammars and dictionaries. He was, in the end, not a genius so much as a man who did an astonishing amount of careful work and did not stop.

He put the same doggedness to the service of the vulnerable. He documented and campaigned against sati, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres, and against infanticide. When sati was at last legally banned in Bengal in 1829, the long weight of his advocacy stood behind the reform.

If he gives me credit for being a plodder, he will describe me justly. I can plod. I can persevere in any definite pursuit. To this I owe everything.

— William Carey

Be still

On the night of 11 March 1812 the Serampore printing works caught fire. Manuscripts, a great dictionary, grammars, and irreplaceable type were destroyed — years of labour gone in a few hours. Carey was away when it happened. He is remembered as saying, when he learned of it, "In one short evening the labours of years are consumed. How unsearchable are the ways of God!" — and for the following Sunday he is said to have chosen as his text Psalm 46:10, "Be still, and know that I am God." He did not rage and he did not quit. The work was begun again, and much of it rebuilt within months. The plodder went back to the bench.

A wretched, poor, and helpless worm

Carey died at Serampore on 9 June 1834, aged seventy-two, having laboured in India for four decades. For a man of such achievement, he arranged for his grave the humblest possible words. He chose for his epitaph two lines from the hymns of Isaac Watts, and nothing about missions or translations or reform:

A wretched, poor, and helpless worm, / On thy kind arms I fall.

— William Carey's chosen epitaph, from Isaac Watts

That is the true measure of him. The man who told a cautious church to attempt great things asked to be remembered as a helpless worm falling on the kind arms of God. He had expected great things and attempted them; and at the last he claimed no credit for any of it. He had said as much of himself all along — that he was no genius, only a plodder who could persevere. It is, perhaps, the most hopeful thing about his whole life. What God did through William Carey, God did through an unschooled shoemaker who simply refused to stop.

faq.q: Why is William Carey called the father of modern missions?
faq.a: Carey was an English shoemaker who argued, against the caution of his elders, that Christ’s command to make disciples of all nations still bound Christians and obliged them to use ordinary means to obey it. He put that conviction into print, helped found the first English Protestant missionary society in 1792, and then gave forty years of his own life to India. His example set the modern missionary movement in motion, which is why the title has stuck to him.

faq.q: How did a poor cobbler teach himself Greek and Hebrew?
faq.a: Born in 1761 into a Northamptonshire weaving family with no money for schooling, Carey was apprenticed to a shoemaker at fourteen and taught himself languages at the workbench, propping a book beside the leather and reading while his hands worked. He learned Latin, then Greek, then Hebrew this way. He also hung a homemade map of the world before him and filled it with everything he could learn about the peoples of the earth and how few had heard the gospel.

faq.q: What was Carey’s “Enquiry,” and how did the Baptist Missionary Society begin?
faq.a: In 1792 Carey published a tract titled An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, surveying the world’s peoples and arguing that the Great Commission was a standing order rather than a relic. That October, at Kettering, he and Andrew Fuller and a few others founded the Baptist Missionary Society, the first of its kind in England. Carey is remembered for offering its guiding image: he would go down into the mine if others would hold the ropes.

faq.q: How long did Carey wait before he saw his first convert in India?
faq.a: He reached Calcutta in November 1793 at the age of thirty-two, and for roughly seven years of preaching and translating there was not a single convert. Then, in December 1800, a Bengali carpenter named Krishna Pal came to faith and was baptised in the river Ganges, the first Bengali believer. Carey had told the church to expect great things, and after long waiting Krishna Pal was the first of them.

faq.q: How much of the Bible did Carey manage to translate?
faq.a: Working from the Danish settlement of Serampore alongside the educator Joshua Marshman and the printer William Ward, Carey helped produce the complete Bible in six Indian languages, including Bengali, Sanskrit and Marathi, and portions of Scripture in some twenty-nine more. He also compiled grammars and dictionaries and taught at Fort William College in Calcutta, turning his salary back into the mission. In his lifetime the Serampore press issued around 212,000 copies of Scripture.

faq.q: How did Carey respond when fire destroyed years of his work?
faq.a: On the night of 11 March 1812 the Serampore printing works burned, consuming manuscripts, a great dictionary, grammars and irreplaceable type, the labour of years gone in a few hours. Carey did not rage and did not quit; he is remembered for calling it unsearchable in the ways of God and for turning back to the bench, with much of the work rebuilt within months. He had long described himself not as a genius but as a plodder who could persevere, and here that was tested.

faq.q: What was the cost of the mission to Carey’s own family?
faq.a: His wife Dorothy had not wanted to leave England and went unwillingly, and in India the family met fever, poverty and grief, losing their five-year-old son Peter to dysentery. Under that weight Dorothy’s mind gave way; she sank into delusions from which she never recovered and was confined for her own safety until her death in 1807. Carey carried on his enormous labours through those same years, and the record does not pretend the suffering was ever tidied away.

faq.q: Did Carey do anything to stop the burning of widows?
faq.a: Yes. He documented and campaigned for years against sati, the burning of widows on their husbands’ funeral pyres, as well as against infanticide, presenting petitions to the government to have such practices ended. When sati was legally banned in Bengal in 1829, Carey, who served as a government translator, had the task of rendering the new regulation into Bengali and worked quickly, believing lives depended on every hour’s delay.

faq.q: How did Carey want to be remembered when he died?
faq.a: He died at Serampore on 9 June 1834, aged seventy-two, after four decades in India without ever returning home. For a man of such achievement he chose the humblest possible grave, asking for no mention of missions or translations but only two lines from the hymns of Isaac Watts: “A wretched, poor, and helpless worm, on thy kind arms I fall.” The man who told a cautious church to attempt great things asked at the last to be remembered as a helpless worm falling on the kind arms of God.

fields.name: David Livingstone
fields.bio: David Livingstone (1813–1873) was a Scottish mill boy turned missionary-explorer of Africa who crossed the continent, exposed the East African slave trade as “the open sore of the world,” and died on his knees in what is now Zambia. Famous as an explorer, he counted almost no converts — and that honest tension is part of what makes his devotion so striking.
fields.bio_html:
There is a difficulty at the centre of David Livingstone’s life, and it is better to set it down at the start than to smuggle it in later. He is remembered as the greatest missionary Africa ever received — his name on schools and hospitals and a town, his body in Westminster Abbey, his face on a stained-glass shorthand for Christian heroism. And in more than thirty years on that continent, the record shows him bringing exactly one African to baptism: a chief named Sechele, in 1849, who afterwards lapsed. One convert. It is an astonishing figure for a man of his reputation, and any honest account has to begin there, because the gap between the legend and the ledger is where the real man is found.

He was the explorer who overshadowed the missionary. He knew it himself. And yet he is worth remembering — not in spite of the failure but partly because of it, and because of what he did with his fame once he had it: he spent it, to the last coin, denouncing the slave trade he called the open sore of the world.

A boy on the spinning jenny

He was born on 19 March 1813 in Blantyre, near Glasgow, the second of seven children in a single room above a cotton mill. It was not poverty of the romantic kind. From the age of ten he worked the mill as a “piecer,” tying broken threads from six in the morning until eight at night, and went to school afterwards, and studied late into the night when a grown man would have slept. The picture most often repeated of him — a book propped open on the spinning frame so he could snatch a line of Latin between passes of the machine — belongs to that tradition of the self-taught poor boy, and whether or not it happened exactly so, it tells the truth about him. He was relentless. He would be relentless all his life, at everything, including the things that did not work.

Out of that mill he made himself a doctor and a minister. He studied medicine and theology in Glasgow, was accepted by the London Missionary Society, and was ordained in November 1840. He sailed for Africa that same month and reached the Cape in 1841. In 1845 he married Mary Moffat, the daughter of the missionary Robert Moffat — a woman who would pay a heavy price for the marriage, as the wives of restless men often do.

Christianity, commerce, and the road forward

His first stations were at Mabotsa, Chonuane, and Kolobeng. It was near Mabotsa, early on, that a lion mauled him and left his left arm crippled for the rest of his life — an injury that, by a grim providence, would one day help identify his body. But the settled work of a mission station could not hold him. Something in him always looked north, to the interior no European had mapped, and he began the long journeys that made him famous: the crossing of the continent, and in 1855 the great falls of the Zambezi that the people who lived there called Mosi-oa-Tunya, “the smoke that thunders.” He renamed them for his queen. That renaming is, in miniature, the whole tangle of his life — genuine wonder and imperial reflex in the same gesture.

He had a theory, and he believed it with all his force. He thought that Christianity, commerce, and civilization, brought together, could open the interior and starve out the Arab-Swahili slave trade that was bleeding East Africa. Legitimate trade would make the trade in human beings unprofitable; the Gospel would follow the roads that trade opened. Modern readers see more clearly than he did how tightly that programme was wound around the machinery of empire, and it is only honest to say so — the paths he opened were walked by others with colder motives. But it would be a lie to reduce his anti-slavery conviction to a cover story. He had seen the slave routes with his own eyes, the chained lines and the bodies left in them, and what he wrote about them was not policy. It was grief.

I go back to Africa to try to make an open path for commerce and Christianity; do you carry out the work which I have begun?

— David Livingstone, Cambridge, December 1857

That appeal, made to the young men of Cambridge, helped bring the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa into being. It is characteristic of him: the greatest fruit of his missionary life may be less the souls he counted than the labourers he sent — a call passed to others to carry out the work he had begun and largely not finished.

The cost, and the failures

The Zambezi expedition of 1858 to 1864 is generally judged a failure. The river he had staked so much on turned out to be unnavigable, blocked by rapids he had not known were there; the expedition was expensive, quarrelsome, and returned little of what it had promised. And it took from him the person who had followed him longest. Mary Livingstone died of malaria on the Zambezi on 27 April 1862. He had dragged his family across a continent in his wake, and his children had grown up largely without him, and now the wife who had borne all of it was buried in African ground far from home.

Here is a life to set beside the legend. One convert, and that one lapsed. A river expedition that failed. A wife dead of fever in the work. Children who barely knew their father. If we are to call this man great, we had better be clear-eyed about what greatness cost and what it did not achieve, or we make his faith into something no ordinary believer could recognise. He was not a man crowned with success. He was a man who kept going forward through failure after failure because he had decided, early and once, which direction his life would face.

…in readiness to go anywhere, provided it be forward.

— David Livingstone, in a letter to the London Missionary Society

The polished version carved on memorials — “I am prepared to go anywhere, provided it be forward” — is a tidying of his actual words, but the direction is exactly right. Forward was the only setting he had.

Lost, and found

His last expedition, begun in 1866, was a search for the source of the Nile, and it swallowed him. For years he was out of contact, feared dead, wandering sick and destitute through country no letter could reach. He ran out of medicine and supplies and, at times, out of everything but the men who stayed with him. In November 1871 the journalist Henry Morton Stanley, sent by an American newspaper to find him or confirm his death, reached the lakeside town of Ujiji and came upon the one worn-out white man in that place.

The greeting Stanley reported — four words that have outlived almost everything else about either man — comes to us through Stanley’s account alone, and it is fair to hold it as the words he recorded rather than a thing independently confirmed:

Dr Livingstone, I presume?

— the greeting as Henry Morton Stanley recorded it, Ujiji, November 1871

Stanley brought supplies, and companionship, and pressed him to come home. He would not. The sick old man turned back inland to keep looking for a river’s source he would never find. Forward, again — even when forward was plainly the wrong medical decision. It is hard to know whether to call that faith or obstinacy. In him the two were never fully separable.

The open sore of the world

If one thing redeems the tangle of his ambitions, it is what he never stopped saying about slavery. He had watched it, close, for decades, and it never became abstract to him. On his last journeys, still ill, still failing, he kept writing against it, and the phrase he reached for was a wound that would not close.

“All I can add in my solitude is, may Heaven’s rich blessing come down on every one — American, English, or Turk — who will help to heal this open sore of the world.”

It reads like a policy note and it is really a prayer — a dying man’s petition, offered in solitude, for anyone of any nation who would help end the traffic in human beings. Those words are carved on his memorial in Westminster Abbey, and of all the sentences he left, they are the ones most worth keeping. This was the true burden of his heart, clearer at the end than any map he ever drew.

The last morning

He died on 1 May 1873 at the village of Chief Chitambo, near the Bangweulu swamps in what is now Zambia, worn out by dysentery and malaria. The scene that has been handed down — that his attendants found him in the early morning kneeling at his bedside as if in prayer, his head resting on his hands — comes from the report of the two African men who were with him to the end, Susi and Chuma, and it reached the wider world shaped by Victorian editors who knew a good ending when they saw one. It should be held as their treasured testimony and the church’s cherished tradition, not as a thing any of us can prove.

Those who were with him remembered finding him at daybreak on his knees at the side of his bed, his face in his hands — a man of relentless motion, still at last in the posture of prayer. So the account most often repeated has it, from the two who loved him best.

What is not in doubt is what those two men did next, and it may be the plainest sermon in the whole story. Susi and Chuma buried his heart under a tree in the African soil he had given his life to, and then carried his body roughly a thousand miles to the coast — a journey of some nine months — so that it could be sent home. His crippled arm, the lion’s old work, confirmed that the body was his. He was interred in Westminster Abbey. The one convert of record was a chief who fell away; but two African friends carried him a thousand miles, and that is its own kind of testimony to the man they had followed.

Why he is worth remembering

Livingstone left a motto often attributed to him — “Fear God and work hard” — and it is honest to say that the working hard is easier to document than the fruit. He converted almost no one. His grand programme was entangled with an empire that did not share his heart. His great expedition failed and his wife died in it and his children grew up without him. If we wanted a tidy hero we would have to choose someone else.

But he is the better witness precisely because he is not tidy. His life says that faithfulness is not the same as success, that a man may pour himself out and see almost nothing he hoped for, and be, all the same, not wasted. His deepest work was not the souls he failed to number but the conscience he stirred — the young men he sent, the trade he shamed, the wound he named and would not let the comfortable forget. He went forward when going forward cost him everything and gained him, in his own accounting, very little. And at the end, if the tradition his friends handed down is true, a man who had never learned to be still was found kneeling.

Fear God and work hard.

— a motto long attributed to David Livingstone

faq.a: David Livingstone was born in 1813 into a single room above a Blantyre cotton mill, and from the age of ten he worked the spinning machines as a “piecer,” tying broken threads from six in the morning until eight at night. It caused a sort of dreaminess, in which there is no sense of pain nor feeling of terror.” By a grim providence, that old wound would one day help confirm that the body carried home from Africa was truly his.

fields.name: Pandita Ramabai
fields.bio: Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) was a Sanskrit scholar of Brahmin birth, orphaned by famine, who became a Christian and gave her life to India’s abandoned women. Her faith-supported Mukti Mission sheltered and educated thousands of child-widows and orphans, and she translated the whole Bible into Marathi from the original languages.
fields.bio_html:
She was one of the most learned women India had ever produced — a Sanskrit scholar honoured with titles that few men held, a reformer who argued for the widows and child-brides of her country before audiences on three continents, and, at the end of her life, the translator of the whole Bible into her mother tongue. And she came to all of it from grief. Pandita Ramabai lost her father, her mother, and her sister to starvation before she was twenty, walked thousands of miles across a famine-struck land, buried a husband after sixteen months of marriage, and was left, in her own words, alone to face the world with one baby in her arms. What she built out of that loss still stands and still feeds and shelters the poor today.

A scholar born in a forest

She was born on 23 April 1858, not in any city but in a forest home high on a peak of the Western Ghats, the mountains that run down the western edge of India. Encyclopedias have loosely placed her birth near Mangalore, but her own account is of a hermitage in the hills, and it is worth keeping her version. Her father, Anant Shastri Dongre, was an orthodox Sanskrit scholar with one deeply unorthodox conviction: that women could learn. Against the custom of his caste and time, he taught his wife the sacred language, and his wife in turn taught Ramabai, from about the age of eight to fifteen, until the girl had committed thousands of verses of Hindu scripture to memory.

That education was the making of her. When she came to Calcutta as a young woman and was examined by the pandits there, they conferred on her in 1878 two titles that measured what she had become — Pandita, the learned, and Sarasvati, after the goddess of wisdom. She was barely twenty, a woman, and reckoned among the scholars of the land.

Orphaned by famine, widowed young

But the years that gave her those titles had already taken almost everything else. Between 1876 and 1878 a great famine swept the country, and it fell on her family without mercy. Her father, her mother, and her elder sister all died of starvation. She and her brother were left to wander — by her own reckoning more than four thousand miles across India, on foot, homeless and hungry, watching a nation die around them. Her brother, too, would later die, and she was alone.

In November 1880 she married. It was a bold step: a civil marriage across caste lines to a Bengali lawyer, Bipin Behari Medhavi — the kind of union her father's world would have forbidden. A daughter, Manorama, was born the next year. And then, in February 1882, her husband died of cholera. The marriage had lasted sixteen months. She was twenty-three, twice-widowed of the family she had known, and now left, as she put it, alone with one baby in her arms.

It would have been enough to end most people. In Ramabai it lit a determination. She had seen with her own eyes what her country did to its widows and its unwanted girls, and she resolved to spend her life for them.

Finding the religion, and then finding Christ

Her path to Christ was neither sudden nor simple, and it is important not to flatten it into a single moment. In early 1883 she travelled to England, helped by the Sisters of Wantage, an Anglican community, and later that year she was baptized in the Church of England. By any outward measure she had become a Christian.

But Ramabai herself drew a careful line between what happened in 1883 and what happened years afterward. The baptism was, she came to feel, an act of the mind — she had found the Christian religion, its truth and its arguments, but she had not yet found Christ. That deeper turning came around 1891, a conversion not of the intellect but of the heart. The two were different, and she never pretended otherwise. It is one of the most honest things about her: a woman of formidable learning admitting that learning had carried her only to the doorstep, and that she had to be brought the rest of the way.

Between the two came America. From 1886 to 1888 she lectured across the United States, published a searing book, The High-Caste Hindu Woman, in 1887, and read. Among the books she read were the lives of Hudson Taylor and George Müller — and Müller in particular, the man of Bristol who fed thousands of orphans on prayer alone and kept no endowment, marked her permanently. She had found her model. Whatever she built would be built the same way: by asking God, and not man, for the bread.

Sharada Sadan and the road to Mukti

Back in India, she opened Sharada Sadan in 1889, a home and school for high-caste child-widows — girls married as infants, widowed before they understood the word, and then treated as bad luck for the rest of their lives. It was a beginning, but the work that would define her came out of another catastrophe.

When famine struck again in 1896 and 1897, Ramabai did not wait for the destitute to reach her. She went to them. She toured the stricken villages with a caravan of bullock carts, gathering up the children nobody wanted — outcast girls, child-widows, orphans, women left with nothing — and carrying them back to safety. She acquired land at Kedgaon, some forty miles east of Pune, and there she raised the Mukti Mission. Mukti means salvation, and the name was exact: it was a place of rescue.

The scale of it was astonishing. By 1900 something like fifteen hundred to two thousand people lived at Mukti. They were fed, housed, and educated; they were taught to teach, to nurse, to weave, to stand on their own. It was open to every caste, which in that society was itself a quiet revolution. And it was carried, as she had determined it would be, on prayer.

We are happy, getting our daily bread directly from the loving hands of our Heavenly Father, having no banking account anywhere, no endowment or income from any earthly source, but depending altogether on our Father God. The Lord is our Inexhaustible Treasure.

— Pandita Ramabai, A Testimony of Our Inexhaustible Treasure (1907)

Fifteen hundred and more mouths to feed at Kedgaon, and no bank account, no endowment, no earthly income behind them — only the daily asking of God for the daily bread. Year after year it came. She had read George Müller and believed his God was her God too, and the crowded, thriving mission was her answer.

It was not a boast; it was a report. She had put God to the test she found in Scripture and staked hundreds of lives on the result.

I have responded to the Lord's challenge, "Prove Me now," and have found Him faithful and true. I know He is a prayer-hearing and prayer-answering God.

— Pandita Ramabai, A Testimony of Our Inexhaustible Treasure (1907)

The revival of 1905

By her own testimony, the great spiritual awakening at Mukti did not fall out of a clear sky. It was prayed down. At the beginning of 1905 she gathered a band of about seventy who met every morning to ask God for one thing above all others — the true conversion of India's Christians, herself first among them, and a fresh outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

Around seventy of them met each morning through the early months of 1905, praying for the true conversion of all the Indian Christians, including themselves, and for a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit — a prayer-circle set going deliberately, and kept.

The prayer band grew, and in the middle of that year the answer came. In her account, within about six months the Lord sent a glorious Holy Spirit revival among them — confession, weeping, joy, and changed lives spreading through the mission. It came in June 1905, before the events at Azusa Street in America with which the wider Pentecostal awakening is usually dated; that is a matter of chronology and not of cause, and Ramabai claimed nothing for it but that God had heard her praying women.

The whole Bible in Marathi

Her last great labour was the quietest and, in some ways, the largest. Ramabai wanted the women of India to be able to read the Word of God for themselves, in their own ordinary speech. So she taught herself Greek and Hebrew and set out to translate the entire Bible into Marathi — not from another translation, but from the original languages, into the plain colloquial tongue a village woman could understand.

It took her some fifteen years. She was still checking the final pages as her health failed. It is the fruit of a life that trusted the book completely, and it grew straight out of the conviction she had proved a hundred times over at Kedgaon.

I have come to believe the Word of God implicitly, and I have found out by experience, that it is true.

— Pandita Ramabai, A Testimony of Our Inexhaustible Treasure (1907)

What she leaves

Her daughter Manorama, her helper and successor, died in 1921, a grief the old woman felt to the depths. Ramabai followed her a few months later, dying of septic bronchitis at Kedgaon on 5 April 1922, just short of her sixty-fourth birthday. The Marathi Bible she had all but finished was published soon afterward.

The shape of her life had a strange symmetry. It began in the mountains with a father who dared to teach his daughters, and it ended with a woman handing her daughters — thousands of them, gathered off the famine roads — a Bible they could read. She had once written that the Lord's own question stopped her in her tracks: when she wished someone would care for India's destitute women, she heard the Still Small Voice ask why she did not begin the work herself instead of wishing others would. She began it. She never stopped.

Pandita Ramabai was not a martyr and not a theologian. She was a scholar whom grief drove to the poor, and the poor to Christ. She left behind a mission that still feeds and teaches the outcast at Kedgaon, a Bible in the hands of ordinary women, and a plain, tested testimony that the God who says Prove Me now can be taken at His word.

fields.name: C. T. Studd
fields.bio: C. T. Studd (1860–1931) was an England cricketer who, after his conversion, gave away a fortune and joined the “Cambridge Seven” as a missionary — serving in China, India, and finally the Congo, where he founded what became WEC. A man of fierce, uncompromising, and at times difficult zeal, he lived by the conviction that no sacrifice could be too great for Christ.
fields.bio_html:
In the summer of 1882, a young Englishman walked out to bat for his country at The Oval in the Test match that would give cricket its most famous name. When England lost, a mock obituary announced the death of English cricket and declared that the body would be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia — and so “the Ashes” were born. Charles Thomas Studd was among the best all-rounders England had. Within three years he had walked away from all of it: the fame, the game, and a family fortune, to sail for China as a missionary. He spent the rest of his life spending it, and he died in the heart of Africa at seventy, still refusing every half-measure — a man his own colleagues found as difficult as he was heroic.

A gentleman’s son

He was born on 2 December 1860 at Spratton, in Northamptonshire, into money. His father, Edward Studd, was a retired planter who had made a fortune in India and lived the life of an English country gentleman — horses, comfort, and no particular religion. Charles went to Eton, where he captained the cricket eleven at nineteen, and then to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took his degree in 1883 and became a star of the university game. By every measure his world used, he had arrived before he was old enough to have earned it.

The turn came through his father. In 1877 Edward Studd was converted during the great Moody and Sankey campaign that swept Britain, and the change in him was total. He began pressing the gospel on his sons with the same energy he had once given to sport. In 1878, at eighteen, Charles was converted too.

Then almost nothing happened. For roughly six years he was, by his own later account, a Christian in name and cold in fact — his faith a private matter that changed little and cost less. Cricket was still his life. It is an honest and useful stretch of the story: conversion had not yet become consecration, and he knew the difference only in hindsight.

The Cambridge Seven

What broke the coldness was, first, a death that did not come. In 1884 his brother George fell seriously ill, and standing at what might have been a deathbed Studd found the questions he had been avoiding: what was all his fame worth, if a man could be gone so quickly? Around the same time he heard D. L. Moody preach again, and the zeal of his conversion returned with force. This time it did not stay private. He offered himself as a missionary.

In 1885 he sailed for China with Hudson Taylor’s China Inland Mission, and he did not go alone. Six other privileged young Cambridge men went with him — athletes, an officer, men with prospects — and the group became famous across Britain as the Cambridge Seven. Their departure was deliberately publicized to stir the nation’s conscience about missions, and it worked: that seven men who could have had anything England offered would instead give it up for China was a sensation.

Studd gave up more than a career. Coming into his inheritance, he gave nearly all of it away — a sum variously reported at £25,000–29,000, an immense fortune for the time. He directed large gifts to Moody’s work in Chicago, to George Müller’s orphanages, to George Holland’s mission in Whitechapel, to the Salvation Army’s work in India, and to other causes. He kept back a modest sum for his future wife; the account most often repeated says that she told him to give that away too, so that they might begin married life with nothing but God to depend on. Whether the words fell exactly so, the pattern of the marriage bore it out.

If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him.

— C. T. Studd

That sentence is the key to everything he did and everything he got wrong. He believed it without qualification, and he never learned to let other people believe it at a different pace.

China, marriage, and India

He spent about ten years in China. There he married Priscilla Livingstone Stewart, a fellow missionary, in 1888; four daughters would survive. The Studds worked in the interior in the plain, hard conditions the China Inland Mission expected of its people, and by every sign they were happy in it. But his health, never robust under the strain he imposed on it, broke down, and in 1894 illness forced the family back to England.

He was not built for rest. After a period of deputation work he took a pastorate at Ootacamund, in the hills of southern India, serving there roughly from 1900 to 1906 among English-speaking residents and soldiers. It was quieter work than China, and it was not what his heart was set on. He had begun to think about the parts of the world where no missionary had gone at all.

The heart of Africa

What seized him was central Africa — vast regions he believed had never heard the gospel and had no one on the way to bring it. He was over fifty, his health was poor, and the doctors told him plainly that he must not go. He went anyway.

He had given away a fortune, buried the ambition of a national sporting hero, and worn out his body in China and India. Now, past fifty and against medical advice, he offered God the last thing he had left — the years of an old and sick man — and asked to spend them where no one else would.

In 1913 he founded the Heart of Africa Mission and set out for the Belgian Congo. The work grew, and in time it became the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade — WEC — one of the notable interdenominational missions of the century, which long outlived him. He spent roughly eighteen years in the Congo, latterly based at Ibambi, preaching, planting churches, and driving himself and everyone near him without mercy. The fruit was real and it endured. So did the cost, and honesty requires that the cost be named.

Some wish to live within the sound of church or chapel bell; I want to run a rescue shop within a yard of hell.

— C. T. Studd

Heroic and divisive

The same absolutism that made Studd give away everything made him very hard to work with. His Congo years were plagued with conflict — with fellow missionaries, with his family, and painfully with his own son-in-law, Alfred Buxton, who had once been his closest partner in the field. Missionaries left or were dismissed; those who could not match his ferocity were made to feel they had failed. He has been described soberly, and not by enemies, as an obstinate and unreasonable leader. His late tract The Chocolate Soldier, a blast against soft, comfortable Christianity, captures the militant, no-half-measures spirit that both fuelled the mission and wounded the people inside it. In his last years the home committee moved to remove him from the leadership of the work he had founded.

There was a darker strand still. In his final years, worn by illness and pain, Studd kept an increasingly harsh personal asceticism, and he used morphine regularly for his suffering — a fact that was documented in his lifetime and caused controversy then. It should be neither hidden nor sensationalized. He was an old, sick man in a punishing climate, and the discipline that had once been a gift had hardened into something that hurt him and those around him. A saint is not a man without faults; he is a man whose faults God does not waste.

This is where the reverent thing to do is to tell the truth. Studd was heroic. He was also difficult, rigid, and, at the end, in some measure broken by his own severity. Both are true at once, and the second does not cancel the first. The gospel he preached does not require its heralds to be flawless — only to be forgiven, and to press on.

Only one life

He died at Ibambi on 16 July 1931, at seventy, of untreated gallstones — refusing, to the last, the care his body needed. Those who told the story afterward remembered his final word as “Hallelujah,” and it may well have been; but it belongs to the tradition around him rather than to the certain record, and it is enough to say that he died as he had lived, in the field, at his post.

Among the words most loved by him and long associated with his name is a couplet he sent to his grandchildren in a farewell letter in that last year:

Only one life, ’twill soon be past; only what’s done for Christ will last.

— lines beloved by Studd (authorship debated)

The full poem’s authorship is genuinely uncertain, and it would be wrong to hand it to him without that caution. But he quoted those two lines to his own grandchildren as he neared the end, and no words could more exactly sum up the account of his years. They are his in the only sense that finally mattered to him: he had believed them all the way down.

He asked God for a life poured out with nothing held back, and he received it. There was no single miracle to point to — the answer was the shape of the whole life. A fortune given away, three continents worn out for the gospel, and a mission still carrying the good news across the world nearly a century after he was buried under the Congo soil.

What he leaves

C. T. Studd left no comfortable legacy and no tidy one. He left a worldwide mission, thousands who heard the gospel because he would not stay home, and a life so extreme that admirers and critics have never quite agreed on how to hold it. He gave away a fortune when he was young and his body when he was old, and he was, by turns, magnificent and impossible.

He would not have minded the mixed verdict. He had settled the only question that concerned him at eighteen, and again at twenty-four, and every day after: if Christ was God and had died for him, then nothing was too much to give back. He gave the cricket, the money, the health, and the years, and he counted none of it a sacrifice. Only one life — and he spent it all.

fields.name: John Stott
fields.bio: John Stott (1921–2011) was rector of All Souls, Langham Place, for his whole ministry and one of the principal architects of modern world evangelicalism — chief framer of the Lausanne Covenant and founder of the Langham Partnership. A clear Bible teacher, lifelong single, and disciplined man of prayer, he gave away his royalties to train pastors across the world.
fields.bio_html:
Most lives that shape a movement do so by restlessness — a man moves from cause to cause, church to church, country to country, and the sum of the motion is the influence. John Stott’s life ran the other way. He was born a short walk from All Souls, Langham Place, in the West End of London; he was converted at school and mentored by letter; he was ordained into that one church and stayed there, in one form or another, until he died. From that single fixed point he did more to shape worldwide evangelical Christianity in the twentieth century than almost anyone alive. He is proof that depth in one place can reach further than breadth across many.

A doctor’s son who heard a sentence

He was born in London on 27 April 1921, the son of Sir Arnold Stott, a Harley Street physician and a convinced agnostic, and of a mother of Lutheran background who took her children to All Souls. It was a household of two settlements — the father’s reason, the mother’s faith — and the boy grew up respecting both.

The decisive thing happened at Rugby School. In 1938 a clergyman named Eric Nash — known to a generation of English schoolboys simply as “Bash” — spoke to the school Christian Union, and on 13 February the seventeen-year-old Stott gave his life to Christ. What made the moment last was what Nash did next. He wrote to the boy every week for about five years, patiently, one letter at a time, teaching him how to follow Christ and how to think. Stott never forgot that a man had taken that much trouble over one young convert. The whole shape of his later ministry — the personal attention, the raising up of the next person, the conviction that the church grows by discipling one soul at a time — was set by those letters.

He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, took a double first, and was ordained in 1945. His first post was as a curate at All Souls, the church of his childhood. Five years later, in 1950, at the age of twenty-eight, he was made its rector. He would hold that connection for the rest of his life — rector until 1975, then rector emeritus — one man and one church across six decades.

The disciplined morning

To understand everything he built, you have to start where he started every day, because he started it the same way for most of his adult life.

He rose at about five o’clock. Before his feet were properly on the floor, before the post or the diary or the demands of a large parish could reach him, he greeted God — and he greeted him as three Persons, one at a time, so that the first act of the day was not a request but a recognition of who God is. Then came the reading. He followed the plan of Robert Murray M’Cheyne, the young Scottish minister of a century before, working through several chapters of the Bible each day so that the whole of it passed under his eye, year after year, and the Old Testament and the New were always being read together.

Before the day could make its claims on him, John Stott greeted God by name — “Good morning, heavenly Father; good morning, Lord Jesus; good morning, Holy Spirit” — addressing each Person of the Trinity in turn. Rising near five o’clock, he then read his daily portion on the M’Cheyne plan before the parish, the post, or the diary could reach him. The pattern held for the better part of a lifetime: recognition first, requests afterward.

Then the notebook came out. It was a small thing, held shut with a rubber band, its pages covered in tiny handwriting and ruled into four columns — one for evangelism and new converts, one for people facing hard decisions, one for the sick and the bereaved, and one for everything else. Down those columns ran the names of people he prayed for by name, day after day, many of whom never knew they were on the list. The man who would help write the theology of a global movement kept its foundations in a rubber-banded pocket book, praying through a column of names before most of the world was awake.

It is worth saying plainly what this was and was not. It was not a gift of temperament; it was a discipline, kept when he felt like it and when he did not, for decades. The public influence everyone can see grew out of a private practice almost nobody saw.

One church, and a world of pastors

Out of that fixed point the work spread astonishingly. At All Souls he built a preaching ministry admired far beyond his own tradition — careful, biblical, unshowy, always trying to let the text say its own thing rather than making it say his. Between 1952 and 1977 he led some fifty university missions around the world, and from 1959 he was an honorary chaplain to the Queen. He wrote more than fifty books; Basic Christianity, published in 1958, has sold around two million copies in more than sixty languages, and The Cross of Christ (1986) is generally reckoned his masterwork.

Then there was the matter of the money. Around 1969 Stott founded what grew into the Langham Partnership, and to fund it he did something most successful authors never contemplate: he gave away the income from his own books and speaking. The royalties and honoraria that could have made a bestselling clergyman wealthy went instead to train pastors in the majority world — scholarships for gifted teachers from Africa, Asia and Latin America, help for national preachers, the supply of good books where there were none. He had learned from Bash that the way you serve the church is by building up the next person; he simply did it at the scale of continents, and paid for it out of his own pocket. He lived, all his life, simply and single, in a modest flat, and let his wealth become other men’s training.

In 1974 he chaired the committee that drafted the Lausanne Covenant, one of the founding documents of modern world evangelicalism, holding together in a single statement the call to evangelism and the call to social responsibility. In 1982 he founded the London Institute for Contemporary Christianity, to help ordinary believers think Christianly about their work and their world. In 2005 Time named him one of the hundred most influential people alive. Through all of it he remained, to the students and pastors who loved him, simply “Uncle John” — and, in his spare hours, a devoted birdwatcher who could write a whole book, The Birds Our Teachers, on what the created world had to teach about the God who made it.

I could never myself believe in God, if it were not for the cross.

— John Stott, The Cross of Christ

The line is worth weighing. A man who had thought about the faith as rigorously as any of his generation located the whole reason for his believing not in an argument but in a crucifixion — the point at which, he held, the love and the justice of God meet.

“I would pray more”

Late in his life someone asked John Stott what he would do differently if he had his ministry again. The answer he is reported to have given was not about strategy or books or missions. It was two words about the notebook and the early mornings: he would pray more.

Bash had prayed and written for one seventeen-year-old convert, week after week, for five years. That single patient investment produced a man whose books, missions, and given-away royalties trained pastors on every continent — and who, into his old age, still rose before dawn to pray through his own columns of names. The clearest answer to the older man’s labour was the ministry of the younger, multiplied across the world church.

Coming from that man, it is not false modesty and it is not a platitude. It is the most consistent thing he could have said. Everyone else measured his life by its output — the covenant, the institute, the fifty books, the pastors trained. He measured it by the one hidden practice from which all of that had come, and judged that even he, who had kept it for a lifetime, had not given it enough.

Nothing except Christ crucified

He preached and taught into old age, then withdrew quietly to a home for retired clergy. He died on 27 July 2011, at Lingfield in Surrey, at the age of ninety, with friends reading Scripture and playing Handel at his bedside.

His gravestone carries no summary of his achievements. It carries the verse he had preached and lived by — the apostle Paul’s resolve to know “nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified.” It is exactly the epitaph the life asks for. He held one church for one lifetime, gave his wealth away to raise up others, and built a worldwide influence on a rubber-banded notebook and a five o’clock greeting to the Trinity. The doctor’s son who was written to, week after week, by a man who cared about one convert, spent the rest of his years writing back — in letters, in books, in prayers by name, in pastors he would never meet — the same patient answer.
