faq.a: On 18 October 1966, at the National Assembly of Evangelicals, Lloyd-Jones appealed for evangelicals to leave doctrinally "mixed" denominations and come together in visible evangelical unity; John Stott, chairing, used the chair to disagree, urging Anglican evangelicals to remain in the Church of England. The exchange opened a lasting breach across British evangelicalism. Both men were godly and believed they were being faithful, both paid for it, and the cooling of their fellowship is one of the honest sorrows of the story.

faq.q: How did he die?
faq.a: He preached his final sermon in 1980 and declined through his last months as cancer advanced. Too weak to say much, he wrote a note to his family: "Do not pray for healing. Do not hold me back from the glory." It was the settled verdict of a man who had spent his youth learning to postpone death and his manhood learning what death could not touch. He died peacefully in his sleep on 1 March 1981, St David's Day, and was buried in the west Wales country he had come from.

faq.q: What does he leave?
faq.a: He left a large body of expository sermons still read and heard, a recovered seriousness about biblical preaching, and the memory of a man who gave up one of the most enviable careers in Britain because he had decided what was really wrong with people. "The Doctor," everyone called him long after he stopped practising, and the name kept telling the truth: he had changed patients and changed the disease he was treating, and never stopped taking the case history until the real complaint came out. He believed the deepest trouble in every one of us is curable, and gave up everything to say so.

fields.name: Billy Graham
fields.bio: Billy Graham (1918–2018) was an American evangelist and Southern Baptist minister who, by his organization's count, preached the gospel in person to some 215 million people across more than 185 countries, closing each crusade with the hymn “Just As I Am.” He founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and set the 1948 Modesto integrity safeguards that kept his ministry free of scandal.
fields.bio_html:
He preached the gospel, in person, to more people than anyone who has ever lived — by his own organization's count, some 215 million of them, in stadiums and rice paddies and cathedral squares across 185 countries — and when he came to choose the words for his grave, he asked for none of that. The marker at the Billy Graham Library in Charlotte gives his name, a reference to John 14:6, and four plain words for the work: Preacher of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. That is the whole of the ambition he would own. A man who could fill Seoul with a million people wanted to be remembered as a country preacher who told them about Jesus.

Preacher of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ

— the epitaph Billy Graham chose for his own gravestone

A dairy farm outside Charlotte

William Franklin Graham was born on 7 November 1918, on the family dairy farm near Charlotte, North Carolina, into a church-going Reformed Presbyterian household where the chores started before dawn. It was an ordinary rural Southern boyhood, and nothing in it marked him out.

The turn came when he was sixteen. In 1934 a travelling evangelist named Mordecai Ham held a revival in Charlotte, and Graham — by his own account more curious than convicted at first — went, and went forward, and made his decision for Christ. Every account of his life, including his own memoir, treats that night as the hinge. He did not become a preacher that evening; he became a Christian, and the preaching would take years to find its shape.

It took, in fact, a false start and a long apprenticeship. He enrolled at Bob Jones College in 1936 and lasted only about a semester, finding its fundamentalism airless. He moved to the Florida Bible Institute near Tampa, and it was there, not in any classroom crisis but in the slow settling of a young man's mind, that he became sure he was called to preach. He was ordained in the Southern Baptist Convention in 1939. Then came Wheaton College in Illinois, where he graduated in 1943 with a degree in anthropology — and where he met Ruth McCue Bell, a daughter of medical missionaries to China. They married that same year in Montreat, North Carolina, and stayed married sixty-three years, until Ruth's death in 2007.

Modesto: four resolutions before the fame

Before any of the crowds, there was a small room in Modesto, California, in 1948, and a decision that may have mattered more than any sermon. Graham had watched travelling evangelists wreck themselves and their witness — on money, on women, on lies about their crowds, on rivalry with the local church — and he did not intend to join them. With his three closest associates — song leader Cliff Barrows, soloist George Beverly Shea, and Grady Wilson — he sat down and resolved four safeguards for the work ahead.

They would handle money honestly: no love-offering abuses, a fixed salary, audited and open finances, and no pleading for cash from the platform. They would guard against even the appearance of sexual impropriety — the rule, which later took Graham's name, that none of them would travel, meet, or dine alone with a woman other than his wife. They would tell the truth about numbers, and never inflate a crowd or a count of conversions. And they would not compete with local pastors or criticize them, but work through the churches and hand converts back to them.

It was not a signed document, and no manifesto was published that day; the catchy name, the Modesto Manifesto, came later. They were four spoken resolutions four young men made to keep each other honest. But it is one of the most admirable and best-documented facts of his life, and it goes a long way to explain the plainest thing about him: across six decades at the very top of American religion, he finished without a money scandal and without a sex scandal. The guardrails held because he built them before he needed them.

The tent that would not come down

The breakthrough came in Los Angeles in 1949. Graham and his team pitched a great circus-style tent — the "Canvas Cathedral" — at Washington Boulevard and Hill Street, and scheduled three weeks. The crowds kept coming, and the three weeks stretched to eight. Press attention (the newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst is said to have told his editors to "puff Graham") turned a regional preacher into a national figure almost overnight.

What followed was without precedent. Over roughly six decades he held some 400 crusades across more than 185 countries and territories. The BGEA — the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, which he founded in Minneapolis in 1950 — estimates that he preached in person to around 215 million people, and that more than three million responded to his invitation to come forward. His largest single live audience, more than a million, gathered in Seoul in 1973. These are the organization's own tallies, and are best held as its estimates rather than bare fact; but even discounted, they describe a reach no evangelist before him approached.

The close was always the same. As the congregation sang the old hymn Just As I Am — Charlotte Elliott's words, "just as I am, without one plea" — Graham would invite people to leave their seats and come forward to Christ. That invitation, repeated in hundreds of cities and dozens of languages, is the image the world keeps of him: a tall man with an open Bible, and a slow river of people walking down toward a platform while the hymn went round again.

Around the preaching he built a machine to carry it — the radio programme Hour of Decision from 1950, World Wide Pictures, Decision magazine from 1960, and a team, Barrows and Shea and Wilson, that stayed with him for life.

Carried on prayer

Graham never claimed the fruit was his. He credited prayer as the engine of anything that came of the crusades, and named it, again and again, as one of the keys to the work. That was not only pulpit modesty; it was method. The crusades were prepared on prayer long before Graham arrived in a city. For months beforehand, host cities were organized into local prayer groups and cottage prayer meetings — ordinary people meeting in front rooms to pray for their neighbours by name — and the BGEA regarded this groundwork as essential to whatever happened once the singing began.

Before a single sermon was preached in a crusade city, the work had already been going on for months in people's living rooms — small groups gathered to pray, by name, for the friends and neighbours they hoped to see come forward. Graham insisted the crusades were carried on that prayer, not on his preaching.

It is worth being careful here, because the legend runs ahead of the record. The vivid private-prayer scenes that attach themselves to famous preachers — the exact hours risen, the tears, the words wrestled out before dawn — are mostly devotional embroidery, and Graham deserves better than embroidery. What can be said plainly is enough: he taught the primacy of prayer, he built his life's work on organized intercession, and he refused to take credit that he believed belonged to God and to the people who had prayed.

A sinner who preached grace

He was not a spotless man, and the honest telling of his life needs two hard things in it.

The first is his entanglement with political power. Graham was pastor and confidant to a line of American presidents from Truman to Obama, but he was closest to Richard Nixon, and that closeness compromised him. He came to see it. In his memoir he wrote that Nixon's candidacy had "muffled those inner monitors that had warned me for years to stay out of partisan politics." Asked late in life what he would do differently, he said he would have steered clear of politics, and added:

Looking back I know I sometimes crossed the line, and I wouldn't do that now.

— Billy Graham, Christianity Today, 2011

That is not the language of a man defending himself. It is a mature Christian correcting his own record in public, and it should be read as strength, not merely as stain.

The second is graver. On 1 February 1972, in an Oval Office conversation recorded on Nixon's taping system, Graham made antisemitic remarks — agreeing with Nixon about a Jewish "stranglehold" on the media, and saying it had to be broken, with further disparaging words. When the National Archives released the tapes in 2002, the remarks became public, and there was no softening the fact of them. Graham did not try to soften it. He apologized publicly and without reserve, said the words did not reflect his heart, and spoke of the Jewish people with plain contrition:

I don't ever recall having those feelings about any group, especially the Jews, and I certainly do not have them now.

— Billy Graham, public apology, 2002

This was real sin, and it will not do to file it under "just politics" or "out of character." A man who had preached to millions that they needed grace was shown, on tape, to need it himself — and, shown it, he repented in the open. There is no cleaner illustration of his own message than that. The gospel he preached was never that good men go to heaven; it was that sinners are forgiven. He turned out to be one of the sinners.

A change of address

Ruth died in 2007, and Graham lived on another eleven years at their home in Montreat, in the North Carolina mountains. He had already handed the work to his son Franklin, who succeeded him at the head of the BGEA and Samaritan's Purse. He died at home on 21 February 2018, aged ninety-nine.

The nation marked it in a way it had marked almost no one. He lay in honor in the Capitol Rotunda in Washington — the fourth private citizen in the country's history to be granted it, and the first religious leader — which stirred a small debate about church and state that he would probably have found amusing. Then they took him home to Charlotte and buried him beside Ruth at the foot of a cross-shaped walkway, in a plain plywood coffin built by prison inmates. The most famous preacher of his century went into the ground in a box a convict had made.

Graham liked to say, late in life, that when people heard he had died they should not quite believe it — that he would simply have changed his address, gone home. He was borrowing the thought; D. L. Moody had said very nearly the same thing a hundred years before, and Graham knew it and did not mind. It was the one boast he allowed himself, and it was not really a boast. It was the content of what he had told 215 million people: that there is a home, and a way to it, and that the way is a person. He spent a long life pointing at it. The four words he chose for his stone ask to be remembered for nothing more.

They married in 1943 in Montreat, North Carolina, and stayed married sixty-three years, until Ruth's death in 2007. Graham lived on another eleven years at their mountain home in Montreat.

faq.q: What was the Modesto Manifesto, and did it really keep him free of scandal?
faq.a: In 1948, in a small room in Modesto, California, Graham and his three closest associates — Cliff Barrows, George Beverly Shea, and Grady Wilson — resolved four safeguards for the work ahead: honest, audited finances with no pleading for money from the platform; strict truthfulness about crowd and conversion numbers; cooperation with local pastors rather than rivalry; and a rule against any of them travelling, meeting, or dining alone with a woman other than his wife. It was never a signed document, and the catchy name came later, but the guardrails held. faq.q: What was the crusade that made Billy Graham famous?
faq.a: The breakthrough came in Los Angeles in 1949, where his team pitched a great circus-style tent, the "Canvas Cathedral," and scheduled three weeks. The crowds kept coming and the three weeks stretched to eight, and press attention turned a regional preacher into a national figure almost overnight. faq.q: How many people did Billy Graham preach to?
faq.a: By the count of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, which he founded in Minneapolis in 1950, he preached in person to around 215 million people, with more than three million responding to his invitation to come forward — reaching, by that reckoning, more people face to face than perhaps anyone who has ever lived. faq.q: What was his message, and why did crusades close with "Just As I Am"?

At the close, as the congregation sang the old hymn "Just As I Am," he would invite people to leave their seats and come forward to Christ. faq.q: Did Billy Graham stand against racial segregation?
faq.a: Yes. In 1953, at a crusade in Chattanooga, Tennessee, he found the seating roped off to keep Black and white attendees apart, and when the head usher refused to remove the ropes, Graham walked down and personally tore them down himself. He told the ushers the ropes would stay down or they could hold the crusade without him, and from then on he made integrated meetings his settled policy — a striking stand more than a decade before the 1964 Civil Rights Act.

faq.a: Diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in his seventies, he slowed over the years and handed the work to his son Franklin, retiring to the family home in Montreat, North Carolina. He died there on 21 February 2018 at the age of ninety-nine. fields.name: Henry Blackaby
fields.bio: Henry Blackaby (1935–2024) was a Canadian-born Southern Baptist pastor whose years leading a tiny, struggling church in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, gave rise to Experiencing God (1990), the Bible study read by millions that reframed prayer as listening for where God is already at work and joining Him there. He founded Blackaby Ministries International, wrote more than fifty books, and taught the church to align with God's agenda rather than its own.
fields.bio_html:
Most books about the Christian life tell you how to make a plan and ask God to bless it. Henry Blackaby spent his life teaching the opposite — that God is already at work, that He has a plan of His own, and that the whole task of prayer is to find out where He is moving and to fall in beside Him. It is a small idea and an enormous one. It came not out of a seminary lecture hall but out of a struggling church of about ten people on the Canadian prairies, where a middle-aged pastor had run out of programs and had nothing left to do but watch and listen. What he learned there became Experiencing God, a study read by millions, and the sentence people still repeat when they cannot see the way forward.

A Canadian boy and a long apprenticeship

He was born Henry Thomas Blackaby on 15 April 1935 in Williams Lake, a small town in the interior of British Columbia, and grew up partly on the coast in Prince Rupert, in a devout Baptist family. There is little in the public record of his childhood, and this account will not invent any; the man himself is best met further on, in the work.

He studied English and History at the University of British Columbia, and then, called to ministry, went south to the Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary in California, where he took a Bachelor of Divinity and a Master of Theology. He was not a research academic — the doctorates that later attached to his name were honorary — but he was a trained, careful reader of the Bible, and it showed in everything he built. At seminary he met Marilynn Sue Wells. They married on 3 June 1960, and she would be beside him for the whole of it.

He pastored Southern Baptist churches in California — San Pablo, then Downey — the ordinary settled work of an American pastor with a growing family. By every visible measure his life was set. And then, in 1970, he gave it up.

Ten people in Saskatoon

Persuaded by a fellow Canadian to come home, Blackaby left a comfortable California pastorate to take Faith Baptist Church in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan — a small, struggling congregation, widely described as about ten members, one account calling it a small, dying church. He was thirty-five. He would stay about twelve years.

This is the heart of the story, and it is worth being honest about what we know of it. We do not have a diary of those years, and there is no single lightning-bolt miracle to report. What we have is a pattern, and his own later account of what he was learning. In a hard and unpromising field, with no resources to generate the kind of activity a bigger church runs on, Blackaby stopped asking what he could do for God and began asking where God was already at work — and then adjusting the little church to join it.

The prayer he learned in Saskatoon was not mainly a matter of presenting God with requests. It was listening — watching the Bible, the circumstances, and the church for where God was moving, and asking not "will You bless my plan?" but "what are You doing, and how do I get in on it?" He came to believe God always takes the first step, and that the believer's whole work is to notice and respond.

By his ministry's own account, the results over those prairie years were far out of proportion to the congregation's size: the small church became a seedbed of church-planting across western Canada, helping to start dozens of new congregations and missions and helping establish what became a Bible college and seminary. Those figures come from the ministry's own retellings and are best held loosely as to their exact count; what is not in doubt is the shape of it — a tiny, unlikely church that grew and multiplied as it learned to move when God moved.

The honest answer to prayer here is not a single miracle but a whole ministry. A church of about ten, in a place where nothing was supposed to grow, became the source of many congregations across the Canadian prairies — because, its pastor said, it kept looking for where God was working and joining Him there. The fruit was the answer.

Experiencing God

What Blackaby had learned in Saskatoon he eventually put into a form the wider church could use. Developed first as an interactive Bible-study course and released through the Southern Baptist Sunday School Board — now Lifeway — Experiencing God: Knowing and Doing the Will of God appeared in 1990, written by Blackaby with Claude V. King. It went on to sell millions of copies in English and to be translated into dozens of languages. Later expanded editions added his son Richard as co-author, but the original was Blackaby and King. He called it, simply, his life's message.

Experiencing God is my life's message.

— Henry Blackaby

The study is built around what he called the Seven Realities — a way of seeing the Christian life that runs, in substance, like this. God is always at work around you. He is pursuing a real, personal love relationship with you. He invites you to join Him in His work — not the other way around. He speaks, by His Spirit through the Bible, prayer, circumstances, and the church, to reveal Himself and His purposes. His invitation brings you to a crisis of belief, where you must decide whether you really trust Him. Joining Him requires major adjustments in your life. And you come to know God by experience as you obey and He works through you.

People remember it best in one line — the study's well-known summary, repeated wherever it is taught: watch to see where God is working, and join Him. The book's own phrasing varies by edition (it also puts it as "find out where God is at work and join Him there"), and behind it lies the Gospel of John, where Jesus does only what He sees the Father doing. However it is worded, the counsel is the same, and it reorders everything. Prayer stops being the place where you inform God of your agenda and becomes the place where you receive His.

The relationship comes first

For all its practical bent, the center of Blackaby's teaching was not technique but love. Assignments, he insisted, flow out of intimacy with God and never around it; the love relationship is not a means to the work — it is the point.

The love relationship is why God created you.

— attributed to Experiencing God

And because God cares more about the person than the project, He works on the one He is sending before He works through him. Blackaby said it plainly, and it is a mercy to anyone who has felt unready for what God seems to be asking.

He will always work in you before He works through you.

— attributed to Experiencing God

A wider ministry, and a family in it

After Saskatoon, Blackaby served for a time as a director of missions in the Vancouver area before moving into denominational and writing ministry in the United States. Within the Southern Baptist Convention he worked in prayer and spiritual awakening, and served as a special assistant to the presidents of the International Mission Board and of Lifeway. He founded Blackaby Ministries International, based near Atlanta, to carry the message into churches, denominations, and the workplace, and it continues under his family today.

He wrote more than fifty books. With his son Richard he wrote Spiritual Leadership: Moving People on to God's Agenda, a title read far beyond church staff, into Christian business and nonprofit leadership — and its subtitle is really the whole of his thought in miniature: leadership is not moving people onto your agenda, but onto God's. His language of "joining God where He is working" passed into common evangelical speech, often by people who had never heard his name.

The life bore its most personal witness at home. Marilynn, who married him in 1960, went before him. All five of their children entered Christian ministry — the four sons as pastors, their daughter as a missionary — and Richard in particular carried the work forward and now leads it. A man who taught the church to watch for God's initiative had, it seems, watched for it first in his own house.

What he leaves

Henry Blackaby died in February 2024, at the age of 88. He is a recent figure, and much of the detail of his private life is thin; a devotional reader is better served by what is solid, and what is solid is the teaching and the fruit.

He leaves the church a reordered idea of prayer. Where much of modern religion begins with the self — its plans, its needs, its felt calling — and asks God to underwrite them, Blackaby began with God, already at work, already moving, and asked only that we learn to see it and to adjust. It is the least dramatic of counsels and one of the hardest, because it costs you your agenda. But it is also the most freeing, because it means the outcome was never yours to secure. The church of ten in Saskatoon did not build itself into a movement; it simply kept joining what God was doing. That, he spent a lifetime saying, is what prayer is for.

fields.name: Bill Bright
fields.bio: Bill Bright (1921–2003) was an Oklahoma-born businessman who gave up his career for ministry and, with his wife Vonette, founded Campus Crusade for Christ in 1951. He wrote the Four Spiritual Laws and originated the JESUS film, but devoted his later years to fasting and prayer for revival — undertaking a series of 40-day fasts and giving away his 1996 Templeton Prize to the cause.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the men in this book are known for one thing they did on their knees. Bill Bright is known first for a machine — a student ministry that grew into one of the largest in the world, a four-point gospel tract carried into more than two hundred languages, a film about Jesus that Guinness records as the most translated in history. It would be easy to make him a biography of numbers. But the numbers are the least reliable and the least interesting thing about him, and he knew it. The Bill Bright who belongs in a book about prayer is the old man of the 1990s who set the machine to one side, stopped eating for forty days at a stretch, and spent the last decade of his life pleading with God — and with his own country — for revival.

An Oklahoma ranch, and a business he gave away

He was born William Rohl Bright on 19 October 1921, near Coweta, Oklahoma, and grew up on a ranch, at a small rural school, in a country of cattle and hard work. He graduated from Northeastern State University in Oklahoma in 1944, having studied economics and business, and then did what an ambitious young man does: he went west. In Los Angeles he built a successful specialty foods company — Bright's California Confections, gourmet foods and fine confections — and was, by his mid-twenties, a rising Southern California businessman with a future in front of him.

The turn came through a church. In the mid-1940s, at First Presbyterian Church of Hollywood, Bright came to faith — drawn in and discipled largely through Henrietta Mears, the church's formidable director of Christian education, in a circle that also brought him into the orbit of the young Billy Graham. Sensing a call to ministry, he studied at Princeton Theological Seminary and then at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena, but he left without finishing a degree, convinced God wanted him reaching university students directly rather than sitting in a classroom. He set the promising business aside for good. In 1948, on the 30th of December, he married Vonette Zachary, a schoolmate from back home in Coweta. She is not a footnote to this story. She was his partner in all of it, and in one of its most important chapters she went ahead of him.

The Sunday they became slaves

The founding act of Bright's life was not the launch of an organization. It was a surrender.

On a Sunday afternoon in the spring of 1951, Bill and Vonette knelt together in their home and signed a written contract giving their whole lives to God — choosing, as Bright always told it, to become the bond-servants of Jesus Christ. He described it plainly in his 1996 Templeton Prize address:

That Sunday afternoon, like Paul, we chose to become slaves of Jesus.

— Bill Bright, Templeton Prize acceptance address, 1996

The devotional retellings add detail — that they each first wrote down what they most wanted from life, and that the vision for a student ministry came to Bright not long after — and some of that is reconstructed from memory rather than documented word for word. What is certain, in his own words, is the shape of it: two people, a written act of total surrender, and the language of slavery chosen freely. Out of that afternoon came Campus Crusade for Christ, begun in 1951 as a ministry to students at UCLA. It grew into one of the largest parachurch ministries in the world — thousands of full-time staff and many times that number of trained volunteers, working across scores of nations. In 2011, eight years after his death, the American organization renamed itself Cru.

Four laws, one film, and the trouble with counting

Two things Bright made carried his name furthest. The first was the Four Spiritual Laws, a short booklet that reduced the gospel to four plain sentences a student could read in a few minutes. It opens with the line that became his most quoted:

God loves you and offers a wonderful plan for your life.

— the first of the Four Spiritual Laws

He developed the content in the late 1950s and published it in its enduring booklet form in 1965. It went on to become one of the most widely distributed pieces of Christian literature ever printed — hundreds of millions, and by the ministry's own count billions, of copies in more than two hundred languages. The second was the JESUS film, produced by Campus Crusade in 1979 and drawn from the Gospel of Luke, which became the engine of a worldwide evangelism effort. Guinness World Records lists it as the most translated film in history, rendered into well over a thousand languages and screened worldwide on a scale few films have ever matched.

Here honesty asks for a word of restraint, and Bright would not have minded it. The distribution and viewership totals attached to his work are ministry estimates, not audited figures, and they have climbed steadily with the retelling. The one claim that rests on independent ground is Guinness's. A devotional reader is better served by the plain fact that these were among the most far-reaching gospel tools of the century than by any billion-count, and better served still by what Bright did once the machine was running and famous. He let it go, and went looking for God.

Forty days, and a call to a nation

In July 1994, at the age of seventy-two, Bill Bright stopped eating. He believed God had prompted him to fast and pray for forty days for a spiritual awakening in America — something he had never attempted, and something that frightened him. His own prayer, as he later recalled it, was not heroic:

Lord, I'll fast for 40 days, but you'll have to help me.

He got through it. Somewhere in the third week, by his account, an assurance settled on him that God would indeed send revival — and with it a conviction that he was to summon two million Christians across North America to fast for forty days by the end of the year 2000, praying for revival and for the finishing of the Great Commission. It was not a one-time exercise. He went on to undertake a series of annual forty-day fasts through the rest of the 1990s, and he began to convene large gatherings of Christian leaders to fast and pray together — in Orlando in December 1994, in Los Angeles in 1995, thousands of leaders in all. He wrote to press the case: The Coming Revival: America's Call to Fast, Pray, and "Seek God's Face" in 1995, and later The Transforming Power of Fasting and Prayer, along with practical guides for those who had never tried it.

This is the Bright the older man became: not the entrepreneur of methods but the intercessor who thought his country's deepest need was not another program but a return, on empty stomachs and bent knees, to the God it had drifted from. He put the discipline near the center of everything:

No other Christian discipline meets the conditions of God's promises to heal our land as powerfully as fasting with prayer.

— Bill Bright, Templeton Prize acceptance address, 1996

A prize, given away

In 1996 Bright received the Templeton Prize for Progress in Religion, a monetary award of over a million US dollars, its citation naming him among the most vigorous Christian evangelists in the world. He kept none of it. He gave the entire prize away to fund the very cause the last decade of his life had become — the promotion of prayer and fasting for revival.

The man who had spent decades raising money for ministry took the largest personal award of his life, more than a million dollars, and poured all of it into calling others to fast and pray. The prize for a lifetime of work was turned straight back into the work of the last chapter.

It was in keeping with how the Brights had long lived. A 1997 profile found them on a modest combined salary, owning neither a house nor a car, taking no book royalties or speaking fees personally — the royalties went to the ministry. For a man whose name sat atop an organization of that size, the smallness of his own footprint was the point.

The center of his teaching, running under all the activity, was that a Christian is not asked to imitate Christ from a distance but to be inhabited by him. He put it simply at Templeton:

He actually takes up residence in us. He lives inside of us, at the deepest level of our spirit, filling that former void and emptiness.

— Bill Bright, Templeton Prize acceptance address, 1996

What he leaves

Bill Bright died on 19 July 2003 in Orlando, Florida, of pulmonary fibrosis, at the age of eighty-one. Vonette, who had co-founded everything with him and led major prayer initiatives of her own — a driving force in the movement that gave the American National Day of Prayer a fixed date on the calendar — outlived him by more than a decade.

He wrote no book that will be read as literature, and much of what made him famous is stated in numbers that no one can verify. Strip those away and what remains is sturdier than any of them. A young businessman gave up a career because a sentence about the love of God had gone through him. A husband and wife knelt on a Sunday afternoon and signed themselves over as slaves. And an old man at the height of his renown decided the thing his life still lacked was not another method but hunger — and spent his last years teaching a distracted church the oldest way back to God there is. The gospel he reduced to four short lines had a first line, and he lived as though it were true to the end: that God loves you, and offers a wonderful plan for your life.

fields.name: Loren Cunningham
fields.bio: Loren Cunningham (1935–2023) was the founder of Youth With A Mission (YWAM), who mobilized generations of young people into missions and taught believers to discern and obey the voice of God. From a vision he testified he received in 1956, he built one of the largest interdenominational mission movements in the world, and in his book Is That Really You, God? taught that guidance comes through listening prayer tested by Scripture, circumstances, and counsel.
fields.bio_html:
Most mission movements begin with a strategy. Youth With A Mission began with a question a young man kept asking a room where he was the only person visible — is that really you, God? — and then acting as though the answer were yes. Loren Cunningham spent sixty years teaching ordinary believers, and especially the young, that the God of the Bible still speaks, that his voice can be tested and trusted, and that the whole adventure of a Christian life is learning to hear him and obey. He was not a scholar or a statesman. He was a preacher's son from an oil town in California who believed he had been shown something, and who never got over it.

A preacher's son from Taft

He was born Loren Duane Cunningham on 30 June 1935 in Taft, California, an oil-boom town in the dry hills north of Los Angeles. Faith was not something he had to go looking for; it was the air of the house. His parents, Tom and Jewell Cunningham, were both ordained ministers in the Assemblies of God — second-generation Pentecostal evangelists — so the boy grew up not merely with a father who preached but with two parents who did.

He came to a personal faith of his own as a boy, by the usual accounts around the age of thirteen. As a young man he traveled and sang, ministering in music with a gospel quartet. It was an unremarkable start for a Pentecostal youth of his generation: converted early, useful in the meetings, expected in time to take up the family trade of the pulpit. Nothing in it announced a worldwide movement. What set his life on its course was not a plan but something he could only ever describe as a picture given to him while he prayed.

The waves

In June 1956, a few days short of his twenty-first birthday, Cunningham was in the Bahamas as one of a group of young men who had come to preach and evangelize. He testified that, kneeling in a guest room, he received a vision. In his own account he was suddenly looking at a map of the world — only the map was alive and moving, with waves rolling in and breaking over the continents. As he watched, the waves became young people, going out everywhere to share the gospel.

The waves became young people — kids my age and even younger — covering all the continents of the globe.

— Loren Cunningham, Is That Really You, God?

He was careful, ever after, about how he told it. It was his experience, recounted in his book, not a thing an observer could confirm; and he had a disarming explanation for why the picture came to him in the shape it did. God, he liked to say, speaks in a language you already know.

God speaks in your language, and I was a surfer as a teenager in California, and I saw these waves.

— Loren Cunningham, quoted in Christianity Today (2023)

That is the whole man in one sentence. The vision that would send tens of thousands of young people to the ends of the earth reached its first recipient in the imagery of a California teenager watching the surf. He did not tidy it up into something grander. He took it as it came, and he took it seriously.

He was twenty years old, kneeling alone in a borrowed room, when he believed God showed him young people breaking over the continents like surf. The rest of his life was, in a sense, one long answer to a prayer he had prayed as a boy — and one long test of whether he had heard rightly.

Youth With A Mission

The vision did not become an organization overnight. It waited four years. In 1960 — Cunningham was twenty-four — Youth With A Mission was founded, with Lausanne, Switzerland commonly named as its birthplace; it was incorporated in California in February 1961, after he had left the Assemblies of God to give himself wholly to the idea. The two dates are not a contradiction. One is a beginning; the other is the paperwork that caught up with it.

The idea itself was almost scandalously simple. The mission field had long been the preserve of the trained, the ordained, the middle-aged. Cunningham believed the young — teenagers straight out of high school, students, anyone across the denominations who would say yes — could be mobilized to go, on short-term and long-term missions alike. Many told him it would not work. It worked. YWAM grew into one of the largest interdenominational mission movements in the world, active in most countries on earth.

Two structures carried the work and are worth naming. The first was the Discipleship Training School, YWAM's foundational course — the doorway through which a young person entered the movement, learning to know God before being sent to make him known. The second was the University of the Nations, headquartered in Kona, Hawaii, which he and his wife Darlene helped to found, joined by Dr. Howard Malmstadt, to train Christians for service across every field of human life.

Cunningham himself went further than almost anyone. He is reported by YWAM and by his obituaries as the first person to travel to every sovereign nation on earth — together with every dependent country and more than a hundred territories and islands — for the sake of the gospel. He would not have wanted the record to be about him. When people reached for a title, he waved it away.

Please, just call me Loren.

— Loren Cunningham, reported in 2023

Is that really you, God?

For all the scale of the movement he began, the thread that ran through Cunningham's teaching was quieter and more personal: he believed that God still guides those who will listen. His best-known book, written with Janice Rogers and first published in 1984, took its title from the very question a believer asks when he thinks he has heard something — Is That Really You, God? Hearing the Voice of God. Its whole subject is discerning God's guidance, told through his own story and the stories of his co-workers: they listen, they obey, and they watch what God does.

The teaching was never a technique for extracting instructions from heaven. Hearing God, in Cunningham's account, flows out of relationship with him, not out of a method — you learn a friend's voice by knowing the friend. And what is heard must be tested. Guidance, he insisted, is confirmed by Scripture, by circumstances, and by godly counsel; anything that contradicts the Bible is refused, however vivid it feels. Prayer, on this reckoning, is not only asking. It is listening, and then the harder thing — doing what you heard.

That was the pattern of his own life, drawn out to sixty years. An ordinary man kept saying yes to what he believed God had said, submitting each prompting to the Book and to wiser heads and to the slow verdict of events, and out of that ordinary obedience a worldwide work was built. He would have resisted any grander telling. The movement was not the achievement; the listening was.

A vision received on his knees at twenty grew, over four decades of asking, testing, and obeying, into one of the largest mission movements in the world — young people from most nations of the earth sent out to preach. He always credited it not to strategy but to a God who speaks, and to the plain willingness to believe he had.

His later years kept the same shape. He gave himself increasingly to seeing the whole Bible read and heard in every nation — the same instinct that had always driven him, that God's word belongs to every person, carried into old age. It was of a piece with the waves: a gospel meant for all the continents, and young people to take it there.

Kona

He did not walk that road alone. In 1963 he married Darlene, née Scratch, who is recognized as a co-founder of YWAM and who was his ministry partner for the whole of it. They had two children, Karen and David, and grandchildren survive him. The home they made in Kona, Hawaii, became the heart of the movement's training.

In March 2023 he was diagnosed with Stage 4 cancer. He died on 6 October 2023 at home in Kona, aged eighty-eight. He left no reputation as a great orator and founded no denomination. What he left was a question, put into the mouths of hundreds of thousands of ordinary Christians who had learned it from him — is that really you, God? — and the conviction, tested across a long obedient life, that the God who answers is worth spending everything to hear.

He was the least imposing kind of leader the modern missionary movement produced, and perhaps for that reason the most encouraging. He was a young man who thought he had heard something, checked it, believed it, and obeyed it — and then kept checking, believing, and obeying until he was old. Nobody, on his account, is too young or too ordinary to be sent. You have only to learn the voice, and go.

fields.name: Derek Prince
fields.bio: Derek Prince (1915–2003) was a Cambridge philosophy fellow and Plato scholar, converted in a WWII army barrack room, who became a systematic Bible teacher heard worldwide and a lifelong intercessor — especially in prayer and fasting for Israel and the Jewish people. He helped found the Shepherding movement in the 1970s and was the first of its leaders to publicly repudiate it.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the men in this book learned to pray before they learned much else. Derek Prince came at it the other way round. He was a professional philosopher, a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, a scholar of Plato who read the Bible the way he read any old text — as a problem in language and logic, evidence to be weighed by a mind trained to doubt. He was, by his own account, a skeptic. And then, in the worst years of a world war, in an army barrack room, the book he had been analysing answered back. The rest of his long life was spent teaching other people to take it as seriously as it had taken him — and, above all, to pray it.

A scholar who did not believe

He was born Peter Derek Vaughan Prince on 14 August 1915 in Bangalore, in British India, into a British military family. His gifts showed early. He won a scholarship, at around fourteen, to Eton College, where he read Greek and Latin, and went on to King's College, Cambridge, where he held a fellowship in Ancient and Modern Philosophy — an academic post, a professional philosopher's chair. He was steeped in Plato. He had also studied Hebrew and Greek, a competence that would later give his Bible teaching its careful, text-first grain.

None of it made him a believer. As a young don he approached Scripture as a set of documents, not as revelation — a work of ancient philosophy to be examined, and found wanting or interesting, but not obeyed.

The barrack room

He enlisted in 1940 and served, as a non-combatant, in the Royal Army Medical Corps — a hospital orderly, a medic. Somewhere in that upheaval he began reading the Bible, he said, as he would read any philosophical work: to understand it, to master it. By his own testimony the reading went on for some nine months. Then, in a barrack room — the ministry he founded places it at Scarborough, in Yorkshire, in the summer of 1941 — the analysis broke open into an encounter. He met, he insisted ever after, not a text but a living Christ.

He came away convinced of two things, and he would repeat them for the next sixty years: that Jesus Christ is alive, and that the Bible is, in his words, a true, relevant, up-to-date book.

Jesus Christ is alive, and the Bible is a true, relevant, up-to-date book.

— Derek Prince, on the two convictions he drew from his conversion

That is the whole of his later ministry in a sentence. Everything he did afterward was a working-out of those two claims by a man who had been paid to be sceptical and had stopped being able to.

He served roughly three years as an army medic in North Africa, through the desert campaign, and was discharged in Jerusalem. There, in the years around the founding of the State of Israel in 1948, a second burden was laid on him that never lifted — a lifelong sense of responsibility toward the Jewish people and their land.

The teacher

What Cambridge had made him did not go to waste; it was converted. After the war he taught and pastored — in London, then in Kenya from the late 1950s, where he worked as an educator and administrator. In the early 1960s he moved to the United States, pastoring in Seattle, Minneapolis, and Chicago before settling in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, where his publishing work — later Derek Prince Ministries — took shape. In 1981 he moved his base to Jerusalem, and taught worldwide almost to the end of his life.

His manner was unmistakable, and it is the through-line from the philosopher to the preacher. Even his obituary called him logical and reserved. He did not shout or dramatise. He defined his terms, built from the text, and distrusted hype — a scholar's plain here is what the Bible actually says. Through a daily radio ministry his teaching was carried, in his lifetime, worldwide in many languages, and he wrote dozens of books. He aimed always at the same thing: to make ordinary believers competent readers and doers of Scripture, dependent on the book and not on him.

Ruling by prayer

If there is a spine to Derek Prince's life, it is intercession. He taught on prayer, fasting, and spiritual warfare across decades, but the burden gathered into one book above the rest: Shaping History Through Prayer and Fasting, first published in 1973. Its claim is bold and simple. Ordinary believers — not only prophets and statesmen — praying and fasting on the authority of Scripture, can change the course of nations.

He did not argue it only from theory. He pointed to things he had lived near: the North African campaign he had served in, the founding of Israel he had witnessed, the end of the Stalin era, the coming of Kenyan independence — reading each, in faith, as something prayer had helped to shape. His model was Daniel, the exile who fasted and humbled himself and prayed his people's Scriptures back to God until history moved. That was the pattern Prince pressed on his readers: not vague, wishful praying, but standing on God's own promises and proclaiming them — believers taking up what he called their office as a kingdom of priests, whose work is to rule by prayer.

Prince taught that the single most consequential thing a believer can do for the world is to intercede — to fast, to humble oneself, and to pray Scripture back to God on the authority of His promises. He did not hold it out as a technique. He held it out as the ordinary Christian's real power over the course of nations, and he practised it: the teaching on fasting, those close to him said, plainly came out of his own.

The burden that had settled on him at his discharge in Jerusalem never left. To the end of his life he urged Christians to accept a responsibility to intercede for Israel, for Jerusalem, and for the Jewish people — a duty he thought the wider church had forgotten. He was influential in the founding of Intercessors for America, whose work drew on Shaping History. When he moved his own home to Jerusalem in his later years, it was not retirement to a view. It was an intercessor moving to the place he had been praying for since 1948.

Deliverance — central, and contested

Any honest account has to name what Prince became equally known for, because he did not hide it. He was one of the most prominent twentieth-century teachers of deliverance — the practice of casting out demons — and he taught that Christians themselves could be, in his term, demonized, and could need deliverance. His book They Shall Expel Demons is a standard text of that movement, and he practised what he taught.

It is genuinely contested ground. Many Christians reject the idea that a believer can be demonized, or are wary of the practice altogether, and the disagreement is serious and sincere on both sides. It belongs in the record, plainly, as central to his ministry and as something a thoughtful part of the church has never accepted. A devotional reader is owed the fact and left to weigh it.

A movement he helped lead, and repented of

The hardest chapter is one Prince himself came to call an error. In the early 1970s he was one of the so-called Fort Lauderdale Five — with Bob Mumford, Charles Simpson, Don Basham, and Ern Baxter — who founded and led what became the Shepherding, or Discipleship, Movement. It taught that every believer should submit to a personal "shepherd" over his life.

The teaching drew serious and sustained criticism. In practice, followers were said to need a shepherd's approval for the major decisions of their lives — marriage, moves, money, work — and critics charged the movement with authoritarian, controlling excess. It is not a small footnote, and it should not be smoothed away.

What sets Prince apart is what he did with it. He was the first of the five to leave, and to repudiate the teaching publicly, in 1983 — not with excuses but with repentance. His own summary has become the line most quoted about the whole affair.

I believe we were guilty of the Galatian error: having begun in the Spirit, we quickly degenerated into the flesh.

— Derek Prince, on leaving the Shepherding movement (1983)

He was neither a cult leader nor a bystander to a minor disagreement; both descriptions distort it. He was a gifted teacher who helped build something that went wrong, saw it, named it in the plainest scriptural terms, and walked away first. He went on reflecting on the danger of manipulative spiritual authority for years afterward. That a leader of his stature would say we were wrong in public is itself part of the witness this book is here to record.

A houseful of daughters, and the end in Jerusalem

His long ministry was married to another. In the mid-1940s he married Lydia Christensen, a Danish missionary who ran a home for children in Jerusalem, and by joining her household he became father to a houseful of adopted daughters, girls of varied backgrounds she had already taken in. Lydia was considerably older than he was, and their marriage bound his life to the land he prayed for. She died in 1975. In 1978 he married Ruth Baker; Ruth died in Jerusalem in 1998.

Derek Prince died at his home in Jerusalem on 24 September 2003, aged eighty-eight, in his sleep. He had gone on teaching almost to the last. He was buried in the city he had carried in prayer for more than half a century.

He leaves an unusual example. Most of the praying men remembered in these pages came to Scripture in simplicity and never left it. Prince came to it as a critic, was overcome by it, and then spent his life persuading ordinary people that the book he had once weighed and doubted was strong enough to rest a life on — and to move the history of nations through their prayers. He got things wrong, and said so. But the two convictions he carried out of that barrack room he never let go of, and the second of them — that the Bible is a true, relevant, up-to-date book — he turned, for fifty years, into a summons to pray.

fields.name: Timothy Keller
fields.bio: Timothy Keller (1950–2023) was a Presbyterian pastor who founded Redeemer Presbyterian Church in secular Manhattan in 1989 and wrote widely read books including The Reason for God and Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God. A brush with thyroid cancer drove him to rebuild his prayer life, and facing pancreatic cancer at the end he wrote movingly of the nearness of God and the deepening of prayer.
fields.bio_html:
Timothy Keller spent his working life explaining Christianity to people who did not believe it — the doubters, the artists, the young professionals of secular Manhattan who had come to New York to get away from the churches of their childhood. He was patient with them, and famous for it. What is less remembered is that the man who taught a skeptical city about God spent decades feeling that he had under-taught the one thing that mattered most, and did not learn to pray deeply himself until a cancer diagnosis drove him to it in middle age. He wrote his best-known book on prayer at sixty-three, out of that late and costly schooling. And then, at the very end, the doctrines he had preached for half a century had to be tested in his own body — and he reported, without drama, that they held.

A nominal faith made real

He was born on 23 September 1950 in Allentown, Pennsylvania, and raised in the eastern part of that state. He was baptized Catholic — his mother was Italian-American — and the family later attended a Lutheran church, so that religion was always around him without ever quite becoming his own. By his own account he did not come to a serious, personally-held Christian faith until he was at university.

That happened at Bucknell, where he took his degree in 1972. As a student he was drawn into a living evangelical faith through InterVarsity Christian Fellowship on the campus — the ordinary machinery of a student ministry, a few friends and some books and a Bible studied seriously, doing its ordinary work on a young man who had grown up with the forms of religion but not its heart. It is worth pausing on how undramatic that is. No crisis, no vision — a college student moving, over a season, from nominal religion to something he would give the rest of his life to.

He went on to Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, taking his M.Div. in 1975; among his teachers there were Richard Lovelace and Roger Nicole. Later he earned a Doctor of Ministry from Westminster Theological Seminary in Philadelphia, in 1981, working on urban mission under Harvie Conn. His theology settled where it would stay: Reformed, confessional, Presbyterian, in the tradition of the two writers he cited most warmly all his life — C.S. Lewis, whose reasonableness he borrowed, and Jonathan Edwards, whose sense of the beauty of God he never stopped preaching.

In 1975 he married Kathy, born Kathy Kristy — Kristy is a maiden name, not a nickname. She is central, and not as background. She had trained at Gordon-Conwell too; she edited and sharpened his work, co-authored The Meaning of Marriage with him, and was a full partner in everything that followed, not least in the founding of Redeemer. They had three sons. Nearly every good thing his ministry produced was, in some real sense, a thing the two of them made together.

Hopewell, and then the hardest city

His first pastorate was not a glamorous one. From 1975 to 1984 — about nine years — he served West Hopewell Presbyterian Church in Hopewell, Virginia, a blue-collar, small-town congregation. This was his apprenticeship: the unrecorded labour of visiting, burying, marrying, and week-by-week preaching that makes a pastor before anyone has heard his name. He learned there to speak plainly to people who had no patience for jargon, a habit that would serve him strangely well in a very different place.

In 1989 he and Kathy did an unlikely thing. They moved to secular Manhattan to plant a new church — a Reformed, confessional congregation aimed at exactly the skeptical, professional, largely unchurched New Yorkers least likely to want one. Redeemer Presbyterian Church was, on paper, a bad idea. It grew instead into thousands, meeting across multiple services, and became one of the most studied models of thoughtful urban ministry in the English-speaking world. Keller preached as though skeptics were always in the room, because they were; he answered their objections respectfully and pointed past himself to Christ rather than scoring points.

The less we attempt to make this world into a heaven, the more we are able to enjoy it.

— Timothy Keller, “Growing My Faith in the Face of Death,” The Atlantic (2021)

Out of Redeemer came institutions larger than any one congregation. With D.A. Carson he co-founded The Gospel Coalition, a network for gospel-centered evangelicalism. He co-founded and chaired Redeemer City to City, a church-planting organization that helped start hundreds of churches in cities around the world. He wrote steadily — The Reason for God in 2008, which made him a bestseller; The Prodigal God the same year; Counterfeit Gods; Every Good Endeavor; some thirty books in all. In 2017 he stepped down from the senior pastorate to give his remaining strength to training and to writing.

The cancer that taught him to pray

For all of this, Keller was candid that his own prayer life had lagged behind his teaching. The turn came around 2002, when he was diagnosed with thyroid cancer and treated for it. He and Kathy have said plainly, on the record, that the brush with mortality drove them to rebuild their prayer life from the foundations — they began praying together every night, and reworked the devotional habits of decades. He would later admit he had under-taught prayer for years and had to be taught it himself.

After the thyroid diagnosis, Tim and Kathy Keller began praying together every night — not as a spiritual flourish but because, as they told it, a man who had preached for years suddenly found he did not know how to pray under the shadow of death, and could not afford to stay that way.

The book that grew partly out of that discipline was Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, published in 2014. Its argument is simple and hard to hold together: that prayer is at once awe — the adoration of God’s glory — and intimacy — the finding of his grace — and that to lose either is to lose prayer. He wanted to unite two streams the church usually sets against each other: the communion-centered tradition that savours God’s presence, and the kingdom-centered tradition that asks and labours and aligns itself with God’s will. Mature prayer, he insisted, holds both. And it is never free-floating technique or self-soothing; it is response, conversation and encounter with a God who has already spoken in Scripture, and he sent readers to the Psalms and to Augustine, Luther, Calvin, and Owen to learn how.

Prayer, then, is both awe and intimacy, struggle and reality.

— Timothy Keller, Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God (2014)

Facing his own death

In 2020 Keller was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, an advanced case, and was treated for roughly three years. He had, as it happened, just published a short book called On Death — a teacher of others on dying who was now handed his own.

What followed is the reason his name belongs among men of prayer. He did not fall silent, and he did not perform. He wrote and spoke about facing death, the nearness of God, and a felt reality of Christ that he said grew sweeter as his strength failed — that the things he had preached for fifty years stopped being doctrines held at arm’s length and became, in his phrase, real. The clearest record of it is an essay he published in The Atlantic in March 2021, “Growing My Faith in the Face of Death,” which he opened by setting his 1975 ordination beside his own diagnosis. In it he refused both denial and despair, and made the plain argument that had always been under his winsomeness:

If there is a God great enough to merit your anger over the suffering you witness or endure, then there is a God great enough to have reasons for allowing it.

— Timothy Keller, “Growing My Faith in the Face of Death,” The Atlantic (2021)

The prayer life the Kellers rebuilt in 2002, under the first cancer, was what carried them through the second. Keller’s own testimony in his last years was that the awe and intimacy he had spent a lifetime describing had become, at the end, experienced fact — that the deepened prayer of two decades earlier bore its fruit exactly when it was needed most.

He was discharged to hospice care on 18 May 2023, and died the next day, 19 May 2023, in Manhattan, aged seventy-two. No reliable last words survive, and this account will not manufacture any; the honest record is not a deathbed scene but the years of writing in which a dying man kept teaching the church how to hope.

What he leaves

Keller was, in his last decade, a contested figure as well as a beloved one. Admirers across the church prized his patience with doubters; some critics to his right thought that same gentleness inadequate to a harder cultural moment, and some to his left faulted him on social and political questions. It is fair to record that he was widely loved and also widely argued over, and fair to leave the arguments there — he would not have wanted a biography to adjudicate them for him.

He is also, it should be said, one of the most misquoted Christians of the internet age; a great many lines attributed to him were never his. One that genuinely was his to use, though not to coin, is a gospel summary he loved to repeat — that we are more sinful and flawed than we ever dared believe, yet more loved and accepted in Christ than we ever dared hope. The phrasing descends from Jack Miller and from his own teacher Richard Lovelace; Keller reworked and carried it, and made it his signature, but it was never original to him, and he would have been the first to say so.

What he leaves, in the end, is not chiefly the institutions or the bestsellers. It is the witness of a man who taught Christianity brilliantly for twenty years before a cancer made him learn, late and humbly, to pray — and who, when a second cancer came, found the practice ready and the promises true. That is the more encouraging story for an ordinary reader. Nobody is too accomplished, too fluent, or too far along to be taught prayer from the beginning. Keller was, and he counted it the best thing that ever happened to him.
