William Sunday, a bricklayer, enlisted in the Twenty-third Iowa Infantry in the summer of 1862, and four months later, on the 19th of November, his wife gave birth to a third son in a two-room log cabin near Ames, Iowa, and named the boy after the soldier who was away. Private Sunday died of disease in a camp at Patterson, Missouri, on the 22nd of December, a little more than a month after the child was born. The boy who would one day draw larger crowds than any American evangelist before him began his life as one of the war’s many small casualties: fatherless, poor, and very soon on his own.

A soldier’s orphan

His mother, Mary Jane, kept her three boys together as long as she could, with help from her father. But the wolf, as Sunday put it, scratched at the cabin door, and at last she told her sons she was sending two of them to the Soldiers’ Orphans’ Home. Woken at a hotel in Ames for a train in the small hours, he saw that his mother’s eyes were red. “All the time Ed and I slept,” he said, “mother had been praying.” She put an arm around each boy on the platform and sobbed as though her heart would break.

He spent about two years in the orphanages at Glenwood and Davenport. By fourteen he was shifting for himself — doing farm chores in Nevada, Iowa, attending the high school there without graduating, working as a school janitor. He liked to say he had crawled out of “the university of poverty and hard knocks.”

The fastest man in the National League

In Marshalltown, Iowa, where he ran with the fire brigade team and played ball for the town, he was noticed by Cap Anson, the captain of the Chicago White Stockings, the champions of the National League. In 1883, not yet twenty-one, Sunday went straight from the Iowa sandlots to Chicago. He never became much of a hitter, but he was reckoned the fastest runner in the league, and the bleachers loved his diving catches and head-first slides. He played five seasons in Chicago and then moved to Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

A curbstone recruit

One Sunday afternoon in Chicago — in 1886 or 1887; the sources differ — he and several teammates came out of a saloon and sat down on a curb. Across the street a band from the Pacific Garden Mission was playing horns and trombones and singing the gospel hymns he had heard his mother sing in the log cabin. The memories came flooding back, and he sobbed. A young man from the band invited them down to the mission. Sunday stood up and spoke to his friends.

I’m through. I am going to Jesus Christ. We’ve come to the parting of the ways.

— Billy Sunday, recalling the street corner in Chicago

Some of them laughed and some mocked. He went to the mission again and again, and there, after conversation and prayer with Mrs. Clark, the wife of the mission’s founder, he made his decision. “I groped my way out of darkness into the arms of Jesus Christ,” he said long afterwards, “and I fell on my knees and cried ‘God be merciful to me a sinner!’” He dreaded the ridicule waiting at the ballpark, but the first man to meet him inside the gate the next morning was the team’s great star, Mike “King” Kelly: “Bill, I’m proud of you! Religion is not my long suit, but I’ll help you all I can.” Anson and the rest followed with the same encouragement.

The change in him was plain to teammates and fans alike. He gave up swearing, gambling and the saloon, refused to play ball on the Lord’s Day, and joined the Jefferson Park Presbyterian Church, where he threw himself into the mid-week prayer meeting and the Christian Endeavor society. There he met Helen Amelia Thompson — Nell — the capable daughter of a prosperous Scottish Presbyterian in the dairy business. Her father did not want a professional ballplayer for a son-in-law; her mother took Billy’s side, and in the end her father relented. They were married in the Thompson home on the 5th of September, 1888, and spent their honeymoon travelling with the team. For the next forty-seven years he would make almost no decision without her.

The parting of the ways

Sunday’s Christianity kept pulling him away from the diamond. He was in demand at YMCA meetings, though he was then a poor, stumbling speaker. In the spring of 1891, bound by a three-year contract with Philadelphia, he put the question to God in the plainest terms he knew: if God wanted him out of baseball and in Christian work, let the club release him before the 25th of March. On the 17th a letter came from the club’s president granting the release. Then the Cincinnati club arrived with a contract for $3,500 and a first month’s pay in advance. His father-in-law told him he was a fool not to take it.

Sunday went home and went to bed, but he could not sleep. By his own account he “prayed that night until five o’clock,” until he “seemed to get the thing straight” — and then he said, “No, sir, I will not do it.” He had asked God for a sign, the release had come, and he would not go back on his word.

He went to work for the Chicago YMCA as an assistant secretary for about eighty-three dollars a month — money that was sometimes months late. For three years he visited the sick, prayed with the troubled, and carried invitations into saloons, learning at close range what drink could do to a family. In 1893 he became the assistant to J. Wilbur Chapman, one of the best-known evangelists of the day — his advance man, organizing prayer meetings and choirs, driving tent pegs, and listening night after night to a master preacher at work. Chapman taught him to build a sermon, and pressed on him the importance of prayer.

Then, over the holidays of 1895–96, a telegram came: Chapman was returning to the pastorate, and the work was over. Sunday had a wife, two children, no job, and no money. He could not go back to baseball.

“I laid it before the Lord,” he told the journalist William T. Ellis, “and in a short while there came a telegram from a little town named Garner, out in Iowa, asking me to come out and conduct some meetings.” He knew no one there. He had eight sermons, enough for ten days. He went in January 1896 — and from that day, he said, he never once had to seek an invitation to preach.

I have just gone on, as the Lord opened the way, trying to do his work. I had no plan for this sort of thing. It is all the Lord’s doings.

— Billy Sunday, to William T. Ellis

The sawdust trail

For twelve years he worked what he called the “kerosene circuit,” some seventy small towns, most of them in Iowa and Illinois, without electric light. When a snowstorm in Salida, Colorado, flattened his tent in 1906, he began to insist that towns build him plain wooden tabernacles, their floors strewn with sawdust to deaden the noise. In the Puget Sound country, among loggers who knew what it was to follow a sawdust trail home out of the forest, walking forward at the invitation became “hitting the sawdust trail.” From 1908 Nell travelled with him and ran the whole enterprise, leaving the younger children with a nanny; a staff grew around them, among them the song leader Homer Rodeheaver.

On the platform Sunday was unlike anything American religion had seen. He ran, stood on the pulpit, smashed chairs, and slid across the stage like a runner stealing home, in a torrent of slang. Many ministers were scandalized, and not without reason — he could be coarse and cruel. But beneath the performance lay something the crowds did not always see.

Before a hammer was lifted on a tabernacle, the churches of a city were divided into districts and blocks for cottage prayer meetings, held wherever possible in the homes of the unconverted. Conversions were often reported before the evangelist arrived.

Before the Pittsburgh campaign of 1913–14, in the weeks of December alone, 4,137 prayer meetings were held in private homes across the city, with a combined attendance of 68,360 people. With such a sea of prayer beneath him, Ellis concluded, any preacher could have had a revival.

Sunday’s own habit was the same. Ellis heard him pray in his room before going out to preach, in exactly the plain, conversational way he prayed on the platform.

I never preach a sermon until I’ve soaked it in prayer. Never.

— Billy Sunday, from his sermon “Teach Us to Pray”

Between 1915 and 1917 he preached in Philadelphia, Boston, Detroit, Buffalo and other great cities, and in the spring of 1917, as the United States entered the First World War, he held his largest campaign, in New York, from April to June. More than 98,000 people came forward, and he gave the entire offering there to war charities, as he gave his Chicago offering to the Pacific Garden Mission where he had been converted. Over his career something like a million people walked the sawdust trail. His most famous sermon was against strong drink, and he did as much as any man to arouse the nation for Prohibition; on the night it took effect in January 1920 he staged a mock funeral for “John Barleycorn” in Norfolk, Virginia.

Trials

The honest record has shadows. The campaigns made the Sundays wealthy, and critics questioned the offerings. His patriotism could curdle into harshness; in the 1920s he accepted gifts from members of the Ku Klux Klan and, hired by coal operators, spoke contemptuously of striking miners. After the war the crowds thinned, but he kept preaching wherever he was invited.

The deepest sorrow was at home. The children had been raised largely by others while their parents travelled, and the three sons struggled with drink and failed marriages; the Sundays paid money to keep scandals quiet. In 1930 Nora Lynn, the nanny who had become family, died. In 1932 their daughter Helen died after a long, wasting illness. In 1933 their eldest son, George, whom they had rescued from financial ruin, took his own life. Sunday had once prayed aloud before a tabernacle crowd, with a candour that made the critics wince, words that read very tenderly now.

Well, Jesus, I’m not up in heaven yet. I don’t want to go, not yet… I don’t want to leave Nell and the children. I like the little bungalow we have out at the lake.

— Billy Sunday, a tabernacle prayer

Early in 1935 he suffered a heart attack, and his doctor told him to stay out of the pulpit. He did not. About a week before he died he preached on the jailer’s question, “What must I do to be saved?” — the question that had found him on a Chicago curb half a century before. He died on the 6th of November, 1935, at the Chicago home of Nell’s brother, William Thompson, just short of his seventy-third birthday, and was buried in Forest Home Cemetery at Forest Park, Illinois.

He was a man of large faults and larger zeal. He was a soldier’s orphan who never forgot his mother praying through the night, and a ballplayer who asked God for a sign and kept his side of the bargain. The chair-smashing has dated. What remains is the simple gospel he heard from a mission band on a street corner and preached for forty years: that any sinner, however far gone, may still get up, turn his back on the old crowd, and go to Jesus Christ.

fields.name: Charles S. Price
fields.bio: Charles S. Price (1887–1947) was an English-born Pentecostal evangelist who, as a liberal Congregational pastor in Lodi, California, went to Aimee Semple McPherson’s 1921 San Jose meetings to expose them and was converted instead. His healing campaigns across North America drew huge crowds, notably in Victoria and Vancouver in 1923, and his book The Real Faith (1940) taught that true faith is not worked up but imparted by God.
fields.bio_html:
Charles S. Price spent the first dozen years of his ministry explaining God away. He was a gifted, popular, well-read preacher who could account for every religious feeling by the laws of psychology, and who never once, by his own confession, asked a sinner to come to Christ. Then he went to a tent meeting in San Jose to gather material for a sermon that would expose it, and the meeting exposed him instead. He spent the rest of his life as a healing evangelist, preaching to arenas of ten thousand — and, at the height of it, wrote a book confessing that his heart had been heavy for those who went home unhealed.

A Sheffield boy who drifted

Charles Sydney Price was born on 7 May 1887 in Sheffield, England. He never knew his mother. She died while he was still very small, and he was told that before she died she took him in her arms and dedicated him to the service of the Lord. His father married again, and Charles grew up loving his stepmother dearly. It was her insistence, and his parents’ sacrifice, that gave him a good schooling; he attended Wesley College, a Methodist school.

Somewhere in those years, he wrote, he began to drift. He came to think his parents’ faith old-fashioned and rather narrow. He worked for a time with a Sheffield law firm and was fascinated by the courtrooms, but he grew restless, and as a young man of about twenty he crossed to Canada, where the legal career he hoped for did not come and he ended up doing rough work instead. From Canada he felt drawn to Spokane, in Washington State.

A lamp post in Spokane

One night in early autumn he was leaning against a lamp post in Spokane, listening to a little band of mission workers sing in the street. When the meeting ended, an old woman stopped him and asked whether he knew that God wanted him. He was uncomfortable, excused himself rather rudely, and hurried off. Halfway across the Monroe Street Bridge he stopped. A feeling of dread and awe had come over him, a sense that God had spoken through her. He turned round and walked back to the mission. When the leader gave the altar call that night, he later wrote, he sprang to his feet, squared his shoulders and marched to the front, and gave himself to God.

He threw himself into the work of that Free Methodist mission, and before long he was ordained into the Methodist ministry. He married and began to raise a family. Then came the turning point he would regret all his life. News had reached Spokane of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Los Angeles, and Price, convicted, promised to meet with some workers to pray to be filled. On his way to that prayer meeting an older minister caught him by the arm and begged him not to wreck his future. Price spent the afternoon in the man’s study instead and went home with half a suitcase of books. He did not go to the prayer meeting.

The books did their work. He came to believe, he said, that he could explain every religious emotion from the standpoint of psychology. Pastorate followed pastorate, and his reputation climbed. He left the Methodists for the broader Congregational Church, spent a season in Alaska, and then took pulpits in Santa Rosa and Oakland, California. In the First World War he spoke from Oakland’s theatre stages as one of the “Four Minute Men,” work that earned him a letter from President Woodrow Wilson. At last he came to the First Congregational Church of Lodi, a fine church with generous people.

I never gave an altar call—never led a soul to Jesus—never preached the glory of the born-again experience. I was spiritually blind, leading my people into the ditch.

— Charles S. Price, The Story of My Life

The tent at San Jose

In 1921 Aimee Semple McPherson held a great tent campaign in San Jose, and members of the Lodi church began coming home from it saying they had been saved. Price laughed, and then grew bitter. He put an advertisement in the newspaper announcing that his next Sunday sermon would be titled “Divine Healing Bubble Explodes,” and drove to San Jose with pen and paper to take notes.

The first shock was the sponsor’s name on the banner: William Keeney Towner, pastor of the First Baptist Church in Oakland, a friend from Price’s Oakland years. The tent held about six thousand and was packed. Towner found him in the crowd, gripped his hand and told him that this was real and that it was what he needed. The only empty seat was in the section reserved for the crippled. The altar call undid him; he did not sleep that night. The next night the preaching, as he put it, punctured his theology until it looked like a sieve.

Back in his hotel room after that second night, Price threw himself on his knees and cried out to God. By his own account the heavens were black above him and no answer came, yet in sincerity of heart he promised God that he would change. The following evening he sat on the platform among the ministers praying for strength to do what he had resolved.

When the call for sinners came, he stood. A prominent minister beside him put a hand on his shoulder and whispered that she was calling for sinners, for people who needed to be saved. Price whispered back that he knew, and went down the steps. As he knelt, he wrote, the glory of God broke over his soul and an ocean of divine love rolled across his heart; he threw up both hands and shouted Hallelujah. Night after night afterwards he tarried in prayer at the Baptist church, and one night, praying for hours in a corner behind a piano until Towner came and urged him into the middle of the room, he was baptized in the Holy Spirit.

He went home to Lodi fully expecting to lose his pulpit. Instead the church was packed the next Sunday, and he told them plainly what they would hear from now on.

As long as I am pastor, you will hear one burning message from this pulpit—Jesus Christ and Him crucified.

— Charles S. Price, The Story of My Life

More than eighty people knelt at his first altar call. Prayer meetings multiplied, attendance reached a thousand, and a Lodi Gospel Team of close to a thousand members drove out in convoys to hold street meetings in nearby towns. When church authorities began to interfere, the revived congregation formed an independent church, Bethel Temple. On 17 August 1922, with a sad parting, Price left Lodi for the evangelistic field.

Arenas of ten thousand

His first campaign was in Ashland, Oregon, where the churches closed their own services to join him. When the first person he prayed for fell under the power of God, he admitted, he was afraid. Then came Albany, Roseburg and Eugene, and in April 1923 an invitation from Methodist ministers in Victoria, British Columbia. The meetings outgrew the Metropolitan Methodist Church and moved to an arena. Among those prayed for was Ruby Dimmick, a young woman crippled for years and the daughter of a Methodist minister; her healing was reported across Canada and the United States. In May he went on to Vancouver, where the Denman Arena held ten thousand, and its owner, Frank Patrick, reckoned that more than a quarter of a million people came in three weeks.

Honesty requires the rest of the story. The healings were contested from the start. Later in 1923 a committee of Vancouver ministers, doctors and others followed up some 350 people who had been prayed for, and reported that most showed no lasting change and that thirty-nine had died within months. Some who had endorsed him drew back, saying they had supported his preaching rather than his healing. Price’s supporters answered with testimonies of people still well years later, and he went on returning to Canada; converts from those campaigns helped fill Pentecostal churches in British Columbia and the prairies for a generation.

From 1926 he sent out a monthly magazine, Golden Grain, carrying his sermons and the testimonies of the healed. He held campaigns across Canada and the American Midwest, and in the late 1930s preached in Europe and the Middle East. The travelling was relentless, and it cost him. His marriage did not survive those years; he and his wife separated and later divorced. It is a sorrow his public story tends to pass over.

The faith that is given

The weariness of that life shows through in his own pages. One night in a tabernacle, with some five hundred sick people waiting to be anointed and no strength left to preach, he looked through a crack in the wall at the sufferers and felt like running away.

“Oh, Jesus,” he cried, dropping to his knees on the office floor and weeping, “I can’t. I have not the strength.” He wrote that a still, small voice answered in his heart, asking why he did not take the Lord’s strength instead. He walked out without his notes, and at midnight he was still laying hands on the sick. Going home, he was not too tired to kneel again and thank God for what He had done.

Out of such nights came his best-known book, The Real Faith, published in 1940. It opens with a confession. For years, he wrote, he had known that something was wrong. He had gone home from meetings with shouts of victory ringing in his ears, only to weep before the Lord for those who dragged their sick bodies home as needy as they came. He would not shrug off the gap between what was preached and what happened. His answer was that faith cannot be worked up by effort of will; it is not the same as believing a promise, but a gift that God Himself imparts to the heart.

We have made faith a condition of mind, when it is a divinely imparted grace of the heart.

— Charles S. Price, The Real Faith

The book is full of prayer rather than technique. He tells of a woman confined to an institution, whom he prayed for one morning with no visible answer, while her husband held him by the coat and begged him not to give up.

Price called his own church and others to a whole day of prayer for her. About four o’clock that afternoon, praying near the altar, he felt the Spirit of the Lord come upon him and rose to announce that the answer was on the way. He telephoned the husband. The next day, after a brief time of prayer and anointing, he wrote, she was delivered and went home to her husband and children.

Just as honestly, he recorded nights when nothing happened and he felt, in his word, empty. When two men once pressed him to settle a controversy, he admitted he did not know the answer.

Brethren, the important thing is not what you believe, but in whom you believe.

— Charles S. Price, The Real Faith

In 1945 he felt the Lord calling him to stay at home, and he gave his last years in Pasadena to writing, local preaching, rest and prayer. He died there on 8 March 1947, aged fifty-nine, and was buried at Forest Lawn in Glendale. Golden Grain went on being mailed out for years after his death, and The Real Faith is still reprinted today.

He was not a theologian, and he carried griefs and failures along with the triumphs. But the man who once explained every emotion by psychology ended his life insisting that faith was not something he could produce, and that every good thing he had seen had come from Jesus alone. That confession is still what his books make.

fields.name: John Foxe
fields.bio: John Foxe (c. 1516–1587) was an English Protestant historian and preacher, a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, who left the university for his convictions and went into exile on the Continent during the reign of Queen Mary. His Actes and Monuments (1563), known ever since as Foxe's Book of Martyrs, told the sufferings of Christian martyrs from the early church to the Marian burnings and became, after the Bible, one of the most widely read books in Protestant England.
fields.bio_html:
John Foxe was born at Boston, in Lincolnshire, about 1516, and was elected a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, which he resigned in 1545 over his Protestant convictions. When Mary came to the throne he fled to the Continent, and at Strasbourg and Basel he gathered the accounts of those who were dying for the Reformed faith in England.

Returning under Elizabeth, he was ordained by Bishop Grindal and published his Actes and Monuments in 1563 — the book the world calls Foxe's Book of Martyrs. He enlarged it through several editions, preached at St Paul's Cross, and pleaded for mercy even for those whose beliefs he opposed. He died in London in April 1587 and was buried at St Giles, Cripplegate.

fields.name: Arthur T. Pierson
fields.bio: Arthur Tappan Pierson (1837–1911) was an American Presbyterian pastor, Bible teacher and tireless advocate of world missions, who preached on both sides of the Atlantic and wrote more than fifty books. A friend of D. L. Moody, C. H. Spurgeon and George Müller, he filled Spurgeon's pulpit at the Metropolitan Tabernacle in London from 1891 to 1893 and was a consulting editor of the Scofield Reference Bible. His George Müller of Bristol (1899) became the authorized memoir of his friend's life of faith.
